That's why a key doesn't get "changed," it gets rotated: you create the new one, drop it into every place the old one was, and only then delete the old one.

terms.short: A tool you operate by typing commands into the terminal instead of clicking buttons.
terms.long: CLI stands for command line interface. Many tools in the course come in two flavors: Codex CLI and Codex on the web, Claude Code in the terminal and Claude in the browser. The terminal version can almost always open and change your files, and the browser one can't, so choosing between them isn't a matter of taste — it's a matter of how much access you're handing over. If you pick the CLI, also pick the specific folder you let it into.
terms.analogy: A remote with twenty buttons versus the two buttons on the TV itself. It does a lot more, but you need to know which one to press.
terms.confusion: With the terminal. The terminal is the window you type into; a CLI is a specific program you use from inside it, like npm, git, or claude. Plenty of different CLIs can live in that same window.

terms.short: Someone who could hire you and hasn't yet.
terms.long: In the course it shows up in two places. In the first-call sales script — twenty minutes, eight ordered questions to learn their problem, their timeline, their budget, and who actually decides. And in the n8n flow that classifies messages coming through the website: hot if they ask for pricing, a demo, or a meeting; warm if they ask specific questions with no urgency; cold if it's just curiosity; and separately, whatever's spam. What you need to decide is what to do with each temperature, because treating them all the same is exactly what lets the hot ones go cold.
terms.analogy: Someone walking into the shop to browse. They might leave without buying, but that's not the same as someone walking past without even glancing at the window.
terms.confusion: With the English word "lead," which means literally a clue or a thread to pull on. You'll see both in the course and they're the same thing: the tools almost always say "lead," and in your own head you can keep calling it a prospect.

terms.short: Downloading a full copy of a project that lives on GitHub onto your own computer.
terms.long: The command is git clone, and it brings down the files along with their entire history at once, not just the latest version. In this course you'll almost never need it: the path taught is going to github.com and downloading the zip, or telling Claude Code to do it for you. It comes up for real in the advanced projects, when you check that your project starts up cleanly in a blank folder, just like it would for a new teammate downloading it for the first time. If a tutorial starts by cloning from the terminal, look for the mouse-click version before wrestling with the black window.
terms.analogy: Photocopying an entire file, old paperwork included, instead of just taking the latest sheet.
terms.confusion: With cloning a voice in ElevenLabs, which also comes up in this course and has nothing to do with it. Talking about GitHub, cloning means pulling files onto your computer; talking about audio, it means copying how a person sounds. Same word, different world.

terms.short: The hosted version of a tool, run and billed by them instead of by you.
terms.long: It's not a separate concept from "the cloud": it's the same thing, tacked onto a product's name. In the course you see it mostly as "n8n cloud," which is n8n installed and maintained by them for a monthly fee, versus self-hosting it for free and handling maintenance yourself. When a menu offers you "Cloud" and "Self-hosted," it's really asking who pays for the machine and who fixes it when it breaks at eleven at night. If you're starting out, pick Cloud without a second thought — setting up your own server before you have a working flow is the classic trap.
terms.analogy: The difference between joining the neighborhood gym and buying weights for your living room. Same exercise, different bill and different responsibility.
terms.confusion: With Cloudflare or any brand with "cloud" in the name. "Cloud" on its own isn't a company — it's a label meaning "this version runs on their computers, not yours."

terms.short: A company that sits in front of your website to speed it up and protect it, and also sells domains.
terms.long: In the course you see it in two different places: in Claude's connector catalog, alongside Notion, Figma, or Sentry, and underneath everything related to domains, since it's one of the most popular places to buy a domain name and manage its DNS records. What it does for your site is filter traffic before it reaches your server and cache copies of your pages to serve them faster. Decision: if you buy your domain there, that's where you'll come back to when connecting your published site, and those changes take anywhere from minutes to hours to show up everywhere.
terms.analogy: The building's doorman. Filters who comes in, keeps copies of the most-requested packages, and if things get chaotic, nobody reaches your door.
terms.confusion: With hosting. Hosting is the computer your site lives on; Cloudflare sits in front of it. That's why a site can be perfectly up and running and still not be visible from outside — the problem's at the door, not in the house.

terms.short: The percentage of your code that automated tests actually run at least once.
terms.long: It shows up after running tests, as a table with a number: 100%, 72%. What it's telling you is which parts nobody's ever looked at, and that's exactly where bugs hide. In the course's assistant project you hit 100% on the logic file and then set a required minimum, so if someone adds a function without testing it, GitHub flags it red and everyone sees. What coverage doesn't tell you is whether those tests actually check anything useful.
terms.analogy: The paperwork from a vehicle inspection. It tells you what got checked, not whether the car is any good.
terms.confusion: With quality. It's the classic mistake, and it shows up in one of the course's quizzes: if your tests don't catch anything, multiplying them just multiplies the green on the screen. Coverage measures how much ground got covered, not how much was actually demanded.

terms.short: Having someone else, or the AI, read your changes before they go into the good version.
terms.long: On GitHub it happens inside a pull request: the screen highlights additions in green and removals in red, and you approve or request changes. Working solo you won't do team reviews, but you will do the version that helps you: take that red-and-green screen, paste it to the AI, and ask what could break. It's the last cheap moment to catch a mistake, because after this it's published and the client sees it.
terms.analogy: Having someone reread your email before you hit send. Costs a minute, saves you the awkward reply.
terms.confusion: With asking the AI to write the code. Writing and reviewing are two different passes, and combining them in the same message rarely works: whoever just wrote something tends to think it's fine — and so does the AI.

terms.short: OpenAI's tool that reads your project folder, edits files, and asks permission before touching anything.
terms.long: It's OpenAI's answer to Claude Code, and in the course it always shows up in that trio: Claude Code, Codex, or Cursor — pick one. In the lesson on reviewing what the AI writes, it comes up as an example of a tool that actually executes things for real, so it can hand you the real output of what ran. That gives you a lever: when it says "executed," demand the actual output and check it. The decision isn't which one is best — it's not trying all three at once and learning none of them properly.
terms.analogy: Switching drill brands. The holes come out the same, the button's in a different spot, and it takes you an afternoon to get used to it.
terms.confusion: With GitHub Copilot. Copilot suggests the rest of the line while you type; Codex takes the whole job and comes back with files already changed. One works alongside you, the other works on its own.

terms.short: The way a file stores letters. If it doesn't match what the program expects, you get garbled symbols.
terms.long: The right one is called UTF-8, and it's the one to use always. In the course you see it written inside code as encoding="utf-8", and on Windows you also have to tell the console explicitly with a line before running anything, or "how much did it cost" comes out as hieroglyphics. It's not a bug in the program or the AI — Windows still defaults to an old encoding for files.
terms.analogy: Two people reading the same page in different alphabets. All the letters are there; each one sees something different.
terms.confusion: With encryption. Encoding stores letters in a specific format that anyone can decode; encryption hides them so only whoever has the key can read them. In English the words sound even more alike, which is exactly why people mix them up.

terms.short: Software whose guts are published: anyone can read them, copy them, and change them, usually without paying for the software itself.
terms.long: Almost all the plumbing tools in the course are open source: n8n, Node, Ollama, the Python libraries that show up in the projects. Being open gives you two very concrete advantages: you don't depend on a company deciding to shut down, and thousands of people have already hit your exact bug and written about it online. The financial decision it forces on you isn't the obvious one: the program is free, but what you call from inside it almost never is.
terms.analogy: A recipe published in a book. The recipe is free; the ingredients you still pay for at the supermarket.
terms.confusion: With completely free. n8n is open source and the model it calls still bills per run; a connector can be free while the service on the other end charges by usage. When someone tells you "this is free, it's open source," the right question is: free the software — and what it consumes?

terms.short: The tool's waiting line: your video doesn't come out instantly, it gets queued.
terms.long: On Higgsfield and other video tools, hitting generate puts you in a queue, and at peak times it takes a while. On a free plan you go behind paying users. The patience-meets-budget decision it forces: the costly mistake is hitting generate again thinking it didn't register, because now two are queued and you pay for two. Check your history before repeating.
terms.analogy: A deli counter ticket number. Not being served yet doesn't mean you were forgotten, and grabbing another number doesn't move you up — it puts you in line twice.
terms.confusion: With something having crashed. If you're in the queue, your job is alive and will show up in your history. And if you're producing daily, factor the queue into your delivery planning — it's not a minor detail.

terms.short: A set of things stored together under one name, all sharing the same shape.
terms.long: The word shows up two ways in the course. The everyday one: your prompt collection, your case collection with the correct answer written in by hand, your reusable script collection. And the technical one: in document and vector databases, "collection" is what SQL would call a table. Either way, the same rule applies: it's only a collection if its pieces share a format — if each one is shaped differently, you can't search or compare them.
terms.analogy: A tidy crate of records. It's a collection because every one fits the same slot and sits the same way; drop magazines in there and it's just a junk drawer.
terms.confusion: With a folder. A folder just stores whatever you throw in; a collection also demands everything inside share the same structure, which is exactly what makes it useful six months from now.

terms.short: Each field a table stores, with its name and type, the same across every row.
terms.long: Name them in lowercase, no accents, no spaces: date, email, amount, status. That name is what your automations use to find the data, and it's where the course's most-repeated rule comes from: on a sheet or table that's already automated, nothing gets renamed or reordered. Insert a column in the middle and no error goes off — the amount just quietly starts getting written where the email used to go.
terms.analogy: The printed boxes on a paper form. Shuffle their order halfway through the stack and whoever's filling them in keeps going as if nothing changed.
terms.confusion: With a row. A column is the type of data ("email"); a row is one specific case ("marta@example.com"). Columns almost never change; rows grow every day.

terms.short: An instruction you type into the terminal and run by hitting Enter.
terms.long: Things like node -v, which asks for the version, or npm install, which downloads a project's pieces. In this course you're not meant to memorize any of them: you paste them when the AI or a guide hands them to you, and that's fine — that's not learning the terminal, that's pasting a sentence. The two habits that prevent nearly every disaster are checking which folder you're in before hitting Enter, and never pasting a command you don't understand, no matter how convincing whoever gave it to you sounds. A deletion command doesn't ask twice.
terms.analogy: Ordering at a counter with no menu posted. Say clearly what you want and you get it; get one word wrong and there's nobody there to correct you.
terms.confusion: With a prompt. You talk to a prompt and it interprets what you mean; a command runs literally, letter by letter, and one extra space breaks it or turns it into something else entirely.

terms.short: A save point in the project, with a sentence explaining what changed.
terms.long: It's not saving a file: it's freezing the state of the entire project at a specific moment, named and dated, so you can come back to it. You make one before any big change and after anything that works. The message matters more than it seems: it's the only thing that'll orient you six months from now.
terms.analogy: The family photo before the renovation. If you don't like the result, at least you know how things looked before.
terms.confusion: With a backup. A commit lives inside the project itself; lose the folder and you lose the commits with it. That's what pushing to a remote server is for.

terms.short: Running the same cases through two versions of a task and counting which one gets more right.
terms.long: It's the only way to stop arguing from gut feeling about which prompt is better. In the "give examples" lesson you do this: prepare five real cases of your own, always the same ones, and run them through three versions of the task in three fresh chats. Note how many of the five come out right for each version, and keep the shortest version that matches the longest one's results. The rule: clean chats and the same cases every time, because changing two things at once means you're not comparing anything.
terms.analogy: Testing two routes to work. It only counts if you leave at the same time both days; leave at seven one day and nine the next and you've measured traffic, not the route.
terms.confusion: With asking the AI which of its two answers is better. It'll answer, confidently, but it's just rereading its own text and hasn't verified anything. You're the one who counts what's actually correct.

terms.short: A pre-built, named piece of screen you reuse in several places without rewriting it.
terms.long: A button, a product card, the site header: you build it once and drop it wherever needed. Change it in one place and it changes on every screen at once. When you copy code from v0, you're taking a component, not the whole app — which is exactly why the first thing to ask is which file in your project it goes into and how another screen uses it. Skip that question and you've got a gorgeous button plugged into nothing.
terms.analogy: Ikea furniture. Assemble the shelf once, then put the same one in three rooms without reading the instructions again.
terms.confusion: With the whole screen. A component is one piece; the screen is the whole assembly. v0 and Lovable hand out very flashy pieces, and people mistake that for a finished app — show it for what it is, or you'll commit to an impossible deadline.

terms.short: An "if this happens, do that; otherwise, do the other thing" inside a program or a flow.
terms.long: It's the piece that lets a flow make decisions instead of always repeating the same thing. In n8n it has its own node, the IF node, where you fill three slots: what data you're checking, which operator you pick from the dropdown, and what you're comparing it against. That's where you build the course's validation gate: if the model's confidence drops below 0.7, that case goes to human review; otherwise it continues on its own. The real decision is what happens down the "otherwise" branch: leave it empty and those cases vanish silently, with nobody the wiser.
terms.analogy: The traffic light at a warehouse gate. Green enters, red waits, and nobody has to stand there deciding truck by truck.
terms.confusion: With a filter. A filter discards what doesn't qualify and that's the end of it; a conditional sends each case down a different path, and both paths keep existing. Validating means separating, not throwing away — rejected cases still need somewhere they can be counted.

terms.short: A pre-built piece that plugs a tool into a service, with nothing for you to program.
terms.long: In n8n they're the nodes that already handle Gmail, Slack, or Google Sheets; in Claude and ChatGPT it's the "Connect" button that hooks up your Drive or your calendar. What almost nobody checks before clicking: a connector never brings just one loose capability — it brings a whole bundle of permissions. The course has the calendar case: it asks for "view, edit, share, and delete," and it's either the whole bundle or nothing. Turn on only what you'll actually use, because with four connectors live at once the AI starts confusing similar tools.
terms.analogy: A travel plug adapter: it comes pre-made, you just plug it in. But check what voltage it lets through before plugging in a hair dryer.
terms.confusion: With integration. The connector is the specific piece plugging in a service; integration is the two tools actually working together. You can have a connector plugged in and no integration doing anything at all.

terms.short: GitHub warning you that two changes touched the same piece of a file and it doesn't know which one wins.
terms.long: It shows up when merging: the same paragraph got edited two different places, and the tool refuses to choose for you. It's not a breakdown and you haven't broken anything — it's a question waiting for an answer. At your level, the quick way out is closing that pull request without merging, deleting your copy, and redoing the change directly on top of the good version. If you insist on resolving it by hand without knowing how to read code, odds are good you leave the file worse than it started.
terms.analogy: Two people have each hand-corrected the same sentence in a contract, differently. Nobody signs until someone decides which sentence stays.
terms.confusion: With a program error. An error means something failed; a conflict means there are two valid options and it's waiting on you to pick one. That's why it can't be fixed by retrying or restarting — it's fixed by deciding.

terms.short: A person saying yes knowing exactly what to, and able to withdraw it later whenever they want.
terms.long: It has to be clear, specific, informed, and revocable. An "I agree" checkbox above text that explains nothing doesn't inform anyone, so it doesn't count as consent no matter how much it looks like one. In the course you run into this on the web form that sends text to a model: the user has to be able to know, before typing, that it's going out to a third party. And watch the most common mix-up, because consent isn't always the applicable basis — often what actually protects you is the contract you already have signed with that client.
terms.analogy: Signing off on a construction quote. If the paper doesn't say what's being done or how much it costs, your signature doesn't mean you agreed to anything.
terms.confusion: With the checkbox itself. The checkbox is the gesture, not the consent. What makes it valid is what the person could actually know before checking it, and a general site policy written three years ago doesn't cover what your brand-new form does.

terms.short: The browser's hidden panel where the red errors on your webpage show up.
terms.long: Open it with F12 on Windows, Cmd + Alt + J on a Mac, or right-click anywhere on the page and choose "Inspect." Red messages are real errors; yellow ones are warnings you can almost always ignore. When your page does nothing on a button click, the error doesn't show up on the page — it shows up here, and copying it whole and pasting it to the AI is the difference between fixing it in two minutes or spending two days. One thing that trips up everyone the first time: the console only records what happens while it's open, so open it before reproducing the bug.
terms.analogy: A flight recorder that only starts recording from the moment you switch it on.
terms.confusion: With the terminal. The terminal belongs to your computer and runs commands; the console lives inside the browser and only reports what happens to that one page. And confusingly, "console" also refers to Google's or OpenAI's billing dashboard, which is a completely different thing.

terms.short: A hidden screen inside the browser where your page logs everything happening to it, errors included.
terms.long: Open it with F12 on Windows, Cmd + Alt + J on a Mac, or right-click anywhere on the page and choose "Inspect." The screen splits and a row of tabs appears; of all of them, you only need "Console." Red lines are real failures, yellow lines are warnings you can safely ignore. You don't need to understand what it says, and that's the whole point: your job is to select it with the mouse, copy it in full, and paste it to the AI — including the lines underneath starting with "at" that look like garbage.
terms.analogy: A building's incident log. Nobody reads it daily, but when the elevator stops, it's written down there, exactly what time and which floor.
terms.confusion: With the terminal. The terminal is the window on your computer where you start the project and it reports what's happening server-side; the console lives inside the browser and reports what's happening to the page on the viewer's screen. When something breaks, check both, and when asking for help, say which one you're pasting.

terms.short: A value you name once, and it never changes while the program is running.
terms.long: It's for whatever's set in stone: the tax rate you apply, the email that alerts land in, your webhook's address. It shows up clearly in the course's Apps Script code, where the webhook address sits in a constant at the top of the file, with a comment right next to it spelling out that it's a secret and never gets shared. Putting it at the top has a practical reason: when it changes, that's the one and only place you need to touch, instead of hunting for it through the whole file.
terms.analogy: The phone number taped to the fridge door. It's always in the same spot, and nobody has to go looking for it.
terms.confusion: With a variable. If the value changes while the program runs, it's a variable; if you decide it once and it stays, it's a constant. Being constant doesn't make it safe: a key placed there is still sitting inside the file, visible to anyone who opens it.

terms.short: The specific question you send a database so it hands you back some rows.
terms.long: A query says three things: from which table, with which filter, and how many rows you want. This is where the course's most important data decision sits: the permissions filter belongs inside the query, not afterward in your own program. Ask for the top five results and then strip out what that person isn't allowed to see, and you end up with one — plus you've already pulled confidential text into your program's memory that you shouldn't have read at all.
terms.analogy: Asking at the hardware store for "size-4 steel screws, ten of them." Ask instead "bring me all the screws" and sort them yourself afterward, and you've hauled off the whole box.
terms.confusion: With the database. A query is the question, written each time; the database is what's stored, and doesn't move. Two different queries against the same data can return different numbers, and both can be correct.

terms.short: A sealed box holding your program and everything it needs, so it runs the same on any computer.
terms.long: It's what Docker spins up when you start a project: inside goes the exact version of Python or Node, the packages, and your code, while your own computer stays outside, just providing the engine. In Docker Desktop you see them under the "Containers" tab: what's running, on which port, and how much memory it's using. Whatever gets written inside disappears when it's switched off, so a database needs a named volume — a separate storage location that survives the shutdown. And if a container shows up gray with "Exited (1)," the cause isn't in that message — it's in its logs.
terms.analogy: A shipping container. Doesn't matter if it's a truck, a train, or a ship — inside, everything sits arranged exactly the same way.
terms.confusion: With the image. The image is the frozen recipe; the container is the dish, served and running. From one single image you can spin up twenty containers at once.

terms.short: Everything a model has in front of it at the moment it responds.
terms.long: It includes your instructions, the current message, everything said before, and any document you've pasted in. It's a space with an edge: once it fills up, the oldest material stops being available, which is why a very long conversation starts contradicting itself. The fix isn't pushing it harder — it's opening a fresh conversation and pasting in only what actually matters.
terms.analogy: A work desk. It fits what it fits, and whatever falls to the floor stops existing for whoever's working.
terms.confusion: With memory. A model doesn't remember across conversations unless someone puts that information back in front of it.

terms.short: Models that can hold hundreds of pages in front of them at once, not just a handful of messages.
terms.long: Today's big apps handle windows of 200,000 to a million tokens — somewhere between a hefty novel and seven of them. It might seem like that means you never have to be careful anymore, and it's actually the opposite: quality drops off well before it fills up. It reads the beginning and the end closely; the middle gets skimmed, and that's usually exactly where the decisions you made two hours ago are sitting. Use that space for pasting in one whole document, not for dragging along four hundred messages of conversation.
terms.analogy: A massive table. Sure, everything fits — but finding the one sheet you need among eighty becomes a whole new problem.
terms.confusion: With memory. A large window doesn't make it remember yesterday — close the chat and it empties out just the same. And it's not free either: everything you're carrying gets resent every turn, and you pay for it, in money or in quota, each time.

terms.short: A character, product, location, or style continuing to look the same across several images or shots.
terms.long: It's one of the hardest things to nail in AI image and video work. A single piece can look gorgeous on its own and still fail as a series because the face, the product's color, the lighting, the clothing, or the logo size shifts between shots. Improving it means working with a reference image, a fixed style recipe, a seed when the tool allows one, and reviewing all the pieces side by side, not one at a time.
terms.analogy: A series of catalog photos: if every t-shirt looks like it's from a different store, the catalog falls apart even if each photo is pretty on its own.
terms.confusion: With style. Style is the overall look; continuity is keeping an identity consistent across different outputs.

terms.short: The secret word that proves it's you when logging into an account from a screen.
terms.long: In the course, a password protects exactly what an AI can't click on your behalf: the Google permissions screen, the button that deletes an old key, your provider's dashboard. A person types it with their own finger; a program can't. That's why, whenever a lesson tells you "this one's on you," there's almost always a password behind it. The decision is where yours lives: in a password manager, never in a notebook, an email to yourself, or a document shared with the team.
terms.analogy: Your house key. You use it, you carry it, and if you lose it, you change the lock that same day.
terms.confusion: With an API key. A person types a password, usually paired with a code sent to their phone; a key gets used by a program alone, a thousand times a minute, with no second question and no warning to anyone.

terms.short: Small bits of information a website leaves in your browser to recognize you next time.
terms.long: Some are essential, like remembering you're logged in; others are for tracking and advertising, and those need the person's permission. That's why the banner pops up on every site you open, and why, the day you publish your own, you'll have to add one too. In the course it comes up on the list of screens people always forget to design and in the pre-publish review. The rule: a banner with only an "accept" button isn't enough — rejecting has to be just as easy, and advertising cookies don't load until the person says yes.
terms.analogy: The stamp put on your hand walking into a club. It lets them recognize you coming back in, and some places use it to track exactly how many spots you visited that night.
terms.confusion: With the banner that announces them. The cookie is the stored data; the banner is just the way permission gets asked. The classic mistake is a pretty banner that loads advertising cookies anyway before anyone's clicked anything — at that point the banner isn't doing anything at all.

terms.short: A copy of your work stored elsewhere, that you've actually tested opening and know it works.
terms.long: In the course it comes up three times, always the same way. First you duplicate the project folder by hand; then GitHub does it for you, and keeps every version, not just the latest; and in n8n you also need the key that keeps your other account connections encrypted, because restoring without it leaves them listed but broken. Proof a backup works is having opened it: a folder dated today that you've never checked isn't a backup, it's a folder with a nice name. And know exactly what it costs to use it, because that's what keeps you from relying on it alone: restoring means the service has to be stopped.
terms.analogy: The spare tire. It takes up trunk space all year, and the day you get a flat is when you find out whether anyone ever checked it had air in it.
terms.confusion: With the change history some chats keep. That history lives inside the conversation: open a new chat or delete the old one, and it's gone with it. A file saved on your computer isn't.

terms.short: Moving text as-is from one place to another with Ctrl+C and Ctrl+V, without retyping it.
terms.long: It's the gesture you'll repeat most in the whole course, in both directions: pasting the ready-made prompts we give you into the chat, and pasting what it hands back "ready to copy and paste" into a file, the terminal, or an n8n box. The problem isn't the gesture, it's pasting without reading: going in, that's how a key or a client's phone number ends up inside a chat. Going out, the phrase "here's the complete file" can quietly overwrite forty lines of your own that you won't miss until something stops working. Rule: read what you paste, and duplicate the folder before pasting over anything that was already working.
terms.analogy: A photocopier. It doesn't read what you put on it: if the original has your ID number in the corner, the copy carries it too, and it's now outside your own folder.
terms.confusion: With cut and paste (Ctrl+X), which removes the original instead of duplicating it; hit the wrong shortcut on unsaved text and it's gone. The costlier mistake, though, is different: pasting a big block over your own file without having copied the folder first.

terms.short: The name Microsoft gives to almost all of its AI assistants, so on its own it doesn't tell you which one.
terms.long: Copilot means exactly that, and Microsoft uses it for the one in Windows, the one in Word and Excel, the one in the Edge browser, and the coding one, called GitHub Copilot. In the course, when the lesson on choosing a model puts it alongside ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini, it means the coding one inside the editor. When someone tells you "use Copilot," your first question has to be which one — the answer changes the price, the account you need, and even the window you type into.
terms.analogy: Like the word "insurance" at an insurer: car, home, and life insurance are all called that and don't cover the same things.
terms.confusion: With GitHub Copilot, which is just one of them — the code-completion one. If what you're being shown lives inside Word or the Windows taskbar, it's not the one this course is about.

terms.short: A helper that keeps suggesting while you work, while you're the one who still decides and signs off.
terms.long: It's how the course wants you to use AI most of the time: it proposes the text, the code, or three versions of your idea, and you accept, correct, or throw it out. GitHub Copilot is the literal example, with its gray suggestion and its Tab key, but a chat you ask for three drafts does exactly the same job. The trap is momentum: accepting on reflex without reading turns a copilot into the pilot without anyone deciding that on purpose. If you're going to say yes to everything without looking, the tool isn't the problem.
terms.analogy: A rally co-driver. Calls out the turns, warns of danger, and never once touches the wheel for the whole race.
terms.confusion: With an agent. A copilot proposes and waits until you say yes at every step; an agent decides and executes on its own, only checking in wherever you've placed a stop point.

terms.short: The [ and ] symbols. In the course they mark the blanks you need to fill in before sending a prompt.
terms.long: Every template in the course writes its blanks in capital letters between brackets: [PRODUCT NAME], [PRICE IN EUROS], [THREE TECHNICAL SPECS FROM THE LABEL]. The capitals aren't decoration — pasted into the AI's box, they jump out at a glance so you can see exactly what's missing. And if you forget to fill one in, the AI usually asks about it instead of making something up, because a bracket full of capital letters doesn't look like real data. The rule it forces on you: give every blank a name that explains itself, [PRODUCT NAME] and never [X].
terms.analogy: The shaded boxes on a tax form. They're there so you can't turn the page without noticing something was missing.
terms.confusion: With brackets inside a JSON blob or a piece of code, where they're part of the format and shouldn't be touched. The course's brackets are a marker for you: the moment you fill in the blank, the brackets get deleted too.

terms.short: What it costs you every single time the flow fires once.
terms.long: It's the number that lets you sleep easy, or the one that sinks the project, and in the course it's almost always the former: classifying 420 emails a month with a small model runs about €0.06 a month in model cost. You calculate it by adding what the model charges for input and output, plus whatever the platform charges per run. The decision is checking what happens when you triple the volume: if the number's still trivial at that scale, the project holds up; if it spikes, you need a different approach before selling anything.
terms.analogy: What one load of laundry costs in water and electricity. Barely noticeable alone; the real number comes from multiplying by the year's four hundred loads.
terms.confusion: With a monthly subscription. You pay the subscription whether anything runs or not; cost per run only shows up when something actually fires. That's why a program stuck in a loop overnight can multiply it by a thousand, and why the real safeguard isn't watching it — it's not having available credit to burn.

terms.short: What you pay for every chunk of text that goes into and comes out of the model.
terms.long: What you send and what you receive get billed separately, and what you receive is usually a fair bit pricier. That has a practical consequence: a long prompt repeated a thousand times costs more than a short one, and asking for brief answers genuinely saves money. Before turning on anything that runs unattended, set a spending cap in the provider's dashboard.
terms.analogy: A taxi that charges by the meter, and the return trip runs triple fare.
terms.confusion: With a chat subscription. A monthly subscription and API credit are two separate things, billed separately.

terms.short: The computer's processor, the one running everything else. It can run an AI model, just very slowly.
terms.long: It's your machine's general-purpose brain: it opens the browser, runs your spreadsheet, and if it has to, it also runs a local model — just badly. On an office laptop with no graphics card, an 8B model will write at about five words a second, slower than you can read, with the fan roaring. That's where people decide Ollama is garbage, when what actually happened is they picked a model too big for their machine. The rule: no graphics card, drop down a model size before giving up.
terms.analogy: A kitchen knife versus an electric chopper. You can still dice the onion with the knife — it just takes twenty times longer and you end up in tears.
terms.confusion: With RAM. They're two separate limits and they show up differently: memory decides whether the model fits at all or just won't start; the CPU decides how fast it writes once it's loaded. If you're getting an out-of-memory error, swapping processors fixes nothing.

terms.short: The data a tool uses to log into another one on your behalf.
terms.long: In n8n, Zapier, or Make, it's saved once and reused at every step. When something suddenly stops working without anyone having touched it, an expired credential is the first suspect. And while it was down, cases didn't sit there waiting — they got lost.
terms.analogy: The set of keys you leave with the doorman. Keeps opening the door until you change the lock.
terms.confusion: With an API key. The key is a piece of data; the credential is that data already saved and configured inside a tool.

terms.short: The saved data n8n uses to log into a service on your behalf.
terms.long: You create it once, inside n8n, and then reuse it in every node that talks to that service — you never paste the key again. It comes up as soon as you connect Gmail or Google Sheets, and it's the first thing to check when a flow that was working starts throwing a 401 error — meaning "I don't know you" — with nobody having touched anything. Watch for this, it's the part that actually stings: while the credential was expired, cases didn't wait at the door — they were lost.
terms.analogy: The set of keys you leave with the doorman. You don't come down to open the door every time; he opens it on your behalf until you change the lock.
terms.confusion: With an API key. A key is the raw piece of data a service hands you; a credential is that same data already saved and verified inside n8n, with its own name and green checkmark.

terms.short: The unit that many image, video, or audio tools spend every time they generate something.
terms.long: They don't always map onto one image or one video: a longer generation, a higher resolution, or a pricier model can consume more credits than a quick test. The practical rule is checking the counter before and after a test generation, noting it down with the date, and multiplying by your monthly volume. In video, spending credits without a storyboard or a reference image usually means throwing attempts at the wall until something works out by luck.
terms.analogy: Tokens at an arcade machine: every attempt spends one, whether it goes well or not.
terms.confusion: With a monthly subscription. You can be paying for the plan and still run out of usable credits to actually produce anything.

terms.short: A sentence like "if I do this, I see that," answerable only with a yes or a no.
terms.long: It's what decides whether a job is actually done, and you write it before you get an answer, not once it's already let you down. In the "verifiable task" lesson you draft between three and six, and the proof one is good is that you can check it just by looking at the screen: "I press the button and it opens WhatsApp with the message already written" counts; "works correctly" doesn't. Watch for this: the AI will tell you it meets all six with total confidence, because it's rereading its own text, not testing it. Checking them is your job, with your own hands.
terms.analogy: Inspecting a renovation. You don't ask "does it look good?" — you turn on the tap, check that water comes out, and confirm nothing drips underneath.
terms.confusion: With the goal. The goal is "sell more"; the criterion is "my exact three prices show up and no data I didn't provide." You can't check the goal in two minutes, and you can check the criterion — that's the whole difference.

terms.short: The sentence that says when a job is finished, written so you can look at it and answer yes or no.
terms.long: It's the sixth piece of a well-formed task and the one most people skip: it doesn't describe what you want, it describes how you'll know it's already there. It always takes the same shape, "if I do X, I see Y," with a specific value inside and a result you can check with your own eyes in under a minute. You'll run into it twice in the course: asking for a website or a form, and handing a task to an agent, where it's also the only thing that makes it stop instead of spinning and spending. The decision it forces on you is deliberately uncomfortable: you have to decide what counts as done before anything gets built, because if you write it afterward you'll write it looking at what's already in front of you and approve it.
terms.analogy: When you drop off your car at the shop, the work order doesn't say "make it run well." It says "replace front brake pads, check right-axle noise." That's why you can pick it up without arguing with anyone.
terms.confusion: With acceptance criteria — they're similar enough it barely matters, but the nuance is useful: definition of done tells the machine when to stop, acceptance criteria tells you whether to accept it. The real mistake isn't mixing them up, it's writing "works well" or "looks professional," which can't be checked with a yes or no.

terms.short: The program where a company stores its customers and everything it's ever discussed with them.
terms.long: CRM stands for Customer Relationship Management. In the course, the CRM is HubSpot, and it's the final destination of the leads flow: every contact ends up there with their temperature, their interest, and their summary. It's the place where a duplicate costs the most, because the same client logged three times means three salespeople calling them the same day. And realize this before connecting anything: writing to a client's CRM means touching their real data, not a test file.
terms.analogy: The old-school salesperson's notebook, but shared: if he writes something down, you see it that same afternoon.
terms.confusion: With a contact spreadsheet. A spreadsheet stores data; a CRM also stores the history and where each deal stands. A spreadsheet is fine to start; the trouble starts when three people touch it at once.

terms.short: The short way of writing a recurring schedule: "every Monday at 8:00."
terms.long: In n8n's scheduled trigger you usually fill in dropdowns (every how many days, at what time, what minute) and never see a cron expression anywhere. It shows up when you want something the dropdowns don't cover, like "Monday through Friday every two hours": then you switch to Cron mode and write five numbers separated by spaces — minute, hour, day of month, month, and day of week. Before trusting it, open the three dots top right, Settings, and check the timezone: if it says America/New_York, your 8:00am summary will land at two in the afternoon.
terms.analogy: A washing machine's timer dial. You don't explain the wash cycle to it, you just set the time you want it to start.
terms.confusion: With a countdown timer. Cron doesn't say "in two hours," it says "when the clock hits this." If what you actually want is the flow to wait a while partway through, that's a different box entirely.

terms.short: The rules that decide how a webpage looks: colors, sizes, margins, and where everything sits.
terms.long: CSS stands for Cascading Style Sheets. It can live inside the HTML file itself or in a separate file ending in .css. In the course you'll almost always see it embedded right inside index.html, so the page opens with a double-click and nothing needs installing. When you pull your brand colors from Figma and hand them to the AI, this is where they end up.
terms.analogy: The paint, curtains, and layout of an already-built house. You change it without touching a single brick.
terms.confusion: With HTML. If text is missing or an extra button showed up, that's HTML; if it's ugly, misaligned, or overflows on mobile, that's CSS. And if the button does nothing when clicked, it's neither of those — that's JavaScript.

terms.short: A table stored as plain text: one row per line, columns separated by commas.
terms.long: CSV stands for comma-separated values. You open it in Excel and it looks like a spreadsheet, but underneath it's a plain text file with no colors, no formulas, and no tabs. In the course it's the format you work with when processing things in batches: the delivery project stores an emails.csv with each email and its category, and the batch recipe reads comments.csv and writes classified.csv. It's the meeting point between your ordinary spreadsheet and a script, a file of instructions the computer runs straight through.
terms.analogy: A shopping list scrawled on a napkin with commas. Same information as the pretty table, just no borders or colors.
terms.confusion: With an Excel file. An .xlsx stores formulas, formatting, and multiple sheets; a .csv stores only the raw table data. Save an Excel file as CSV and you lose everything else with no warning, and if any text field contains commas, double-check the result before trusting it.

terms.short: Storing a model with less precision so it takes up less space and runs faster, losing a bit of quality.
terms.long: It's what makes it possible for a model that was born weighing forty gigabytes to fit in five and run on an ordinary laptop. You'll run into it on Hugging Face, in file lists with names like Q4 or Q8, where the number tells you how much it's been compressed. And here's the good news: Ollama already ships models pre-compressed by default, and that's the right choice ninety-five percent of the time. So the decision, most of the time, is not deciding anything and just going with what comes preset.
terms.analogy: An MP3 versus the original disc. You've thrown away detail almost nobody notices, and twenty times more songs now fit in the same space.
terms.confusion: With model size, the B in 8B. Parameters are how many internal dials it has; quantization is how much detail each dial is stored with. A quantized 8B is still an 8B, just half the size. Dropping from 8B to 3B does change the model; quantizing doesn't.

terms.short: Being able to prove with paperwork that what you built respects the law and the rules that apply to you.
terms.long: In the course it's a checklist you go through before delivery, not an abstract idea: privacy, security, ownership of what you generated, licenses, and the client's internal policies. Underneath, it's very concrete things: having a note of what data you process and why, having a contract with the model provider (because they're also processing that data on your behalf), and knowing whether they process it outside the EU. The word that sums it up is "prove": if you can't show it to someone, you're not compliant, even if you're doing everything right. And whatever isn't resolved gets delivered as a visible, written flag — not swept under the rug.
terms.analogy: A bar's fridge temperature log. You can have kept it perfect all year, but if the inspector asks for the paper and it's not there, it's as if you never had it.
terms.confusion: With having a secure system. You can have everything locked down tight and still be out of compliance — say, by storing customer data you never needed to collect. Security is nobody getting in; compliance is what you're doing being allowed and written down.

terms.short: A fixed payment that repeats every month, either you paying a provider or a client paying you.
terms.long: In the course you see it in both directions. The kind you pay: the automation tool's cloud plan runs around €20/month, while self-hosted on your own computer it's free. And the kind you charge: the €45/month maintenance fee in the accounting-firm case, which is what turns a one-off job into recurring income. In exchange it commits you to reviewing the system every month, so you have to decide and write down what's included in that fee. Skip writing it down, and the fee ends up paying for unlimited support.
terms.analogy: A gym membership: charged on the 1st whether you go or not, which is exactly why the membership needs to spell out what it includes.
terms.confusion: With a one-time payment. The one-time payment covers building it; the monthly fee covers keeping it alive, and that's neither the same thing nor the same cost. In the proposal they go on two separate lines, so the client sees the second number isn't a hidden markup.

terms.short: A code editor with AI built right in: you point it at a file, say what you want, and it proposes the change.
terms.long: It's built on top of Visual Studio Code, so if you've seen one you've seen the other, and it only downloads from cursor.com because there are lookalikes out there. It shows you what's about to change marked in green and red, and you say yes or no before anything gets saved. In the course it always shows up as the third option alongside Claude Code and Codex. It's the tool for someone who already writes some code and wants to move faster — if you've never programmed, this isn't your first stop.
terms.analogy: The same car as always, but with the co-driver sitting inside instead of talking to you over the phone. You still drive; you just get warned about the exit in time now.
terms.confusion: With GitHub Copilot. Copilot finishes the line you're typing; Cursor has your entire project in front of it and you can ask for changes that touch several files at once.

terms.short: A screen with the handful of numbers you check every day to know if things are going well.
terms.long: It's a single screen pulling together the important figures of something already up and running, so you don't have to open five different places every morning. You build one once you have a flow running on its own: in the course's operations kit, the dashboard carries four figures and no more — cases per day, percentage approved without correction, minutes saved, and monthly cost. The decision isn't which chart to add, it's what to leave out, because nobody looks at a dashboard with twenty charts. And a dashboard nobody looks at is worse than having none, because it gives you a feeling of control without giving you any.
terms.analogy: A car's dashboard. It shows speed, fuel, and temperature, and it doesn't show every injector's pressure, even though the car knows it perfectly well.
terms.confusion: With "panel," which is the same thing under a different name; Docker, for instance, calls its own "Dashboard." The real mistake is confusing it with a report: you read a report once and it tells a story; you check a dashboard every day and it only has to tell you whether today needs action.

terms.short: A pile of data already collected and organized in one place, ready to train a model or test it.
terms.long: It literally means "set of data." You'll never touch the giant datasets models are trained on, but you will touch small ones: the twenty test cases you use to measure whether your assistant answers well, the list of emails you're about to classify, the folder of invoices you're feeding it to read. That's where the decision that matters shows up: if that set carries names, phone numbers, or client data, deciding which server it gets uploaded to stops being a technical question and becomes a data-protection-law one.
terms.analogy: The shoebox with every receipt from the year. It's not the accounting yet — it's the raw material the accounting gets made from.
terms.confusion: With a database. A database is a live system, with its own program, that you query and write to every day. A dataset is still material — collected, frozen, and used to train or measure, precisely because it doesn't change.

terms.short: Data that causes real harm if it leaks: health, political or religious views, union membership, sexual orientation, data about minors.
terms.long: European data protection law calls it specially protected and sets a much higher bar for it than everything else. In the course it shows up in two very specific places: the rule to never copy a phone number, address, card, or a client's allergies into a flow's notes, and the operations kit's warning that if health data or data about minors shows up, you stop and consult someone. This doesn't get solved with a line in a legal notice. The rule: if your project touches it, you don't build it alone — someone with a legal signature reviews it.
terms.analogy: A medical record. A name on a list is uncomfortable if it leaks; a diagnosis sticks with someone for life.
terms.confusion: With ordinary personal data. All sensitive data is personal, but not the reverse. An email is personal; a depression-related sick leave is sensitive, and at that point sending less isn't enough — you have to stop and ask.

terms.short: Names, amounts, and phone numbers made up on purpose so you can test something without using real people's data.
terms.long: It's what you use when you need a specific value and don't want to plug in a real one: an Oscar Smith, a made-up 555-0100, a $1,480 invoice. It shows up in three places in the course: writing definitions of done, because "the user enters their data" can't be checked while a specific name can; testing an n8n flow before wiring it to the real inbox; and preparing a screenshot or a workflow file you're about to show or publish. A warning the course repeats: data you invent always comes out too clean, so copy the shape of ten real cases (odd accents, two-word replies, forwarded emails) and then fill it with made-up content.
terms.analogy: A shop-window mannequin. It wears the clothes exactly like a customer would, useful for checking how the size falls, but if it topples over, nobody gets hurt.
terms.confusion: With anonymizing. Fictitious data has nobody real behind it — you made it up from scratch. Anonymized data did have someone real behind it, and you've stripped out what identified them. If yours is real and just tweaked, it's not fictitious, and the rules that apply to it aren't the same.

terms.short: Anything that lets you tell who's being talked about: name, email, phone, ID number, account number.
terms.long: It's much broader than people think, and that's exactly the trap: an email and a phone number identify a person better than their surname does, so dropping the surname anonymizes absolutely nothing. In the course you touch it the moment a form, an email, or a WhatsApp message enters your flow, and in the security project you write a filter that masks it before sending it to the model. The instant personal data is involved, the project falls under the GDPR, the European data protection law, and you need to know what you're using it for, what basis you're relying on, and how long you're keeping it. It doesn't matter how small your company is or whether you're getting paid for it.
terms.analogy: A club's member list. Doesn't matter that you strip the surnames — with a phone number and an email, anyone can figure out who to call.
terms.confusion: With data that seems to belong to "nobody in particular." The classic mistake is thinking a work email doesn't count — it does. The other one is believing that if the provider doesn't train on your data, you're already clear to send it; not training on it doesn't mean you had the right to send it in the first place.

terms.short: Data that's technically there but unusable: extra spaces, misspellings, or inconsistent formats.
terms.long: Whatever comes in from a form is almost always dirty: "New," "NEW," and "new " are three different states as far as a program's concerned, which is why your dashboard's count never adds up. It also shows up when pasting from a website, which drags along invisible junk that later breaks searches. The rule: clean it on the way in, as its own step, not by patching every query afterward. A piece of dirty data that gets in multiplies across every place that copies it.
terms.analogy: Unwashed fruit in the basket. You can rinse each piece right before you eat it, or wash it all at once when you get back from the store. The second one only has to happen once.
terms.confusion: With incorrect data. A phone number written as " 600 111 222" is dirty but true; a made-up one is spotless and false. Cleaning catches disorder, not lies.

terms.short: Fixing bugs, plainly named: literally "removing the bug."
terms.long: You'll see it written in English everywhere: a "Debug" button, a debug mode that shows far more detail on screen, a checkbox that turns on messages that normally stay hidden. The word comes from "bug," the seventy-year-old name for a defect. Turn on debug mode in any tool and be ready to see a lot more text than usual: that's normal and exactly what you want, because that's where the detail the normal view hides from you lives. Remember to turn it off before publishing — that detail sometimes includes paths, keys, and data that shouldn't be visible from outside.
terms.analogy: A car's mechanic mode: same dashboard, but showing every sensor reading instead of three warning lights.
terms.confusion: With "depurar," the Spanish word for the same idea. The useful distinction is different: "debug" on its own usually refers to the mode or the button, while the actual work of hunting the cause is debugging. If someone asks you to turn on debug, they're asking for information, not for a fix.

terms.short: The step that catches repeats and sets them aside before they mess up your data.
terms.long: It's idempotence turned into a node: you compare a field that shouldn't repeat (the email, the order number, the alert ID) against what you already have, and decide. In the course's leads flow it sits right after receiving the form and right before creating the record in the CRM, the program where clients get stored — that order isn't negotiable. Put it after, and you've already dirtied the database and now have to clean it by hand.
terms.analogy: A doorman with a guest list: checks the ID and, if you already came in, doesn't count you twice.
terms.confusion: With deleting duplicates afterward. Cleaning up later is mopping up the mess; deduplication is stopping it at the door. If you find yourself manually deleting repeated rows every week, that's the sign this step is missing.

terms.short: A mode that spends several minutes reading websites and hands you back a report with links.
terms.long: It's what Gemini's button is literally called. You press it before typing your question, it takes five to fifteen minutes, and it delivers pages of text with sources listed alongside. It's for when you genuinely need to check twenty sites, not for asking a single figure, and it eats a good chunk of your daily quota. And you still have to open the links: it can search well and summarize poorly, or lean on a ten-year-old blog post.
terms.analogy: Sending someone to the library for the whole morning instead of asking from your desk. They come back with a dossier — and you still have to read the dossier.
terms.confusion: With a regular web search, which checks two or three pages and answers in ten seconds. Deep research costs minutes and quota, so save it for questions that actually deserve it. And don't mistake "long and full of links" for "verified": nobody has checked that report.

terms.short: Explaining out loud what you built and why, answering questions from whoever's evaluating you.
terms.long: It's one of five ways you get evaluated, and the only one you can't pass by copying: the project proves you built something, the defense proves you understand what you built. The questions are almost always the same: what problem does it solve, why did you pick these tools, what part always behaves the same way and what part does the model decide, what does each run cost, and what happens when it fails. And there's a written rule: nobody gets certified who can't explain what happens when their system breaks. The decision it forces on you comes before the defense itself: if you can't answer "what if the service your system depends on goes down?", you haven't finished — you've just been lucky.
terms.analogy: The interview after you send your resume. The paper says what you've done; the conversation shows whether you actually did it.
terms.confusion: With the demo. A demo shows it works and can be pre-recorded; the defense comes after, when you're asked about what the video doesn't show. That's why a recording never counts as a defense.

terms.short: The character that marks where one piece of data ends and the next begins.
terms.long: In a CSV, a text file with data separated by a specific character, it's usually a comma — but many Spanish programs use a semicolon instead, because the comma is already used for decimals there. That's why a file downloaded from a bank sometimes opens jammed into a single column: it's not broken, the delimiter just isn't the one the program expected. The same word is used in prompts for markers like INPUT: and OUTPUT: that separate one part of a task from another.
terms.analogy: The painted lines in a parking lot. Same cars either way — put the lines in the wrong place and nobody fits.
terms.confusion: With a decimal separator. In Spain, 12.50 is written 12,50 with a comma, which is exactly why a comma makes a bad delimiter there and a semicolon gets used instead.

terms.short: Markers that separate one piece of a task from another so they don't blur together.
terms.long: They're things as simple as writing INPUT: and OUTPUT:, adding a line of dashes, or opening <context> before a pasted text and closing it with </context> at the end. They exist so the AI knows exactly where your example ends and the real case begins. Skip them and sooner or later it hands you back your own sample as if it were the processed result, and you're left staring at the screen not understanding what happened. The rule: the moment your prompt has two distinct blocks (examples and real case, instructions and pasted material), label them.
terms.analogy: The dividers on a supermarket checkout belt. Without them, your groceries and the next person's end up in the same bag.
terms.confusion: With the brackets around blanks. Brackets mark what you fill in, and disappear once filled; delimiters mark where each part of the message starts and ends, and those stay put permanently.

terms.short: Showing your work running in front of someone, in three minutes, with no surprises.
terms.long: In the course a demo is done in airplane mode: you save the model's responses to disk and replay them, so you don't depend on the client's wifi, don't spend a cent, and get identical results every time you run through it. It runs a strict three minutes and gets rehearsed twice beforehand. What you have to decide is what to show: it's worth showing the failing case yourself, because you've measured 11 out of 12 correct and the skeptic in the room was going to find it anyway. Showing it yourself defuses it; them finding it sinks you.
terms.analogy: A test drive before buying the car: five minutes, on a road the salesperson already knows.
terms.confusion: With a pilot. You drive the demo, it lasts minutes, and runs on prepared data; a pilot is the client using it for weeks with their own real data. A brilliant demo doesn't prove it'll hold up on some random Tuesday in their office.

terms.short: An outside piece your project needs to run at all: without it, nothing works.
terms.long: They're all listed in package.json and download themselves when you run npm install. Every one you add is a promise to your future self: someone will have to update it, and someday a new version will break something. That's why the course has you set this rule for Claude Code in writing: never install new dependencies without first saying what they are, what they're for, and whether it's doable without them. Ten dependencies is a project; fifty is a maintenance problem you accepted without noticing.
terms.analogy: A bar's suppliers. The more you have, the more you can serve, and the more phone calls you get the day one of them doesn't show.
terms.confusion: With a program you install on your computer. Node.js or VS Code you install once and they're good for everything; a dependency lives inside one specific project folder and only works there.

terms.short: The programs that need to be installed on your computer for a project to run at all.
terms.long: Things like Python, Node.js, Git, or Docker: they're not part of your project, but without them it never starts up. You install them once per computer, with winget, brew, or apt depending on your system, and they stay put for every project you ever build afterward. Don't confuse them with a project's own dependencies, which live inside its folder and reinstall themselves on every machine. A rule of thumb that'll save you a thousand times: if something of yours won't run on someone else's computer, the first thing to check is which versions of these they have installed, not the code.
terms.analogy: The kitchen's oven and fridge. The recipe lists the ingredients, but it takes for granted you have an oven.
terms.confusion: With a project's own dependencies, the ones listed in package.json or requirements.txt that fill up the node_modules folder. System ones you install by hand and they're good for everything; project ones install themselves and only work for one.

terms.short: Finding the exact cause of a failure and fixing only that piece, without rebuilding the rest.
terms.long: It's the opposite of what almost everyone does when something breaks, which is asking the AI to rewrite the whole thing. Debugging means narrowing down: getting the failure to happen again on command, reading the actual message in the console or the terminal, and tracing it down to the exact file and line causing it. In this course you practice it in the errors lesson, with the six-point report you hand the AI instead of just saying "it doesn't work." The rule is harsh but saves days: until you can trigger the failure at will, don't touch anything, because you won't be able to tell whether you fixed it.
terms.analogy: A plumber shutting off valve after valve until they find the leaking pipe, instead of replacing the whole house's plumbing.
terms.confusion: With rewriting. Rewriting leaves you different code and a bug you don't know is still there or not; debugging leaves you the same code with one piece changed and certainty about what was wrong. If you ask the AI to fix one small thing and it hands back the entire file, be suspicious.

terms.short: A person's right to ask you to delete their data, and your obligation to actually be able to.
terms.long: It's the famous right to be forgotten: someone writes to you, asks you to delete their information, and you have a short deadline to do it and reply. The hard part isn't deleting — it's knowing where everything is. In the course this gets decided while building the flow, because a person's data ends up scattered between the spreadsheet, n8n's execution log, the chat history, and maybe an email. The rule: if you can't answer "where's everything about this client?" in under a minute, you're not ready to handle an erasure request yet.
terms.analogy: Canceling a gym membership and asking them to remove your photo. If it's on the front-desk computer, on the trainer's phone, and in a WhatsApp group, cancelling the membership doesn't fix any of that.
terms.confusion: With unsubscribing someone from a mailing list. Removing them from the mailing doesn't delete them — their data is still in your spreadsheet and your logs. And it's not absolute either: if a law requires you to keep an invoice, the invoice stays, and you explain why.

terms.short: An editor where you cut video by deleting words from the transcript, like editing a document.
terms.long: You upload the recording, it gets transcribed, and from there you work on the text: delete a written sentence and it vanishes from the video, or strip every "um" at once with one button. It also cleans up audio, and with your voice cloned it can read back a word you flubbed without you having to record again. It's built for recorded lectures, podcasts, and talking-head videos — exactly the material that's the biggest chore to edit in a traditional video editor.
terms.analogy: Correcting a letter with a word processor's spell-check instead of scissors and tape. Cross out the sentence and the page rearranges itself.
terms.confusion: With a standard video editor like Premiere. There you cut watching a timeline and hunting for the exact moment; here you read. For talking-head footage this goes five times faster; for an effects-heavy ad, it's not the right tool.

terms.short: Publishing your project so it exists on the internet, not just on your own computer.
terms.long: It's the moment everything that secretly depended on your machine gets exposed: keys that lived in your local file, file paths with capitalization that never mattered on your system, mismatched versions. That's why a first deploy almost never goes smoothly on the first try, and it's not a sign you did anything wrong.
terms.analogy: Moving house. At your old place everything worked because you knew exactly where everything was.
terms.confusion: With saving your changes. Saving leaves the change on your computer; deploying puts it where people can actually see it.

terms.short: Each individual screen of a presentation.
terms.long: In the course you use them in prepared lessons and, above all, in your project's oral defense. The rule that keeps coming back is one: long text goes in your speaker notes, and the slide keeps just the idea. Write everything out and the audience reads faster than you talk, and stops listening to you. The decision it forces on every one of them is which sentence to cut so only a single idea remains on screen.
terms.analogy: A protest sign. Room for one sentence, readable from a distance, in two seconds. Whatever you really want to explain, you say out loud.
terms.confusion: With the script. The script is what you say; the slide is what's visible while you say it. If both say the same thing, one of them is redundant — and it's not the one talking.

terms.short: The list of what changes between the before version and the after version.
terms.long: It reads in two colors: green for additions, red for removals. It's the screen you check before accepting any change written by an AI, and the habit that separates someone in control of their project from someone flying blind. If a diff touches five files you weren't expecting, stop and ask why.
terms.analogy: Word's "track changes," but for the whole project at once.
terms.confusion: With the final result. A diff doesn't tell you whether the code works — it tells you what got touched.

terms.short: The flow's first box: the one that decides when everything else starts.
terms.long: In the course you see four, and only four: the scheduled one (fires by the clock), the webhook (an outside service pings you itself), the app-polling one (n8n goes and checks Gmail or your spreadsheet every few minutes), and the manual one (starts when you click it). Choosing between them means answering one question: who's the first to know about what matters to me, and can they tell me directly? If you catch yourself setting "every 5 minutes" just to not miss anything, what you actually wanted was a webhook. Swapping a trigger later isn't rebuilding the flow — it's changing the first box and checking the fields still match up.
terms.analogy: Finding out a package has arrived: either you go check the lobby every hour, or the postman rings the bell, or you ask the doorman who's already watching the door.
terms.confusion: With the actions. The trigger only decides the when; what happens next are the actions. And there's fine print that catches everyone: almost every trigger only sees what happens AFTER the flow is switched on, so don't expect it to go back and grab last week's emails.

terms.short: The directory that translates a website's name into the numeric address of the machine it actually lives on.
terms.long: DNS stands for Domain Name System. You'll touch it exactly once in the whole course: the day you connect your own domain and the platform asks you to add some records or switch nameservers. The two options aren't equivalent: switching nameservers hands everything over to the platform and can knock out that domain's email; adding individual records is more tedious but only moves the website. And changes aren't instant — they take anywhere from minutes to a few hours to show up everywhere, so don't touch it half an hour before a meeting.
terms.analogy: A large company's phone switchboard. You say a name, and it connects you to the right extension.
terms.confusion: With the domain. The domain is the name you bought; DNS is the directory that says where that name points. When something "points wrong," the problem is almost never the domain — it's the directory.

terms.short: Turning a video into another language while keeping the original voice's tone.
terms.long: ElevenLabs calls it "dubbing," and it does something that until recently required a whole studio: it takes your video and hands it back speaking another language, sounding like the same person. In the course it comes with a clear warning: always review it, because it translates well on average and fails exactly on proper names and technical terms. The decision it forces on you is who does the reviewing: if nobody on your team understands the target language, don't deliver it.
terms.analogy: A dubbed movie. Same face, same scene, different language. And just like at the theater, you can tell right away when the dubber didn't get the joke.
terms.confusion: With adding subtitles in another language, where the text gets read and the audio never changes. And with voiceover, which is a new voice laid over footage, not swapping out one that was already there.

terms.short: A box that carries a program and everything it needs to run, all bundled together.
terms.long: It solves "it works on my machine": inside the box you always get the exact same version of everything, on your laptop and on the server. The cost is one more layer to learn, so don't reach for it in a small project just because it sounds serious.
terms.analogy: A camping stove: you're not depending on the house having a working kitchen.
terms.confusion: With a server. Docker is the package format; the server is where it actually runs.

terms.short: The start button: a file that switches on every box of your project at once with a single command.
terms.long: It's written in a docker-compose.yml file that sits next to the Dockerfile, and it turns half a dozen options nobody remembers into four commands you actually do remember: "docker compose up -d" to start it, "logs -f" to see what it's saying inside, "down" to shut it off, and "up -d --build" once you've changed the code. It's what makes your project genuinely clonable: someone else downloads it, types one line, and has it running without asking you anything. It's used mostly when there's more than one piece — say your app and a database that need to start in the right order. A weird error naming an image is almost always a typo: postgress with two s's, node:22-slimm.
terms.analogy: The remote that turns on the blinds, the light, and the AC in a room. One button and everything starts in the right order.
terms.confusion: With Docker on its own. Docker is the program that switches boxes on, one at a time, by hand; compose is the written list saying which ones, with what settings, and in what order.

terms.short: The file where you write the box's recipe: which version, which packages, and what runs on startup.
terms.long: It's called exactly that, Dockerfile, no leading dot and no file extension, and it lives in the project's root folder. In the course you ask the AI for it along with two other files, and two rules never get broken: no key ever written inside it, and specific versions of the base images (the pre-built boxes yours is born from) instead of "latest," which means "whatever's newest" and can change under your feet. Next to it goes a .dockerignore, the list of what never makes it into the box, and that's not optional extra — it's what stops your .env from ending up inside and traveling with you to the server. If your program starts and immediately dies, check that the startup filename you wrote here matches the real one.
terms.analogy: A cake recipe, written out. Ingredients, quantities, oven, and time, so it comes out the same whether you make it at your place or your mother's.
terms.confusion: With docker-compose.yml, which sits in the same folder. The Dockerfile says how one box gets built; compose says which boxes start up together, with what settings, and in what order.

terms.short: The living map of your page exactly as the browser has it assembled right now.
terms.long: DOM stands for Document Object Model, and in practice it's what you see in the browser tools' "Elements" tab: the tree of boxes, text, and images that makes up the page. It matters because it doesn't always match your HTML file: if a program paints in a piece after the page loads, it's not in the file, but it is here. And that explains one of the course's most typical errors, the "Cannot read properties of null" that shows up when a program goes looking for a button that hasn't been mounted on screen yet.
terms.analogy: The floor plan is the file; the DOM is the apartment already furnished, with everything you've moved in since.
terms.confusion: With HTML. HTML is the file you wrote and it doesn't change on its own; the DOM is what's assembled on screen right now and changes every time someone clicks something. If you check the source code and can't find text you can clearly see on the page, look for it in "Elements" instead.
