terms.short: Your site's pretty name, like myshop.com, paid for by the year and pointing to wherever it's hosted.
terms.long: When you publish something on Vercel, you get a long address like my-project.vercel.app: it works perfectly, but it's not what you show a client. Your own domain gets bought at a registrar (the shops that sell them: IONOS, GoDaddy, Namecheap, and others) and then connected from "Settings" → "Domains." Watch for one thing that gets expensive: if your company's email lives on that same domain, touching the settings carelessly can knock out your email. And it's a lease, not a purchase: stop paying and you lose it, and someone else can grab it.
terms.analogy: A shop's sign. You can move locations without changing the sign, and change the sign without moving locations.
terms.confusion: With hosting. The domain is just the name — if there's nothing hosted behind it, typing it goes nowhere. And with DNS, which isn't the name but the directory saying which machine that name points to.

terms.short: The same case coming in twice and ending up creating two records where there should be one.
terms.long: It's the number one failure mode of webhooks, the addresses where other services notify you: the same alert arrives twice and you sign the same client up twice. In the course's leads project there's a node literally called Duplicate, whose only job is checking whether that email was already there before touching anything. The decision it forces on you is what to do with the repeat: drop it, update the one you already had, or send it for review. Pick one and write it down, because all three are defensible and the worst option is not having chosen.
terms.analogy: Clicking the buy button twice because the page is slow. Two packages show up, and two charges.
terms.confusion: With two similar cases. The same client writing twice with different questions isn't a duplicate — that's two cases. A duplicate is the same fact, told twice.

terms.short: The program where you open and write your project's files: a notepad with superpowers.
terms.long: It colors your text, flags missing parentheses, and shows every project folder in a column on the left. The most popular one is Visual Studio Code, which is free; Cursor is that same editor with AI built in. In this course you don't need one on day one: the first website is a single file and Notepad gets you through it. Install one when you hit a specific, named wall — not because a video tells you to at minute three.
terms.analogy: A workshop's workbench. You can manage on the floor, but the moment you're juggling three pieces at once, you're glad for the space and the light.
terms.confusion: With the terminal. In the editor you write and save files; in the terminal you run things. They're two separate windows, and plenty of people waste an afternoon pasting commands into the editor waiting for something to happen.

terms.short: One complete run of a flow, from the first box to the last, with its data saved.
terms.long: When someone tells you "this broke yesterday at three," you open that execution and see the flow frozen exactly as it ran: what arrived at each box and where it went wrong. It's not a log entry — it's the entire flow with the real data from that moment. And a warning that saves days: green doesn't mean correct, it means it didn't crash. A filter that blocks everything or a search that finds nothing also comes back green, so the real check is the number showing on the arrow between boxes.
terms.analogy: One month's power bill. It's not the wiring — it's what actually happened over those thirty days.
terms.confusion: With the flow. The flow is the diagram, always the same one; an execution is one specific run with that day's data. A flow has thousands of executions, and each one can be opened separately.

terms.short: Putting one or more samples you've already worked out into the task, so the AI copies the shape.
terms.long: It's the single biggest lever once a task is already well-built. An adjective is an opinion ("friendly tone"); an example is proof the AI has in front of it and can copy without guessing anything. In the "give examples" lesson you run the same five cases through three versions of a task, one with a single sample, one with three, one with five, and you see with your own numbers that the big jump happens between one and three. The rule: examples have to be real, pulled from your own files with personal data covered, because a made-up example teaches a clean world that doesn't exist.
terms.analogy: Showing a new waiter three well-filled-out orders instead of spending half an hour explaining how to fill them in.
terms.confusion: With adding more instructions. An instruction says what to do, and an example says what it should look like — together they work far better than either alone. If you catch yourself writing a third adjective for the same nuance, stop writing and paste an example instead.

terms.short: Turns text into spoken audio that doesn't sound robotic: paste the script, pick a voice, get the audio.
terms.long: It does three things worth knowing: reading text with a catalog voice, cloning a voice (yours, with your permission) to read anything, and dubbing a video into another language while keeping the original voice. It's used for video voiceovers, training audio, answering-machine messages, and podcasts: it's an incredibly fast, cheap narrator that doesn't understand what it's reading, so irony or how a figure gets said is on you to direct. Watch how it's measured, because it's billed by characters, not minutes — every letter counts, and the free plan runs around ten minutes of audio a month and doesn't allow commercial use. Before charging for anything with audio from here, check your plan actually grants you rights over what's generated.
terms.analogy: A radio announcer who records in thirty seconds and charges by the letter. Delivers a flawless voice for a text they never understood.
terms.confusion: With cloning whoever's voice you feel like. Doing it without written permission is a serious legal problem: in Spain a voice is protected as part of a person's identity, and even more so when it belongs to someone well-known.

terms.short: Converting a piece of text into a list of numbers that represents its meaning.
terms.long: It's what lets you compare two texts by what they mean instead of by which words they use. Every time you convert a document you pay for it, so it's done once and saved; reprocessing the same PDF on every run is beginners' most common expensive mistake.
terms.analogy: Placing every piece of text on a set of coordinates. Things about the same subject land close together.
terms.confusion: With a translation or a summary. An embedding can't be read, and it can't be converted back into the original text.

terms.short: The company that processes personal data on your behalf. Your AI model provider is one.
terms.long: You're the controller, because you decide what data gets processed and why; OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, or n8n cloud are processors, because they only process it because you asked them to. That translates into two very concrete things in the course: you need a contract with them (the big providers already offer one baked into their terms, but you have to go find it) and you need to know which region they process your data in. The rule: note it in your record of processing activities with the date you checked. It's literally what a client's legal department is going to ask you.
terms.analogy: The accounting firm that runs your payroll. They handle your employees' data, but you're the one who answers to your employees.
terms.confusion: With having the responsibility taken off your hands. The provider being a processor doesn't clear you of anything: if the data shouldn't have left your system in the first place, that's still your problem. They're responsible for meeting your contract, not for your decisions.

terms.short: The table that decides which letter shows up on screen for each stored byte.
terms.long: It literally means "codification." You'll see it two ways: in the Encoding dropdown when you save a file with Notepad, and written inside project code as encoding=utf-8 every time a file gets opened or saved. Pick the wrong one and the file doesn't break, but accented letters come out as meaningless symbols. The decision is always the same and always easy: set UTF-8 and never touch it again.
terms.analogy: Dialing a phone number with another country's prefix. The digits you press are exactly the same, but someone else picks up.
terms.confusion: With a file's format. Format is whether something is a .csv or a .docx; encoding is how the letters inside get translated. A CSV can be perfectly well-built and still look terrible purely because of encoding.

terms.short: What fits inside the image's rectangle and what gets left out.
terms.long: It's one of two or three things that separate an amateur image from a professional one, along with lighting — and the course's Midjourney guide says exactly that. In video it gets decided on the shot sheet, before generating anything. The money decision it forces on you: framing gets tested in low resolution, which is cheap, and only once it's locked in do you generate the good, high-res version.
terms.analogy: Laying a frame over a big photo. The photo stays the same; what you show and what you hide completely changes what the viewer understands.
terms.confusion: With camera movement. Framing is where you're looking from and what fits; movement is what the camera does from there. They get decided separately, and skipping either one shows in the result.

terms.short: The specific address of an API that a request gets sent to.
terms.long: An API has many: one to create, one to look up, one to delete. The most common mistake isn't getting the address wrong — it's using the wrong method on the right one. When something returns a 404, check the address letter by letter before touching anything else.
terms.analogy: A specific window inside a building. The building is the API; the window is the endpoint.
terms.confusion: With the service's website. An endpoint almost never opens in a browser and doesn't return a pretty page.

terms.short: Adding information to a piece of data you already have by going out and fetching it from somewhere else.
terms.long: An email comes in from a form, and not much else. Enriching means going out for the company, the sector, or the size and attaching it to the record before saving it. In the course you see it in the leads flow, where the AI adds temperature, interest, and a summary to what arrived bare, and in an e-commerce flow that fills out product listings. The rule: every field you add is one more call that costs money and can fail, so only enrich what you're actually going to look at.
terms.analogy: A waiter who takes your order and also remembers you asked for it gluten-free last time. You didn't give them that today.
terms.confusion: With transformation. Transforming rearranges what you already had; enriching brings in from outside what wasn't there. That's why enriching can fail and transforming almost never does — it depends on a service that isn't yours.

terms.short: Deciding which path each case follows based on what it carries.
terms.long: It's what the IF node and the Switch node do: a message comes in, its category or urgency gets checked, and it gets sent down one branch or another. In the course's support flows there are always at least three exits: what gets answered automatically, what goes to human review, and what nobody understood. Sketch those branches on paper before building them, because the classic mistake is leaving cases with no path: if there's no branch for "everything else," that case vanishes and you never find out.
terms.analogy: A mail sorting machine: domestic here, international there, and a separate bin for what won't scan.
terms.confusion: With filtering. A filter lets through or discards; routing discards nothing, it distributes. If you're throwing away cases because they don't fit any category, that's not routing, that's losing work.

terms.short: A sealed space where a project runs with its own stuff, without mixing with the rest of the computer.
terms.long: It's the answer to the classic "it works on my machine and not yours." Each project lives in its own spot, with its pieces' versions pinned, so two projects needing different versions stop fighting over the same computer. In the course you build this at different levels as needed: a separate folder per project to keep versions apart, Docker when you want the box to be identical on your laptop and on the server, and a sandbox when what you're separating isn't versions but permissions, so a program you didn't write can't touch anything outside it. Start with the simplest option: half an hour now beats two lost days a month from now.
terms.analogy: A rented apartment with its own meter. What the neighbor uses doesn't show up on your bill or trip your breaker.
terms.confusion: With just having the project in its own folder. Keeping files tidy isolates nothing: what actually gets separated here is program versions and permissions, not documents.

terms.short: The place you test in: your own computer, with fake keys, where whatever you break doesn't affect anyone.
terms.long: It's one of three environments you'll see written exactly this way on Vercel's dashboard: Development (your computer), Preview (test copies), and Production (the real live site, on your domain). The same project runs in all three, but each setting can carry a different value in each one — that's the whole trick: development gets the test key, production gets the real one. It also includes what you need to start it up: the Python version, packages with their numbers pinned, Docker if needed. When someone says "it works on my computer," they're really saying their development environment and production aren't the same.
terms.analogy: A restaurant's test kitchen. Same cooking, same stoves, but if it comes out wrong, it never reaches the dining room.
terms.confusion: With Python's virtual environment, which is just one project's box of packages. A development environment is the whole package: computer, versions, test keys, and fake data.

terms.short: A separate folder where the pieces of ONE Python project live.
terms.long: Without it, everything you install mixes together across the whole computer, and two projects needing different versions start fighting. You create one with python -m venv .venv, activate it every time you sit down to work, and it never gets uploaded to the internet.
terms.analogy: A toolbox per job site, instead of one shared drawer where everything ends up jumbled.
terms.confusion: With node_modules. Same idea, different language: one's Python's, the other's JavaScript's.

terms.short: The specific thing a client receives and can open: a file, a working flow, a manual.
terms.long: Every project in the course ends in one. The delivery module's is a zipped folder under 100 kB with the offline-capable program, a report of measured figures, and the already-written proposal. The test for whether you actually have a deliverable is this: if you can't say in one sentence what file or thing you're going to hand over, you don't have a deliverable yet — you have an intention. And that test decides the price, because you only go fixed-price once the deliverable is clear.
terms.analogy: In a move, the deliverable isn't "I'll help you move" — it's the boxes inside the new house and the bed assembled.
terms.confusion: With the task. The task is what you do over three weeks; the deliverable is what's left on the table once you're gone. Nobody pays for your three weeks — they pay for what stays.

terms.short: The already-finished process where a model read a huge amount of text and learned to write. It doesn't happen again while you talk to it.
terms.long: Before you ever opened the app, someone fed the machine a brutal amount of text and had it guess the next word millions of times, correcting it every time it was wrong. Nothing gets stored from that as a copy of the data — what's left is a way of writing. That process ended on a specific date, the cutoff, and nothing after it made it in. The practical consequence is harsh: no matter how much you correct it today, tomorrow it won't remember, because your conversations don't train it — if you want it to know something, you have to put it in front of it every single time.
terms.analogy: It's the degree they studied, not this morning's meeting. A plumber with twenty years of experience still won't know where your shutoff valve is until you show them.
terms.confusion: With a chat's memory. What it remembers within a conversation is only the text currently in front of it; open a new chat and it starts from zero. And ChatGPT's or Gemini's "memory" features aren't training either — they're notes saved separately that the app pastes back in front of it later.

terms.short: The .env file: your list of keys, one per line, living in your folder and never uploaded.
terms.long: Named after "environment," and written with a leading dot: .env. Inside go lines like NAME=value, no quotes, no spaces around the equals sign, because those spaces sneak into the value and then you can't figure out why it's not working. To keep it from being uploaded, .env has to appear written in your .gitignore file, the list of what stays on your own computer — and that gets verified, never assumed. If you ever upload it by accident, deleting it isn't enough: the key is already in the history, so you have to go into the provider's console and revoke it.
terms.analogy: Your home safe. The code is the note on the fridge that says "it's in the safe," not a note with the actual combination written on it.
terms.confusion: With .env.example, which looks almost identical by name and does the opposite: that one does get uploaded, because it carries the names with the values left blank.

terms.short: A copy of .env with the key names but no values; that one gets uploaded with the project.
terms.long: It's the map whoever downloads your project reads to know what to fill in before starting it up. Without it, someone downloads it, runs it, it crashes, and they have to call you; with it, they see the list of missing keys and go get them. It also helps you in three months, once you've forgotten what that project needed. The practical rule is simple: the moment you add a new variable to .env, write its line into .env.example right then, not later.
terms.analogy: A blank application form. It tells you which boxes need filling without showing you anyone's actual data.
terms.confusion: With the real .env. They're told apart by the end of the filename and one rule that never fails: if a file has real values inside, it never gets uploaded; if it has empty blanks, it does.

terms.short: A typo in the code: one comma too many, an unclosed parenthesis.
terms.long: The computer doesn't interpret what you meant to say: it either understands the whole instruction or understands nothing at all, and here it understands nothing, so it stops before it even starts. It's the number one suspect when you open your site and get a blank screen with not a single message explaining anything. It usually comes from pasting half-finished code or accidentally deleting a character while editing. The good news: it fixes in one message — copy the full error from the console and paste it, since it comes with the filename and line number attached.
terms.analogy: An order written in illegible handwriting in the kitchen. The cook doesn't improvise — sets the paper aside, and no dish comes out.
terms.confusion: With the program being poorly designed. A syntax error says nothing about whether your idea is good or bad — it only says it's written wrong. It's fixed by changing one character, and afterward the program will do exactly what it was going to do before, well or badly.

terms.short: A separate flow that only fires when another one breaks, existing purely to alert you.
terms.long: In the course's n8n guide you build it with two boxes: an Error Trigger and a Telegram message with the name of the flow that failed, the specific box that broke, the error message, and a link to go check it out. This flow stays switched off on purpose, with the toggle untouched, because it never starts on its own — it starts when something else falls over. What matters comes after building it, and it's exactly what gets forgotten most: you have to go flow by flow, open the three dots top right, go into "Settings," and pick it from the "Error Workflow" dropdown. It's not inherited, and that oversight is what leaves automations failing silently for three weeks.
terms.analogy: The smoke detector in the hallway. Does nothing for years and isn't wired to the kitchen, but the day there's smoke, it's the only thing that goes off.
terms.confusion: With an error branch. A branch lives inside the same flow and catches one specific box's failure so the rest can keep going; an error workflow is a separate flow that fires when anything at all breaks. It's not either/or — normally you have both.

terms.short: The database's blueprint: which tables exist, what columns each has, and what type they are.
terms.long: In the course it lives in a file called esquema.sql that you paste once into Supabase. Keep it even after you've already run it: it's the recipe for rebuilding everything from scratch somewhere else, and without it your database only exists inside someone else's server. The schema is also what stops junk from being stored, because a column declared as a date won't accept "tomorrow" no matter how you ask.
terms.analogy: An apartment's floor plan. It shows where every wall goes, not who lives there or what furniture is in it.
terms.confusion: With the data. You can delete every row and the schema is still there, empty and ready. And watch out for a prompt's output schema: that describes the shape of a response, not of a table.

terms.short: The spec that says which fields a response must carry and what values each one accepts.
terms.long: With a schema you don't ask for a format — you enforce it. You tell it the response must carry category, confidence, and reason, and that category can only be one of your five labels, nothing else. You see it in the course's classifier recipe, and it cuts off cold the day it answers "Invoice," then "invoices," then "looks like an invoice, though it could also be support." The rule: if your process breaks when a weird value shows up, this stops being optional; if you're the one reading the response with your own eyes, building it is just making your life harder.
terms.analogy: A car registration form. They won't accept a letter explaining the same thing — either you fill those exact boxes, or it doesn't get processed.
terms.confusion: With web form validation. A form protects against people, who make mistakes one at a time; a schema protects against a program that's about to throw a thousand responses at you in a row with nobody watching.

terms.short: A set of test cases with the correct answer already written down.
terms.long: It's the only way to know whether a prompt change made things better or worse, because eyeballing it always looks like an improvement. You put together twenty or thirty real cases, note what should come out for each one, and run the list after every change. Without this, changing a prompt is just superstition.
terms.analogy: An exam with an answer key. Without the key, every grader approves whatever sounds right to them.
terms.confusion: With trying it a couple of times by hand. Two loose tests won't catch that you just broke five other cases.

terms.short: Microsoft's spreadsheet. In the course it's where your data comes from and where results end up.
terms.long: It shows up everywhere: the 300-product catalog you upload to a project so the AI stops making up your prices, the invoice you process by hand every Monday and eventually automate, the hours table you use to measure whether things improved. There are even official skills that build you an entire Excel file from scratch. And there's a mandatory check before uploading a `.xlsx` to any chat: open it and check whether it carries client names, phone numbers, or account numbers, because a spreadsheet hides columns and tabs you don't remember adding.
terms.analogy: A shop's account book. The whole business is in there, which is exactly why you need to check carefully which pages you're showing.
terms.confusion: With CSV. A CSV is plain text separated by commas and stores neither formulas nor colors; a `.xlsx` stores formulas, tabs, and formatting. When a program asks you for data, it almost always wants the CSV, and Excel will warn you on export that you're losing things — that's normal, not an error.

terms.short: A failure that goes off while the program is already running, and stops it dead.
terms.long: It's not that the code is written wrong — it's written fine, but on reaching that line it hits something it wasn't expecting, like a missing key or a file that isn't where it should be. In the course's environment project, comprobar.py does exactly this on purpose: it walks through every piece one by one and, if any is missing, throws a controlled exception before a single cent gets spent on the API. The decision you face is whether you let it crash mid-run with an English error message from a library you didn't write, or you trigger it yourself upfront with a message in plain language saying what's missing and how to fix it.
terms.analogy: The supermarket checkout when a barcode doesn't exist. It doesn't overcharge or undercharge you — it just stops and calls the manager.
terms.confusion: With a syntax error. A syntax error shows up before anything even starts, because the computer doesn't even understand the instructions; an exception only shows up once the program is already running and reaches that exact line. That's why an exception can take weeks to surface: until someone makes that one specific click, nothing happens.

terms.short: The window where you see your computer's folders: the yellow folder icon on Windows, Finder on Mac.
terms.long: It looks so basic nobody bothers explaining it, and that's exactly where half the class gets stuck. In the course you use it for three specific things: creating the project folder somewhere sensible, seeing the files the AI just wrote, and dragging them into GitHub or the chat. You need to flip two settings on day one, and only day one: show file extensions, so you know if you have a .html or a .txt, and show hidden files, because .env and .gitignore start with a dot and are invisible by default. On Windows they're under the "View" tab; on Mac press Cmd + Shift + . inside a Finder window.
terms.analogy: An office filing cabinet. Your papers can be perfectly organized, but if you don't know how to open the drawer, they don't exist for you.
terms.confusion: With a web browser. Both have an address bar and both show folders, but one looks inside your disk and the other looks at the internet. If a path starts with C:\ or /Users, it's the File Explorer.

terms.short: The mark a file adds to say which of its pieces others are allowed to use.
terms.long: It's the other half of import: one offers, the other takes. If a file exports nothing, it's a locked box no matter how full it is. The classic error you'll see reads "does not provide an export named X," and it almost always means one of two things: either the name's misspelled with a stray capital letter, or the AI invented a function that doesn't actually exist in that file. And watch a vocabulary trap: in the Mac and Linux terminal, export means something completely different — it's the command that loads a key into that window's memory.
terms.analogy: A shop's counter. What's in the window can be ordered; what's in the storeroom exists, but for someone outside, it might as well not.
terms.confusion: With exporting a document to PDF or Excel. Unrelated: no new file gets generated here and nothing gets downloaded, it just marks what stays available to the rest of the project.

terms.short: The formula between double curly braces that grabs a value from an earlier step in the flow.
terms.long: Written like this, {{ $json.name }}, meaning "the name field of the item that just arrived." It's n8n's glue: without expressions, every node would always write the exact same thing, and you wouldn't have an automation — you'd have a fixed message repeated forever. The first time, n8n generates them for you when you pick a field with the selector; from the second time on, you write them yourself. The classic mistake is getting back "undefined" because the field is actually named something different than you thought.
terms.analogy: A spreadsheet's "=B2". You're not writing the value — you're writing where to go fetch it, every single time.
terms.confusion: With typing the value by hand. Type "Juan" into the email subject and every email says Juan; use an expression and it says each person's actual name. If you see literal text where you expected a value, the braces are missing.

terms.short: A way of searching text by its pattern instead of by exact words.
terms.long: Instead of searching for "Juan," you describe the shape: something starting with sk-, or anything with an at-sign and a dot after it. In the course it lives inside the secrets scanner, a set of instructions that walks every one of your files looking for anything shaped like an API key before you accidentally push it to the internet. You don't need to learn to write them yourself — you ask the AI, explaining what you want to catch. What is on you is testing it against five examples that should match and five that shouldn't, because a badly-written regex fails silently.
terms.analogy: An inbox filter. You're not saying "this email," you're saying "anything from this domain with the word invoice in the subject."
terms.confusion: With plain find-and-replace. Find matches the text exactly as you typed it; a regular expression matches everything shaped that way, even things you've never seen. That's why it's good at catching keys you didn't even know were there.

terms.short: An add-on you plug into a program so it does something it doesn't out of the box.
terms.long: The word shows up in three places in the course and doesn't mean the same thing in each. In Visual Studio Code, an extension adds capabilities to the editor. In Gemini or Claude, extensions and connectors are what let the model into your Gmail or your Drive, and that's where a real decision lives, because each one asks for permissions and you give it the bare minimum. And in Google Sheets, "Extensions" is just the name of the menu you open Apps Script from.
terms.analogy: A drill's attachments. The drill stays the same; one bit drills holes, another drives screws.
terms.confusion: With a file's name extension, the letters at the end: .html, .txt, .css. Completely different thing. On Windows, turn on "File Name Extensions" under the explorer's View tab, or you won't be able to tell if you saved index.html or index.html.txt.

terms.short: The document used to bill: who's charging, who's paying, what was done, how much, and the tax.
terms.long: In the course invoices show up on both sides. The ones you issue, which need a tax ID and VAT to count for anything, and the ones you receive from tools: the AI subscription, the cloud automation tool, hosting. They're also practice material: there's an exercise that sums an invoice column and applies 21%, and an n8n flow that checks incoming ones and pings Slack when a tax ID is missing. What it forces you to decide is separating into two columns what you charge and what it costs you, because savings that don't subtract your own bills convince nobody.
terms.analogy: A supermarket receipt, but with both parties' full names and the tax broken out separately.
terms.confusion: With a quote. A quote comes first and is an offer that can still change; an invoice comes after and is already a debt with a date on it. If something changed along the way, you change the quote and get it re-approved — never edit the invoice directly.

terms.short: The automatic plan B: what happens when the first thing fails.
terms.long: In the course it mostly shows up with a modifier: human fallback. It's the exit you prepare for when the AI isn't sure or a step goes down, sending the case to a person instead of letting a bad answer through. There's also a model fallback: if one provider is down, call another. The decision has to be made before delivery, not after: in any flow you build for a client, you need to be able to point to where a doubtful case ends up and who looks at it.
terms.analogy: The phone number that shows up on a site when the form goes down. It doesn't fix the form — it keeps the client from walking away.
terms.confusion: With a retry. Retrying means trying the exact same thing again, and it's the right move when the failure was temporary, like a two-second outage. A fallback means doing something different. If the actual problem is the task itself, retrying twenty times just racks up the bill and delays the moment someone notices.

terms.short: Your test says something failed, when the answer was actually correct.
terms.long: You'll run into this building the quality project's test suite: you write a rule like "4.95 can't appear anywhere" and the assistant answers flawlessly but still fails the test, because it mentioned that figure to explain when it gets charged. When this happens, the mistake is almost always in your rule, not the model. It does more damage than a real failure: two false positives in a row and nobody trusts the test suite anymore. Before touching the prompt, read the failing case and decide whether you're the one who wrote the bug.
terms.analogy: A car alarm that goes off every time a motorcycle drives by. By the third night you stop getting up — and that's exactly the night it gets stolen.
terms.confusion: With a false negative, the reverse: the answer was bad and your test calls it good. A false positive costs you trust in your tests; a false negative lets you publish the mistake. Both get fixed by looking at the case, not the model.

terms.short: What the people using your work tell you.
terms.long: In the course you collect it two ways. By hand, with the three hard questions you get asked after showing a demo: privacy, maintenance, and cost. And on its own, with an n8n flow that reads incoming messages, classifies them, and flags the ones that need a human to look. What you have to decide is what to do with the uncomfortable feedback, because that's always the useful kind — the one that tells you the tool fails every Monday, or that nobody's used it since March.
terms.analogy: A bar's complaint book: annoying to have, and the only thing that tells you the kitchen is too slow on Saturdays.
terms.confusion: With praise. "It's great" isn't feedback, it's courtesy, and it doesn't let you change anything. Useful feedback is "reviewing what it proposes takes longer than just doing it myself," which sounds much worse and is worth a hundred times more.

terms.short: The technical name for giving several worked examples inside a prompt.
terms.long: You'll see it in OpenAI's and Anthropic's documentation and in any article about prompting. There's nothing to memorize: it's exactly what the course calls a guided example — putting two to five samples you've already worked out into the task. Its siblings are one-shot, with a single sample, and zero-shot, with none. It's worth knowing so you recognize the word when it comes up, and for nothing else.
terms.analogy: It's like calling "filet mignon" what your family's always just called "the good cut of steak." Same piece of meat, dressed up with a fancier name.
terms.confusion: With fine-tuning, which also learns from your examples. The difference is scale: few-shot is five examples pasted into the message and costs nothing; fine-tuning needs hundreds of examples, time, and money. For what you're doing in this course, few-shot has you covered.

terms.short: A drawing pad in the browser where you sketch what your website will look like before it exists.
terms.long: It builds nothing, and it doesn't need to: it's the blueprint, like the one an architect draws on paper before anyone touches a brick. In the course its job is very specific: you do the design, take a screenshot of it, and that screenshot is what you show the AI so it builds the house, telling it to respect the section order and the exact colors. The free plan is more than enough for this, with one catch worth knowing upfront: it only keeps the last thirty days of history, so whatever you broke five weeks ago isn't coming back.
terms.analogy: An architect's blueprint. It's for arguing over where the kitchen goes without knocking down a single wall, and it can't hold up any actual ceiling.
terms.confusion: With a real, working website. In Figma the button is painted, not functional. Show it to a client without a warning and they'll assume it's already built and ask for a delivery date that doesn't exist.

terms.short: The condition that only lets through the rows you care about and drops the rest.
terms.long: It's written with a WHERE clause and it's the part of a query hiding the most decisions. In the search project, the permissions filter goes inside the query, before picking the top five results; filter afterward, in your own program, and you end up with one result — plus you've already read text you shouldn't have. And a date filter like "last 30 days" gives a different number every time you look at it: note next to the value when it's counting from.
terms.analogy: A colander. It matters a lot whether you use it before or after dumping the pasta onto the plate.
terms.confusion: With sorting. A filter removes rows; sorting just puts them in a different order. If a dashboard shows a lower number than you expected, suspect the filter, not the sort order.

terms.short: Exactly what you're going to use that data for. Decided before collecting it, and not changed midway.
terms.long: It's the first question on the course's GDPR checklist, and the one most people skip because it seems obvious. "Improve the service" isn't a purpose because it says nothing; "classify the issue a client writes in and prepare a draft a person reviews" is one. It matters because purpose limits everything else: data collected to fulfill an order can't later be reused to send marketing. The rule: write it in one sentence before building the flow, because it's what determines your legal basis, the notice to the user, and the retention period.
terms.analogy: The reason you give when booking a room. If you booked it for a meeting, you don't throw a party in it just because it was free.
terms.confusion: With describing the project. Purpose doesn't say what your system does — it says what you're using that specific person's data for. If your sentence doesn't mention the person, it's not a purpose yet.

terms.short: Retraining a model on your own examples so it adopts a specific way of responding.
terms.long: It's for style and format, not for feeding it data: if you want it to know your documents, what you actually need is RAG. It costs money, requires hundreds of well-made examples, and needs redoing every time a new model comes out. In practice, almost everything people try to solve this way is better solved with a good prompt.
terms.analogy: Teaching an employee the house's tone. You're not teaching them the catalog — that they just look up.
terms.confusion: With RAG. Fine-tuning changes how it answers; RAG changes what information it answers with.

terms.short: Copying someone else's project into your own account, dragging its history along and staying linked to the original.
terms.long: The button sits top-right on any public GitHub project's page, and in two seconds you have a copy with your name on it that you can destroy without fear. In the course you use it when you find a project that fits and would rather start from there than from scratch. Before forking anything, check two things: the date of the last change, because if it says three years ago, half the pieces no longer fit together, and the license, because if there isn't one, that work isn't yours to use.
terms.analogy: Asking a friend for their recipe and copying it into your own notebook: you tweak it to your taste, but it's still on record whose it came from.
terms.confusion: With "Use this template," the green button some projects show. A template gives you a clean copy, with none of the author's history; a fork drags the whole history along and stays linked to the original. To kick off your own project, a template is more convenient.

terms.short: A program that rearranges your code: indentation, spacing, and line breaks, all made consistent.
terms.long: It doesn't change what the code does, only how it looks, and it usually fires automatically on save. It sounds fussy and it's one of the most useful things there is when working with AI: if everything's written in the same format, a diff only shows what actually changed, instead of two hundred lines that just moved around. Watch the name, though — in Zapier the "Formatter" is something else entirely: a flow step that cleans up text and dates before writing them to a sheet.
terms.analogy: Word's justify-text button. The words are exactly the same, and it reads far better.
terms.confusion: With a linter. A formatter rearranges without asking and never complains; a linter touches nothing and warns you about problems. They almost always sit together in the editor and do completely different jobs.

terms.short: The exact shape you want the response in: how many parts, in what order, under what names, and how long.
terms.long: It's the single ingredient that saves you the most manual work, because it decides whether you can paste the result as-is or spend ten minutes trimming it. In the course you never ask for it in words ("keep it tidy") — you draw it. Write FORMAT in capitals and underneath sketch the empty response with the blanks between brackets, putting the limit right inside the blank, like [max 45 characters]. The rule: if you're the one reading it, ask for plain text or a table; if another program is going to read it, ask for JSON.
terms.analogy: A warehouse's pre-printed shipping form. You don't ask "log the order for me" — you hand over the paper with the boxes and have them filled in.
terms.confusion: With tone. Tone is how the response sounds; format is which pieces it carries and in what order. You can nail the tone perfectly and still spend the morning manually splitting up the text.

terms.short: A sheet of fields someone fills in that fires off your flow when submitted.
terms.long: It's the cleanest entry point there is, because you control the fields and the data always arrives in the same shape. In the course's leads project, the site's form sends what gets filled in to an n8n webhook (an internet address n8n gives you to receive notifications), and from there it gets cleaned, classified with AI, and logged. What surprises everyone the first time: a form simply dropped onto a page sends nothing anywhere on its own — you have to tell it where the data goes.
terms.analogy: A doctor's intake form. Everyone fills in the same boxes, which is exactly why the front desk can process it without calling you.
terms.confusion: With an email asking for the same thing. In an email, everyone writes whatever they want and you have to guess; in a form, you own the fields. If a flow keeps breaking on odd data, the input was almost always free text.

terms.short: The block of boxes and the submit button where people leave their information for you.
terms.long: What almost nobody tells you is that a form, by itself, sends nothing anywhere — it's a pretty drawer with no bottom. Someone has to collect what people write and deliver it to your email, a spreadsheet, or your CRM, and that's where the course's automations come in: the form fires, and n8n or Zapier do the rest. It also forces a legal decision that isn't optional: the moment you ask for a name and an email, you're processing personal data, so you need a consent checkbox and a link to the privacy policy.
terms.analogy: A bar's suggestion box. Hanging the box is the easy part — what you actually need is someone who opens it every day.
terms.confusion: With assuming the messages are already reaching you. It's the costliest mistake in this part of the course: you build the form, never test it by filling it in yourself, and discover three weeks later that not a single one has arrived. Send yourself a test before publishing, and another every time you touch the flow.

terms.short: A design tool where you build the site by dragging boxes and publish it without writing a line of code.
terms.long: It starts out looking like Figma, since you're dragging boxes, text, and photos onto a canvas, but it goes where Figma can't: once you like the design, you hit publish and there's a real internet address, with your own domain if you want. It's for sales pages, portfolios, and one- or few-page sites where looks are what matters. The decision it forces on you is where you're stuck: publish there, and your site lives inside Framer — moving it later means rebuilding it.
terms.analogy: A storefront that's already fitted out with rent included. Very convenient, until the day you want to take the furniture to a different street.
terms.confusion: With Figma. Figma draws the blueprint and stops there; Framer builds the house and rents it to you too. If all you need is to show what it'll look like, Figma is more than enough and you're not paying for hosting.

terms.short: A pre-built skeleton that gives you the project's structure so you just fill in the blanks.
terms.long: When you ask Lovable or v0 for a website and folders show up with names you never chose, that's the framework: React, Next.js, Astro. It saves you weeks in exchange for imposing its own way of doing things and its own idea of where every file goes. It matters to you for a very practical reason: when something breaks or you're about to publish, the first thing you have to tell the AI or the hosting service is which framework the project is built with, because the answer changes completely depending on it.
terms.analogy: A prefab house. The walls, wiring, and measurements are already set; you pick the furniture and the paint color, not where the bathroom goes.
terms.confusion: With a library. The distinction comes down to who calls whom: you call a library when you need it, and a framework calls you, because it's the one running the program's overall order. That's why swapping libraries is usually easy, and swapping frameworks means rebuilding almost everything.

terms.short: The part that's visible and the part working behind the scenes.
terms.long: The frontend is what gets painted in the browser: buttons, text, colors. The backend is what happens on a server: talking to the database, checking permissions, calling other APIs. The rule that prevents disasters: secret keys always live in the backend, because anything that reaches the browser can be read.
terms.analogy: A restaurant's dining room and its kitchen.
terms.confusion: Mixing one up with the other in terms of security. Putting a key in the frontend is writing it down on the menu.

terms.short: The exact place a piece of data comes from, with a link, so you can go check it yourself.
terms.long: The newspaper's name or the ministry's homepage doesn't count — it's the link to the specific page where the fact is stated, along with its date. You need this because with search enabled, fabrication comes disguised as a source, which is worse than having no source at all, because the link relaxes you and you stop checking. The course has a prompt that demands three things together for every claim: the literal sentence in quotes, the direct link, and that page's date, and if the model can't provide all three, it leaves the claim out entirely. And there's a step almost nobody takes: a link opening proves nothing, because the page can exist and simply not say what it told you it said.
terms.analogy: An invoice versus a "they definitely charged me for it." With the invoice in hand you check the date, the amount, and who issued it; without it, all you have is someone's word.
terms.confusion: With a direct quote. A quote is the sentence; a source is where it comes from. You can have a perfect quote hanging off a page that never contained it — and that's exactly the trap to watch for: open the link and search for the phrase inside with Ctrl+F.

terms.short: The list of what you will NOT be doing, written into the proposal before you start.
terms.long: It's the most important of the five sections a proposal carries, and the one almost nobody writes. The course's examples are very concrete: doesn't include connecting to their existing customer software, doesn't include replying to emails without a person reviewing them, doesn't include migrating the 2019 archive, doesn't include after-hours support. Write it before scope itself — it comes out faster, and it clarifies to you what you're actually selling. The rule is harsh and true: whatever you don't write down as excluded, you'll end up doing for free.
terms.analogy: In a bathroom renovation, if the quote doesn't say the door won't fit, the door ends up getting fit — and nobody pays for it.
terms.confusion: With looking distrustful. The classic mistake is staying quiet about the obvious to avoid a bad impression; then comes "while we're at it, might as well have it reply on its own" and that argument you always lose. A well-written out-of-scope list actually reassures the client, because it tells them exactly how far what they bought goes.

terms.short: Your or your clients' information ending up somewhere it shouldn't: published, at a third party, or in anyone's hands.
terms.long: In the course it has two faces. The cheap one: you accidentally push your .env file to GitHub with the key inside, and someone uses it to burn through your credit. The expensive one: you paste a spreadsheet with forty clients into an AI chat, and that data has already left your system even if the provider doesn't train on it. The decision has to be made beforehand, because what you never send can't leak — and if it's already happened, minutes count, which is why Marina rotated her key in five minutes and the breach cost her €0.00.
terms.analogy: Leaving your wallet open on a bar table. Nobody has to steal it — it's enough that someone just walks by.
terms.confusion: With an attack. Almost none of the breaches in this course are caused by an outsider: you cause it, uploading a file that shouldn't have gone up, pasting a client spreadsheet into a chat, or leaving a key in a shared document.

terms.short: A named chunk of code that does one task, called by that name whenever you need it.
terms.long: You write it once and use it twenty times, instead of repeating the same lines all over the project. You feed it data on one side and it hands back a result on the other, and the name should say what it does — see calculateVAT and you already know plenty. Where this really bites in the course is with fabrications: a model invents functions that don't exist inside libraries that do exist, and that failure is silent. The code reads perfectly, and then either crashes when run or, worse, quietly does something different from what you assumed.
terms.analogy: The "café con leche" button on a coffee machine. You press one and eight things happen inside that you don't have to know about.
terms.confusion: With a script. A script is the whole recipe, run start to finish; a function is one named step the recipe calls when it's needed.

terms.short: When the model, instead of answering you, asks for a specific tool to be run and waits for the result.
terms.long: It's the plumbing underneath almost everything interesting in the course: agents, MCP, n8n's agent node, and the moment ChatGPT searches the internet. What happens under the hood is the model returns a message saying "call lookup_order with number 4471," and stops there. The decision this hands you is the most important of all: since your own program is the one actually executing anything, the place where you draw the line on what's allowed to be touched lives on your side, not the model's.
terms.analogy: A waiter doesn't cook. They call out the order to the kitchen and wait to carry the finished dish back to you.
terms.confusion: With the model executing things on its own. It executes nothing — it only asks. Whoever decides whether that request gets fulfilled, with what permissions, and how many times, is the program around it. That's why "the agent deleted the database" is always, in reality, "someone gave it permission to delete."

terms.short: Turns your text into a fully designed presentation in a couple of minutes.
terms.long: You paste in a script, an outline, or even a long document, and it hands back the slides already built: titles, text laid out, images, and a coherent design you can swap entirely with one click. It runs in the browser, shares with a link, and exports to PowerPoint or PDF. The trap to avoid is the usual one: whatever blanks you leave, it'll fill with generic boilerplate, so the part only you know — the real numbers, the actual examples, the price — you write yourself before pasting anything in.
terms.analogy: A print shop that lays out your text on its own. The brochure comes out flawless; if the text says nothing, you get a flawless brochure that says nothing.
terms.confusion: With Canva. In Canva you start from a template and fill it in by hand, slide by slide; in Gamma you start from your text and it assembles it. If you've already written the content, Gamma saves you the whole afternoon.

terms.short: Google's AI assistant. It shines when you hand it huge documents or entire videos and ask about them.
terms.long: It has two faces worth keeping separate: the chat at gemini.google.com, for using it yourself by hand, and AI Studio, where you get the key so a program can call it on its own. In the course it's one of the four options in the lesson on choosing a model, and the text box you paste prompts into in several exercises. Its free plan is the most generous of the four and lives inside Gmail, Docs, and Drive. If you already work all day inside Google, that's the reason to pick it; if not, it doesn't offer anything special over the others.
terms.analogy: A lightning-fast intern who reads an entire tender document cover to cover while you're still making coffee.
terms.confusion: With Gemini CLI, which is a different thing: the version you install that edits files right in your folder, in the same family as Claude Code and Codex. The chat hands you text to paste yourself; the CLI writes directly to your disk.

terms.short: Asking an AI to draw an image from scratch that never existed, describing it in words.
terms.long: You write what should be visible and the tool hands back several proposals; you pick one and refine it. In the course you work with Midjourney, and the first thing you learn is to describe the way a photographer would: a specific subject, setting, light, framing, with adjectives last or dropped entirely. The decision it forces on you is what you're NOT going to ask it for: it can't write text and it can't draw your logo, so those get added afterward, in an editor.
terms.analogy: A blazing-fast, dirt-cheap illustrator who draws exactly what you describe, has never seen your shop, and can neither read nor write.
terms.confusion: With searching a stock photo site. There you pick from what already exists and know exactly what you're getting; here something new comes out every time, which is why you note down the seed to be able to reproduce a hit.

terms.short: Asking an AI to produce a few seconds of video from a description or a photo.
terms.long: In the course you do this with Higgsfield and Runway, always in shots of five to ten seconds, never asking for a whole video in one go. Each generation spends credits, so what's being asked for gets decided in advance, on the shot sheet: subject, movement, light, duration. The decision it forces on you is where you set the cap: how many attempts you allow yourself per shot before accepting the whole shot needs rethinking.
terms.analogy: Renting a camera operator by the hour who films exactly what you ask but has no idea what your business is about, and charges you the same when the take comes out wrong.
terms.confusion: With editing video you already have. There's no starting footage here — the image gets invented from nothing. Always check hands, written text, logos, and eyes — the four places it tends to break, and exactly where the human eye looks first.

terms.short: A program where you lock up all your keys, instead of leaving them loose in notes or documents.
terms.long: It comes up repeatedly in the course, always at the same moment: you've just created a key and the screen is only going to show it to you once. That's when you copy it into the manager, not Notepad, not an email to yourself. Chrome's own, Apple's Keychain, Bitwarden, or 1Password all work: any of them beats a shared Drive document infinitely. The decision that saves you money: when six people share the same key pasted into a Drive doc and the bill jumps from €40 to €380, nobody can tell who spent the extra €340.
terms.analogy: A hotel room safe. Annoying to open every time, and the only place your passport doesn't get left on the bed.
terms.confusion: With the browser remembering a site's password for you. That only stores logins; a manager also stores loose keys, tokens, and secret addresses — exactly what you'll be handling in this course.

terms.short: The method that means "I'm only going to look, not change anything."
terms.long: It's the one left set on your very first HTTP Request box in the course, the one that checks the dollar-to-euro exchange rate. A GET carries no data inside — it puts everything in the address itself, which is why you can paste that address straight into a browser and see the response before building anything in n8n. It's the fastest way to tell whether a problem is yours or the service's. Since it doesn't change anything on the other end, it's also the only one you can safely retry with your eyes closed.
terms.analogy: Window shopping. You can walk past a hundred times and the store stays exactly the same.
terms.confusion: The classic mistake is assuming a GET is always safe to share. A GET's address can carry your key or a client's email inside it, and those addresses stay written in logs and browser history. Never put personal data there.

terms.short: The system that saves your project's history and lets you go back.
terms.long: It's real undo — not for one file, for the entire project, with dates and explanations attached. It's also what makes working with AI without fear possible, because anything it breaks can just be reverted. Install it before starting anything, not after the first scare.
terms.analogy: A notebook where you log every state of the work and can flip back to any page.
terms.confusion: With GitHub. Git is the program on your computer; GitHub is a website where copies of Git-managed projects get stored.

terms.short: The website where projects managed with Git get stored and shared.
terms.long: Beyond storing copies, it's where changes get reviewed, tasks get tracked, and automated processes fire off every time someone pushes something. For a personal project, its most valuable function is simple: if your computer dies today, your work still exists.
terms.analogy: The cloud where the official copy of the notebook lives.
terms.confusion: With Git. You can use Git perfectly well without GitHub; you can't use GitHub without Git.

terms.short: GitHub's free robot that runs whatever you ask on one of their machines every time you push code.
terms.long: You give it instructions in a text file stored in .github/workflows, and GitHub reads that folder on its own, with nothing to switch on. The detail that throws everyone off: that machine starts empty every single time, so nothing you have installed on your laptop exists there, and it all has to be installed inside the file itself. Two lines you should always add: a minute limit, so a hung test doesn't chew through your quota, and read-only permission, so if someone sneaks in a third-party piece with malicious code, it can't rewrite your repository.
terms.analogy: An intern who borrows your GitHub. Shows up every morning remembering nothing from yesterday, does exactly what the note says, and leaves.
terms.confusion: With Git. Git keeps the change history; Actions is what runs when that history moves. You can use Git your whole life without ever touching Actions.

terms.short: An assistant that lives inside your code editor, completing in gray the lines you're typing.
terms.long: It installs as an add-on in Visual Studio Code and requires a GitHub account; the free plan gives about 2,000 suggestions a month, plenty for weeks of learning. In the course it's the fourth option in the lesson on choosing a model, and it plays a different game: you don't describe your idea to it, it accompanies you while you write. It's only worth it if you're going to spend real time inside a code editor; if your work is asking things in a chat, you don't need it.
terms.analogy: Your phone's predictive text, except instead of finishing a word it finishes twenty lines. And like your phone's, it's right a lot and wrong with the exact same confident face.
terms.confusion: With Copilot on its own, Microsoft's assistant in Windows, Word, and Excel. Same name, not the same thing: this one lives inside the code editor and is paid for with a GitHub account.

terms.short: A file listing what never gets uploaded to the internet, not even by accident.
terms.long: It's literally called .gitignore, dot in front, and sits loose in the project folder. Inside go filenames and folder names, one per line: your .env with its keys always goes there, along with node_modules, which is thousands of files that regenerate on their own. Here's the trap that catches almost everyone: uploading the key and then deleting it afterward doesn't help, because the history keeps the old snapshot and the key stays visible one click away, forever. If a key ever leaks, revoke it at the service before touching anything else.
terms.analogy: The note taped on moving boxes that says "this doesn't leave the house." Without the note, it goes on the truck with everything else.
terms.confusion: With deleting the file afterward. .gitignore stops it from being uploaded in the first place; deleting it once it's already up doesn't remove it from history. Order matters enormously: set up .gitignore first, then do your first push.

terms.short: Google's email. In the course it's almost always where data comes from or where the result ends up.
terms.long: It shows up in nearly every automation lesson: emails you care about landing row by row in a spreadsheet, the flow that reads the inbox, the node that drafts the reply. That's where one of the course's most important rules lives: in the Gmail node, if the flow is about to send AI-written text to an outside person, switch the operation from "Send" to "Create Draft." The draft waits for you in your own inbox, recipient already filled in, never actually sent. That decision gets made before the first send, not after the first disaster.
terms.analogy: A mailbox slot. What arrives just arrives; what you drop in doesn't come back, which is exactly why you check the envelope before letting go.
terms.confusion: With your Gmail account as your identity. Your email is one thing; the permissions you grant a flow over it are another. Connect Gmail to n8n or Make and that saved credential can read and write on your behalf until the day you revoke it.

terms.short: A Python notebook that opens in the browser and runs on Google's own computers, for free.
terms.long: You open a page, write chunks of code into boxes, and hit play: each box runs and shows the result right underneath, whether it's a number, text, or a chart. What matters for you is that you install nothing, and Google lends you a stretch of GPU time, the expensive piece that makes models run fast, so you can experiment without wrestling your own computer. What it forces you to decide: that machine shuts itself down after a while and erases whatever was on it, so anything you want to keep gets downloaded or saved to your Drive.
terms.analogy: A computer lab lent to you by the hour. The machines are excellent, and at nine the lights go off and every desktop gets wiped.
terms.confusion: With having Python installed on your own computer. Here the program runs on a Google machine, not yours: your files aren't there unless you upload them, and whatever you leave there isn't sitting at home.

terms.short: Google's hard drive on the internet. In the course it's where the AI pulls your documents from.
terms.long: It comes up in the connector and MCP lessons as the first thing almost everyone switches on: with it enabled you write "summarize the invoice amounts in the January 2026 folder and tell me which ones are over €3,000" and it takes forty seconds for what used to be twenty-five minutes of manual copying. Watch what you're actually turning on: a connector never brings a single loose capability, it brings a whole bundle, and Drive's includes search, read, create, and move. The last two touch your real files, so turn it on scoped to one folder and review before accepting any change.
terms.analogy: An office filing cabinet. Handing the AI the connector is handing over the key: it can browse folders and also pull things out and move them around.
terms.confusion: With uploading a loose file to the chat. Upload one and the AI sees that single file and nothing else; with the connector switched on, it sees the entire folder you've opened up to it, today and three months from now, without you ever uploading anything again.

terms.short: Google's spreadsheet: opens in the browser, saves itself, and a program can write to it.
terms.long: In the course you don't use it for math — you use it as a filing system: each row is a case and each column is one piece of data about it. An n8n flow adds rows without you having anything open, and you see them from your phone a minute later. For that to work, three rules can't be broken: headers in row 1, lowercase, no accents; no merged cells and no total rows; and columns never get reordered, ever, because the automated process finds them by their position. It's free with a Gmail account, and connecting it to an automated process costs nothing either.
terms.analogy: The notebook next to a shop's register. Perfect for jotting things down, disastrous the day three people write in it at once.
terms.confusion: With Excel. They look very similar, but for automation there's a difference that changes everything: Sheets lives online and a program can write to it while you sleep; the Excel file on your desktop can't.

terms.short: The graphics card: the piece that draws video games, and also what makes an AI model run fast.
terms.long: It only matters if you're going to run models on your own computer. On Windows you see it in Task Manager's Performance tab, under GPU, and what you need to check is its dedicated memory, not the computer's overall RAM. The difference is enormous: with a decent NVIDIA card, an 8B model writes at forty or fifty words a second and feels great; without a card, it's about five, and it drags on forever. Modern Macs don't have two separate memory pools but one shared one, which is why they perform surprisingly well without a discrete card; without either a GPU or a recent Mac, either download a smaller model or stick with the cloud.
terms.analogy: A pizzeria's oven versus your home oven. Your home one also makes pizza — what it can't do is make a hundred in one night.
terms.confusion: With the computer's RAM. If you have a dedicated card, its own memory is what's in charge: with 8 GB on the card, an 8B model flies; if it doesn't fit, the work spills over to the rest of the system and speed craters.

terms.short: Forcing the model to answer by looking at a real source instead of pulling from memory.
terms.long: It literally means "putting your feet on the ground," and it's the only real cure for making things up. It can mean searching the internet before answering, reading a PDF you've uploaded, or consulting your own documents. In the course you'll see it by name mostly in Gemini, as "grounding with Google Search." The practical decision you use every single day: a response with clickable links or the exact page cited is worth a thousand times more than the same response without them, and anything without a source doesn't go out to a client.
terms.analogy: An appraiser who actually visits the house before pricing it, instead of quoting a number over the phone from memory.
terms.confusion: With RAG. Grounding is the goal — the response resting on something real; RAG is one path to it, using your own documents. Searching Google is also grounding and isn't RAG. And watch out: resting on a source doesn't guarantee it was read correctly, so opening the link is still on you.

terms.short: A limit that stops a system from doing something it shouldn't.
terms.long: It can be a check before acting ("if the amount is over €500, a person has to approve it"), a closed list of allowed values, or a spending cap. You set these up before switching on anything that runs unattended, because the day you need them it'll already be too late to add them.
terms.analogy: A barrier on a mountain road. It doesn't drive for you — it keeps you from going off the edge.
terms.confusion: With an instruction in the prompt. Asking the model to behave isn't a limit — a limit is code that physically prevents the thing.

terms.short: n8n's screen and every tutorial write it in English, so that's the word you'll actually see.
terms.long: n8n's interface is in English, so in the HTTP Request box you'll find "Send Headers" and "Header Parameters," not a translated term. Each header is a pair: a name and a value, for instance Authorization paired with the word Bearer followed by your key. When you look up an API's documentation (the catalog of what a service lets you ask it for), the section you need is almost always called Headers or Authentication, and that's where the exact name is written. Copy it exactly, capitals and hyphens included — there's no margin here: x-api-key and X-API-Key aren't interchangeable for every service.
terms.analogy: The printed fields on an official form. If it says "Last Name" and you write in the "First Name" slot, it doesn't get processed.
terms.confusion: With a website's header, the banner at the top with the logo and menu, or a Word document's header. Same word, three different worlds. Here it's always metadata on a call between programs.

terms.short: Puts a digital presenter on screen reading your script, and also dubs videos into other languages.
terms.long: You pick an avatar from its catalog, or create one with your own face by recording a couple of minutes, paste in the text, and it hands back a video of someone talking to camera with lip movement synced. The other half of what it does is dubbing: upload your video in Spanish and get it back in English, with your own voice and your mouth moving correctly. It's used for training, product presentations, and social videos when you'd rather not be on camera yourself. And it comes with the usual decision in this category: a person's face and voice belong to them, and using them without written permission isn't a prank, it's a legal problem.
terms.analogy: A TV presenter hired by the hour who reads absolutely anything without complaint and never gets tired. They also don't understand a single word of what they're reading.
terms.confusion: With ElevenLabs. ElevenLabs gives you just the voice, to lay over your own footage; HeyGen gives you the whole person, talking to camera. If what you need is a voiceover, don't bother setting up an avatar.

terms.short: A site where you describe a video shot and it generates it, with you choosing the camera movement.
terms.long: What sets it apart from other video tools is exactly that: camera movement isn't left to chance, you pick it from a list the way you'd call a shot on a real set, and you can start from a photo of your own and set it in motion. It's for five- to ten-second pieces that get edited together afterward: short ads, product video, social content. It's not a production studio — it's a very fast camera operator that sometimes gets it wrong and has no idea what your brand is about. Before putting a shot into a client's work, check two things about your plan: whether it allows commercial use and whether it removes the watermark, because the free tier doesn't.
terms.analogy: A rented camera operator who delivers the take in thirty seconds, charges per take, and never read the script.
terms.confusion: With Runway. Higgsfield generates new shots with the movement you choose; Runway is built for fixing and extending video you already have. The question that separates them: am I starting from nothing, or starting from footage?

terms.short: The list of every save the project has had, newest to oldest, with a date and a note.
terms.long: Every save leaves a complete snapshot of the project, and none get erased when the next one happens. The history is that stack of snapshots, and what you'll actually be reading three weeks from now isn't the code — it's the list of your own notes. That's why writing "changed the button color to blue" instead of "Update index.html" decides whether your ability to go back is worth anything. Open it on GitHub by clicking above the file list, and from any point you can download the project exactly as it stood that day.
terms.analogy: A bank statement: every line with its date and description. If every description just says "payment," the statement is useless.
terms.confusion: With a backup. A backup stores how everything looks today; history stores how it looked every day along the way. A backup saves you from losing your hard drive; history saves you from a change that broke something two weeks ago that you never noticed.

terms.short: The list of every time your flow has fired, with its time and its outcome.
terms.long: It's the third area of n8n's screen, and almost everyone discovers it late, once something's already broken. It should be the other way around: it's the only one that shows you real data instead of configuration, and that's exactly why it's where you actually learn something. It has a real limitation that forces a decision: it's a list you have to go check yourself, and you're not going to check it every day. That's why the course also sets up a phone alert — a failure you find out about nine days later has already cost you money.
terms.analogy: A water meter's log. It records every time the tap opened, but if nobody reads it, the leak keeps running.
terms.confusion: With a log you build yourself in a spreadsheet. Execution history lives inside n8n and gets pruned; your own "Log" tab is under your control, readable without opening n8n, and it's what lets you answer a client in thirty seconds about what happened with their order.

terms.short: A table that opens in a browser or in Excel, saves itself, and the whole team understands.
terms.long: It's where almost every automation in the course starts: an incoming email lands as a row and you see it from your phone a minute later. It handles a few thousand rows fine; past that it gets sluggish, and with several automations writing at once they start stepping on each other. For a robot to use it there are three rules: headers in row 1, lowercase, no accents; no merged cells, no total rows; and columns never get reordered, ever.
terms.analogy: The notebook by a shop's register. Perfect day to day, disastrous the day three people write in it at once.
terms.confusion: With a database. A spreadsheet lets you put anything in any cell; a database stops you, and that friction is exactly what saves you once volume grows.

terms.short: The file where colors, font sizes, spacing, and borders live.
terms.long: It's called that because it separates appearance from content: what your page says lives in one place, how it looks lives in another. It's usually a file ending in .css, though in your very first website in the course it sits inside the file itself, between style tags. The advantage of keeping it separate is that changing one color there changes it across all twenty pages at once. And watch the exact filename: the errors lesson has a two-day story about lost time because the stylesheet got accidentally saved as styles.css.txt and the browser never loaded it.
terms.analogy: A letter's text versus the typeface it's printed in. Change the font and the letter still says exactly the same thing.
terms.confusion: With the page's content. If the stylesheet fails to load, your site doesn't vanish — it shows up in black and white, default font, everything stacked top to bottom. That's actually a great clue: if the content's all there, the problem is appearance, not structure.

terms.short: Mac's program installer. You type brew install and it downloads it and leaves it working.
terms.long: It shows up in the "what to install" lesson, always under the Mac tab: `brew install node@20` or `brew install python@3.12`. It doesn't come preinstalled — you set it up once from its website, and after that the `brew` command just works. The course deliberately trips you up on this in a quiz: Homebrew is Mac and Linux only, so on Windows the terminal will tell you it doesn't recognize "brew," and the equivalent there is `winget`. A two-second check that saves half an afternoon: before pasting a command, check whether the tutorial has a tab for your system.
terms.analogy: The neighborhood appliance store that delivers the appliance and installs it for you. You give them the name; they handle the cable and the outlet.
terms.confusion: With pip and npm. All three install things, but each in its own territory: brew installs programs for the whole computer, pip installs Python packages, npm installs Node pieces. Grab the wrong installer and the error will say it doesn't recognize the name you typed, not that you're in the wrong place.

terms.short: An action that fires on its own at a fixed point in a process.
terms.long: It gets defined once, and from then on it always happens, with nobody having to remember: before saving, after every change, when a task finishes. It's useful precisely because it doesn't depend on anyone's discipline.
terms.analogy: A door's automatic closer. Nobody has to remember to shut it.
terms.confusion: With a webhook. A hook fires inside your own tool; a webhook is a notification that goes out to another service.

terms.short: Renting the place where your website lives so anyone can see it, with power and maintenance included.
terms.long: In the course, the hosting you use is Vercel: it takes your project's files, assembles them, and publishes them at an address you can send over WhatsApp. What you're getting isn't just space — it's also the security padlock, the connected domain, and the button to roll back to yesterday's version.
