terms.short: The program you use to open webpages: Chrome, Edge, Firefox, or Safari.
terms.long: It's the window through which you enter almost everything in this course: ChatGPT, Claude, n8n in the cloud, GitHub, or your own website. It also opens things sitting on your own computer, not on the internet, like a site of yours in testing. Whenever a lesson tells you to open something, unless it says otherwise, this is where.
terms.analogy: The car that gets you to different addresses. The car isn't the city, just like the browser isn't the internet.
terms.confusion: With the internet. The browser is the tool; the internet is the network it takes you to. And with the search engine: Google is a page you open inside the browser, not the browser itself.

terms.short: A site where you publish your website by dragging a folder, no terminal, no card required.
terms.long: It's the shortcut in the "your first website" lesson: you go to the drag-a-folder page, drag in the folder containing your `index.html`, wait about twenty seconds, and you have an internet address you can send over WhatsApp. Before dragging, leave only that one file inside and clear out any numbered versions you saved along the way. On price: the free plan is enough as long as it's just you and a few friends, and the jump to paid runs around $20/month. Decision: drag-and-drop for showing off a test; connect it to GitHub for something you're going to change every week and let it publish itself.
terms.analogy: A photo booth at a train station. You walk in, drop your coins, walk out with the photo. Not a photo studio, but it'll do for the ID card.
terms.confusion: With having a domain. Netlify gives you an ugly address with random words and its own ending; the nice name gets bought separately and connected afterward. Publishing and having your own name are two separate steps, in that order.

terms.short: The number identifying a person or company to Spain's tax authority. Without it, an invoice doesn't count.
terms.long: It comes up two very different moments in the course. One practical: the n8n flow that reviews incoming invoices and pings Slack with the reason "Missing Tax ID" — exactly the kind of oversight that's costly and that a machine catches better than you would. One about privacy: a client's tax ID is personal data, so it never gets pasted into a free chat or left loose in a project file that later gets pushed online. If you're going to handle someone else's clients' tax IDs, you need their signed contract, not their verbal okay.
terms.analogy: It's the invoice's ID card. Without that number, the paper is a nice story that's worth nothing.
terms.confusion: With older business tax number formats people still mention out of habit. In Spain that separate designation went away years ago: individuals and companies all use the same tax ID system now.

terms.short: The folder where all of a JavaScript project's borrowed pieces get downloaded.
terms.long: It weighs somewhere between two and three hundred megabytes and holds tens of thousands of files you'll never open in your life. It never gets uploaded to the internet and regenerates entirely with an npm install, so deleting it is no tragedy. Here's the decision: if you go to push a project to GitHub and see thousands of files in the list, stop, write the line node_modules into .gitignore, and watch that list shrink to a few dozen.
terms.analogy: A shop's back storeroom. It takes up more space than the shop floor, nobody's shown it, and if it empties out, you restock it with an order.
terms.confusion: With your code. Your code is one-of-a-kind — lose it and it's gone; node_modules gets written by the machine on its own and always comes back identical. If it's missing when you unzip a project, that's normal, not a bug.

terms.short: The program that lets your computer understand website code without opening a browser.
terms.long: The `.js` tag is for JavaScript, the language almost every website is written in. For years only the browser, the program you view pages with, understood that language; you install Node on your own machine to run it without opening one. In the course it shows up in the "what to install" lesson and in the one about seeing your project actually running: it's what lets you have the site up on your own computer, seeing every change instantly, without publishing every test online. Decision: don't install it "just in case" — install it the day your project grows past a single loose page.
terms.analogy: An interpreter you hire to live at home. You used to have to go to the embassy for a translation; now you have one in your living room.
terms.confusion: With npm. Node is the engine that runs the code; npm is the parts store that comes in the same box. They install together, which is why many people think they're the same thing, but when an error mentions npm, the problem's in the parts, not the engine.

terms.short: Each box in an n8n flow. It does exactly one thing: read, filter, write, or notify.
terms.long: Open a node and you always see three columns: on the left, what arrived from the previous step; in the center, what you configure; on the right, what it returns. Learning n8n is looking at that right-hand column after running it and checking it carries what you expected, before building the next box. Chain six boxes without ever checking those columns and you end up with a flow you have no idea how to fix. And the decision is about scope: cram three steps into one node, and the day it fails you won't know which of the three broke.
terms.analogy: A station on an assembly line. It receives the part, performs one operation, and hands it to the next station.
terms.confusion: With the whole flow. The flow is the complete diagram, with its own name; a node is one single box inside it. When a tutorial says "add a node after the trigger," it means "put one more box to the right of the trigger and connect them with an arrow."

terms.short: n8n's all-purpose box: the one that calls any service without its own dedicated box.
terms.long: It's the first one you build in the course: click the roundest icon, type HTTP into the search, leave the method on GET, paste an address, and run it to see what comes back. It matters more than it looks like, because n8n ships pre-built boxes for Gmail or Slack, but for the rest of the world — your accounting firm's API, a local service nobody's integrated — this is the only door in. Its routine is always the same: method, address, header if you need to identify yourself, body if you're sending data, run, and read the right-hand column.
terms.analogy: A screwdriver with interchangeable bits. It's not the most comfortable option for any single screw, but it opens every one.
terms.confusion: With integration boxes (Gmail, Sheets, Slack). Those come with their fields pre-built and permissions sorted out; with HTTP Request you build it all by hand. If an integration box exists, use it — you'll get there faster with half the failures.

terms.short: The box that splits the flow into two paths based on a condition: yes on top, no underneath.
terms.long: Inside it you write a condition — the amount is over $500, the subject contains a word, the confidence the AI gave exceeds 0.7 — and n8n sends each item down one output or the other. In the course you use it as a validation gate: what looks fine follows the normal path, and anything doubtful gets diverted to a "Review" tab with an alert to your phone. And the decision is where to put it: always before the box that spends money or sends something to a client, never after.
terms.analogy: Airport security. Either you pass, or you get pulled aside to the other table. Nobody stays stuck in the middle.
terms.confusion: With the Switch node. IF only has two outputs: met or not met. Need to sort into three or more groups (urgent, normal, discarded)? Chaining IFs spirals out of control fast — what you actually wanted was a Switch.

terms.short: The box that tidies up data: renames fields, keeps only what you want, and fills in what's missing.
terms.long: In n8n you'll see it labeled "Edit Fields (Set)," the same box under two names, which is exactly why it's confusing to look for. It's for putting things in order between two steps: a service hands you back twenty fields with ugly names and you keep four, giving them your own names, or you add the date and the flow's name before writing the row to a log sheet. It does nothing outward-facing, which makes it low-risk: if something twisted ends up arriving, the Set node is where you fix it without touching the rest of the flow.
terms.analogy: The plating step. The food's already cooked — here you just decide what goes on the plate and how it's presented.
terms.confusion: With real transformation. Set positions, renames, and adds fixed fields or simple expressions (the formulas between double braces). It's not built for complex calculations or splitting lists apart. The moment what you want needs code, it stopped being a Set job.

terms.short: Like an IF, but with several outputs: it sorts each case down whichever path it belongs on.
terms.long: You give it a list of rules and each one gets its own arrow: orders over $1,000 this way, orders from outside the country that way, everything else through the default output. It's what you use once you've classified something with AI and want to handle each category differently: urgent to your phone, quotes to a sheet, everything else to a folder. The classic trap is forgetting the default output: an odd case ends up with nowhere to go, vanishes with no error, and nobody notices for months.
terms.analogy: A post office sorting station: one tray per region, and one last tray for whatever doesn't fit anywhere.
terms.confusion: With the IF node. IF is a yes-or-no gate; Switch is a fan of options. Catch yourself chaining three IFs one after another, and you were already overdue for a Switch.

terms.short: The set of boxes making up your flow, and also the catalog n8n offers you to build one.
terms.long: On the right of the screen sits the node panel, which is a search box: type "Gmail," "HTTP," or "IF" and the box shows up. Only three families matter: what starts the flow, what decides or arranges data, and what does something outward-facing (sending, writing, charging). The practical decision is how many to add and what to call them: four boxes with names in your own language get diagnosed in a minute; twenty called "HTTP Request1" never get diagnosed at all.
terms.analogy: A hardware store's display wall. It's all hanging up there, but for today's fix you grab four pieces, not forty.
terms.confusion: With community nodes. Official ones ship built-in and survive updates; community ones get uploaded by individual people and can stop working overnight. In your first flows, stick to the official ones.

terms.short: Keeping names, dates, and amounts in one consistent format so they can be compared.
terms.long: The course defines it this way: converting names, dates, amounts, or text into a stable format, right after checking no required field is missing. It's what makes "John Smith," "john smith," and "JOHN SMITH" count as the same person, and stops two different ways of writing the same date from counting as two different days. Without it you can't deduplicate or filter properly. It forces you to decide up front what your own house format is, regardless of what format the outside world sends things in.
terms.analogy: A video rental shelf: last name first, all caps. Doesn't matter how it's written on the box — it always gets shelved the same way.
terms.confusion: With data cleaning. Cleaning removes what's extra or broken; normalizing gives the same shape to what remains. They go together and in that order: clean first, then normalize.

terms.short: Getting every record into the same fields and the same shape, regardless of where it came from.
terms.long: A case coming in by email, another through a form, another via WhatsApp arrive with different field names and in no particular order. Normalizing converts them all to the same record before they move on, so the rest of the flow never has to know where each one came from. In the course's flows there's a box called Normalize and right after it another called Validate, and that order matters: first you give them all the same shape, only then do you check whether they're valid.
terms.analogy: Transferring whatever comes in by letter, phone, or in-person into the same form. From there, it doesn't matter who brought it.
terms.confusion: With validating. Normalizing changes the shape of the data without judging it; validating doesn't touch it, it just says whether it passes or not.

terms.short: A Google tool where you upload your documents and it only answers from what's inside them.
terms.long: You load PDFs, notes, and links, and from there it answers citing the exact page of your material instead of pulling from what it knows about the world generally. It's the zero-setup version of what the course calls RAG: asking AI about your own documents. Use it to study or prep for a meeting, but before uploading client data there, check what GDPR requires of you, because that's personal data sitting on someone else's server.
terms.analogy: A test-taker you've only handed your own study material to: they'll recite the chapter and tell you the page it's on, but won't tell you anything that isn't in those pages.
terms.confusion: With Gemini, also Google's. Gemini answers from everything; NotebookLM deliberately confines itself to what you've uploaded, and that limitation is exactly what makes its answer verifiable.

terms.short: The message a flow sends a person to tell them something it's done.
terms.long: An email, a Slack message, a phone alert. In n8n there's a checkbox almost nobody fills in, and it's the most important one on the settings screen: the error notification, set to "Notify me immediately." Skip it, and the day the flow breaks, you won't find out — and the worst part of an automation isn't that it fails, it's that it fails silently for three weeks. Separate the channels: routine notices, silent; failures, on a separate channel that's actually allowed to make noise.
terms.analogy: The alert that the package is out for delivery, versus the driver calling because they can't find your door. They can't sound the same.
terms.confusion: With an alert. A notification reports what happened, good or bad; an alert fires because something crossed a limit. Make everything notify the same way, and you'll stop checking and miss exactly what mattered.

terms.short: A shared online notebook where the team puts notes, tables, and documents, all in one place.
terms.long: It blends a text document with a data table: a page can carry a list with statuses and filters inside it, and everyone sees it instantly from the browser. In the course it shows up mostly from the other side, as one of the connectors ChatGPT and Claude offer to plug in so the AI can read what's in there. And that's exactly where the app-connecting lesson lands its point: every connector switched on is one more place to search, and with too many plugged in, the AI starts looking for something in Notion that was actually in Drive.
terms.analogy: An office corkboard, except it has drawers inside the cork itself. Everyone pins things there, and pin too much and nothing's visible anymore.
terms.confusion: With Obsidian. Both are for notes, but Notion belongs to a company and everyone shares it, while Obsidian is yours, on your own disk. A quick way to tell them apart: if "where's the document?" gets answered with a link, it's Notion.

terms.short: The package installer for JavaScript projects.
terms.long: With npm install you download everything a project needs, reading the list from the package.json file. It leaves two traces worth understanding: node_modules, the heavy folder that never gets uploaded, and package-lock.json, the ticket recording each piece's exact version, which does get uploaded.
terms.analogy: The errand runner who fetches every ingredient on the recipe.
terms.confusion: With npx. npx runs a tool without leaving it installed; npm installs it.

terms.short: A command that downloads a tool, runs it once, and doesn't leave it installed.
terms.long: It ships inside Node. It's for one-off jobs: you scaffold a website's skeleton with one command and never touch that particular tool again for months. Since it downloads fresh each time, you always run today's version, not one frozen a year ago on your disk. In the course it shows up when starting n8n and in GitHub Actions' publish step. Clean rule: use it once, use npx; use it every day, actually install it for real.
terms.analogy: Renting a cement mixer for the weekend. You use it, return it, and it never takes up garage space or gets old on you.
terms.confusion: With npm. They're spelled nearly identically, come in the same installer, and show up on the same documentation page, but they do opposite things: npm stores, npx runs. That's why npm always expects a command of its own after it, like install or run, not a tool's name.

terms.short: Someone else's computers, always on inside a data center, that you rent by the month instead of buying.
terms.long: In the course, "the cloud" comes up every time you choose between paying a fee or setting something up yourself: n8n in the cloud versus n8n on your own computer, your site on Vercel versus your site on a machine of your own. What you're buying isn't the computer — it's someone keeping it on, updated, and backed up. What you pay is a flat fee or usage-based billing, and what you give up is your data living somewhere you don't control. The practical decision is always the same: cloud to get started and for small clients, your own machine only once volume is high or the data can't leave the building.
terms.analogy: Renting a spot in a guarded parking garage instead of building your own. You pay monthly, but you're not the one fixing the gate.
terms.confusion: With plain internet. The internet is the road; the cloud is the warehouses along it that someone else maintains for you. A program can use the internet without being in the cloud: your computer requesting data from an API (the window one program uses to ask another for things) is exactly that.

terms.short: The value meaning "there's nothing here," set deliberately instead of making a value up.
terms.long: It means empty, nothing. It's the single most valuable instruction you can give a model that's extracting data from text: if a value isn't there, put null — don't infer it, don't fill it in, don't invent it. Skip that instruction and the model fills the gap with something plausible, you believe it, and that's exactly how a fabrication ends up saved in your database. In the course's tables you'll also see NOT NULL, its opposite: that field can never be left empty.
terms.analogy: A form field crossed out with a line. Not an oversight — it's a deliberate statement that there was nothing there, and that statement is worth as much as data.
terms.confusion: With zero, or with an empty string. Zero is a quantity, an empty string is text with no letters, and null is the absence of a value. An invoice for zero dollars and an invoice nobody's filled in aren't the same thing, and mixing them throws off any sum.

terms.short: An empty slot in a record: not a zero, but "there's no data here."
terms.long: It shows up when a column is allowed to stay unfilled. It's useful and treacherous, because calculations involving nulls don't crash — they return null, and on a dashboard that shows up as a blank cell nobody notices. In the course's metrics SQL you'll see a nullif wrapped around a division, a function that turns zero into empty precisely so the division doesn't blow up the day there are no cases yet. If a value is essential, declare it not-null and let the database stop you.
terms.analogy: An unfilled form field. Not the same as writing "$0" — one says we don't know, the other says there's nothing to charge.
terms.confusion: With zero and with an empty string. All three look almost identical on screen and behave differently: zero adds up, an empty string can be compared, and null spreads emptiness to anything it touches.

terms.short: A piece of data with labeled slots: every value comes attached to the name of what it is.
terms.long: It's how almost all information travels between programs. In JSON you recognize it by the curly braces: {"category": "invoice", "urgency": "high"}. When you ask a model to classify something, this is exactly what you need to demand back, with a specific line: respond with only the JSON object, no explanation, no code block. Wrap it in a friendly paragraph or code fencing and the next step in the flow breaks.
terms.analogy: A hand-filled client card: every field with its label on top and its content underneath.
terms.confusion: With an array. You ask an object for something by name ("give me the urgency"), an array by position ("give me the second one"). And an object isn't a database — it's how a piece of data travels, not where it's stored.

terms.short: Being able to see what a system is doing while it's running.
terms.long: It's three things: logs of what happened, alerts when something breaks, and a handful of numbers you check every day. You set it up the same day you switch something on, not after the first scare, because a system failing silently is worse than one that doesn't exist: people trust it.
terms.analogy: A car's dashboard. It doesn't drive, but it tells you you're about to run out of gas.
terms.confusion: With looking at results. Results tell you what came out; observability tells you why.

terms.short: A notes app that stores them as ordinary text files in a folder on your own computer.
terms.long: No account, no cloud, no subscription needed to use it: download it and start writing. Every note is a file, folders are drawers, links between notes are threads you follow from one card to another, and each card tells you on its own who's mentioned it. In the course it's where what you learn and what works for you ends up, and it has an advantage that's not just sentimental: if Obsidian shut down tomorrow, your notes would still be there, openable in Notepad.
terms.analogy: An old library's index card cabinet, with colored threads connecting one card to another. The cabinet could vanish; the cards stay yours.
terms.confusion: With Notion. Notion lives on the internet and your notes sit on their servers; Obsidian lives on your disk and works offline. If what matters is writing simultaneously with other people, Notion; if it's that nobody can ever take away what you've written, Obsidian.

terms.short: The trick that turns a photo of text into actual text you can copy and search.
terms.long: OCR stands for Optical Character Recognition. It's needed whenever a document is really an image: a scanned contract, an invoice that arrives as a photo, an old PDF. The two-second test for whether you need it: open the file and try selecting a word with your mouse — can't do it, and that's not text, it's a photograph. What you decide afterward isn't the tool, it's how much to trust it: OCR mangles digits when the paper's crooked, has a stamp over it, or is handwritten, so any number that comes out of it and ends up on an invoice gets eyeballed before use.
terms.analogy: A friend reading a handwritten letter aloud to you. They get almost everything right, but you'd better have them spell out the account number twice.
terms.confusion: With AI "reading" a PDF. Many models today look at the image and tell you what it says, which isn't the same as extracting the exact text — they can complete what's illegible because it fits the rest. If you need the literal figure off an invoice, you want extraction, not interpretation.

terms.short: A program that runs AI models inside your own computer, so what you write never leaves for the internet.
terms.long: It's completely free and needs no sign-up: download the program from ollama.com, download a model, and you're set. In the course it shows up in the "what to install" lesson and as the answer for when data can't leave the building. What you pay is electricity, disk gigabytes (a mid-size model takes up around 14 GB), and quality, because the answer will be worse than ChatGPT's or Claude's. You have to decide whether that trade-off is worth it, and it's only worth it when privacy or per-use cost outweighs getting it right the first time.
terms.analogy: Ordering delivery versus having your own kitchen. You don't pay per dish and nobody sees what you're cooking, but you're limited to what fits in your own kitchen.
terms.confusion: With Hugging Face. Hugging Face is the warehouse the models come from; Ollama is the program that puts them to work on your machine. One's the store, the other's the oven.

terms.short: The guided first steps that let someone new start using something without getting lost.
terms.long: It literally means "getting on board," and there are two in the course. Yours, with an initial test to see where you're starting from, a route chosen based on whether you're coming for the basics, the technical side, or the business angle, and a list of what to install before starting. And the client's, which is the first week after delivery: giving them access, the user manual, a short training session, and telling them who to call if something breaks. What you have to decide is how many hours of hand-holding are written into the price — leave it unwritten, and the hand-holding never ends.
terms.analogy: A first day at a new job: where the coffee is, which desk is yours, and who hands you the computer password.
terms.confusion: With training. Onboarding aims for the person to use the thing alone from day one; training aims to get everything out of it, and that's separate hours at a separate price. In the course, training shows up under out-of-scope with a clear cap — say, two hours included, and billed beyond that.

terms.short: Microsoft's folder that keeps copying your files to the internet as you save them.
terms.long: On most Windows machines today it's on by default: Desktop, Documents, and Pictures are already inside it without you doing anything. In the course it comes with a very specific warning in the "your first folder" lesson: your projects go outside it, at a path like `C:\projects\ceramics-website`. The reason is real and it shows: OneDrive touches files while a program is still writing to them, and a file can appear in the list without actually being downloaded, so whatever program tries to open it finds it empty. And yes, moving it out means you lose that backup, which is why you duplicate the folder by hand until GitHub takes over that job.
terms.analogy: A stockroom worker putting boxes away while you're still filling them. Great once you're done, chaos in the middle of the job.
terms.confusion: With a real backup. OneDrive copies a mistake just as fast as a success: delete or corrupt a file, and within seconds it's deleted or corrupted on every one of your devices. Getting back to how it was yesterday needs something else.

terms.short: The same thing as "código abierto" in Spanish, in English: literally "open source."
terms.long: "Source" means the source code, the text a programmer wrote before it became a program. You'll read it exactly like this on GitHub, on tool pages, and in any comparison, since nobody in the field translates it. Where you need to slow down is the license: an "open source" label on the front page doesn't tell you what you're allowed to do with it, and some very well-known projects let you use it in your business but not resell it as a service to others. If you're going to charge for something built on top, read the license before signing the proposal.
terms.analogy: The same thing under two names, like "parking lot" and "car park." And like a rented apartment, what you can do inside is set by the lease, not the sign out front.
terms.confusion: With being able to do whatever you want with it. Being able to look at the code and being able to sell it are different permissions, granted by the license, not the label. It's the difference between being able to walk through a house and being able to rent it out room by room.

terms.short: The company that makes ChatGPT, Codex, and the GPT models. Pay by usage, and the bill comes from them.
terms.long: In the course it shows up less as a brand and more as the source of an API key, the long password you give your program so it can talk to them. You'll use that key in n8n's AI node, in Make's module, and in any project that calls the model on its own. Here's one of the course's most expensive lessons: Rubén left his OpenAI key written inside a project file, pushed the folder to a public GitHub repo, and by Monday had $340 of usage that wasn't his. The decision is where you store that key, and the answer is always a .env file that git never uploads.
terms.analogy: The power company. You never see it, but it's what installs the meter and sends you the bill at the end of the month.
terms.confusion: With ChatGPT. ChatGPT is one of OpenAI's apps, not the whole company. And paying for ChatGPT Plus doesn't give you API credit — two separate registers, two prices that never touch.

terms.short: Coordinating several steps, tools, or models so they work together.
terms.long: It's the difference between one loose call to a model and an actual system: who does what, in what order, what happens if one part fails, and who finds out. Most professional AI work is this, not writing clever prompts.
terms.analogy: An orchestra conductor. Plays no instrument, and without them nothing plays in sync.
terms.confusion: With automating. Automating means something happens on its own; orchestrating means several things happen on their own, in the right order.

terms.short: The file that says what your project's called, what pieces it needs, and how it starts up.
terms.long: It's a handful of lines, and most of them make sense read slowly; you can open it with Notepad. Inside there's a section called scripts with the actual startup command, almost always npm run dev. It's the first place to check when you don't know how to launch a project the AI built you: instead of asking for general instructions, tell it to look at your package.json and report the command actually written there.
terms.analogy: A recipe card and shopping list on the same page: the dish's name, what's in it, and what oven temperature it goes in at.
terms.confusion: With package-lock.json. The first says what you need, and you edit it; the second records each piece's exact version down to the last digit, gets written by the machine, and never gets edited or deleted by hand.

terms.short: You pay once and it's done: covers building the thing, not what comes after.
terms.long: In the course's proposal it shows up as one line in the pricing table: setup as a one-time payment, $900, and right below it, monthly maintenance, $45. Those two lines together are the normal way to bill automation work — one to build it, one to keep it running. The costly mistake is charging only the one-time fee and then spending a year fielding calls for free, because the cheap project generates the exact same volume of support calls as the expensive one.
terms.analogy: Buying the boiler is the one-time payment. The annual checkup is a separate thing, requested and paid separately.
terms.confusion: With a fixed price. A one-time payment says how many times you pay; a fixed price says the number never moves. You can have a monthly fee that's also fixed, and you can have a one-time payment that balloons if the work grows.

terms.short: The four or five colors you use in a project, and none beyond that.
terms.long: It shows up two places in the course. When you ask the AI for a website, the request carries the palette as plain color names with their codes, never as adjectives. And when you generate several images meant to be seen together, the palette is part of the style recipe you paste identically into every request. The decision it forces on you is writing it once and locking it in: let the tool pick per piece and you end up with five results that don't look like they belong together.
terms.analogy: The four cans of paint you buy for the house. You don't choose the color wall by wall — you pick four and paint everything with those.
terms.confusion: With the whole style. The palette is just the colors; the style also covers lighting, photo type, and finish. And watch out: "a nice blue" isn't a palette — a written color code is.

terms.short: The screen with the four or five numbers you check every day to know if things are going well.
terms.long: In the course it gets built on a separate tab of the spreadsheet, never touching a single cell the robot fills in, because touching it breaks things. The test for whether a number deserves a spot there is simple: if it changing never changes a decision of yours, it's out. And watch out for overloading it, because every extra formula slows it down, and a dashboard that's slow to open stops getting checked by week two.
terms.analogy: A car's dashboard. Speed, fuel, temperature. Nobody wants to see every individual bolt's torque up there.
terms.confusion: With a report. A dashboard gets checked at a glance and is always current; a report gets read in full, happens occasionally, and explains the why. And watch the word: Supabase's or Vercel's admin screen is also called a "dashboard," and that one measures nothing.

terms.short: A piece of code someone else wrote that you download and add to your project instead of writing it yourself.
terms.long: Almost everything you install with npm is a package: a calendar, a date converter, a PDF reader. The course insists on a twenty-second check: before installing anything the AI suggested, search the exact name on npmjs.com. Models make up package names that don't exist, and there are people who register those exact fake names with malicious code inside, waiting for someone to install them blindly. That's why you always copy the name from official documentation, never from a forum comment.
terms.analogy: Buying puff pastry already made instead of kneading it. Fine to do, but you check the brand before it goes in the oven.
terms.confusion: With a dependency. It's the same thing seen from two sides: a package is the piece that exists out there; a dependency is that piece once your project no longer starts up without it.

terms.short: Deliberately switching an automation off without leaving cases half-finished.
terms.long: It's not the same as it crashing: here you decide, remove the trigger, the flow stops firing, and whatever was already in progress runs to completion. In the course it's taught as part of documentation: write down where the flow lives, what triggers it, which channel it notifies, and how to switch it off — so you remember six months from now, or so someone else can turn it off. It forces you to decide two things ahead of time: who's allowed to stop it, and what happens to cases still coming in while it's stopped.
terms.analogy: Closing up a shop: you pull the shutter so nobody new walks in, but you still help the people already inside.
terms.confusion: With an outage. In an outage nobody decided anything, and cases get lost without you noticing. A controlled stop is done by you, with notice given and a record of when and why.

terms.short: The slot a function leaves ready for you to pass a value into when you use it.
terms.long: When you write a function to calculate VAT, you don't stuff $100 directly inside it — you leave a slot called "base," and that slot is the parameter. You'll also see them in every call to a model, where parameters are the settings you pass: temperature, max tokens, the chosen model. It matters because a parameter is the difference between a piece that works once and one that works forever: hardcode the value inside the code and the demo works beautifully while the project is worth nothing.
terms.analogy: The boxes on a tax form. The form is identical for everyone; what changes is what you write inside each box.
terms.confusion: With a model's parameters, those "7B" numbers you see on Hugging Face. There the word means something completely different: those are the model's internal weights, used to measure its size and whether it fits on your computer — not to configure it.

terms.short: Taking a piece of text and pulling out its data in order, so the next step can use it without reading it.
terms.long: It means examining a text and separating out the specific fields you care about, always the same ones. You run into it the moment you ask a model to respond in JSON (a record with labels and values) inside an automation: the next step tries to parse that record, and if it can't, the whole flow stops. The course's classic failure is the model returning the JSON wrapped in code fencing with an explanation in front, which makes it unparseable. The decision is where you fix it: it works much better to tell the prompt to respond with only the record, nothing before or after, than to clean up the mess afterward with an extra step.
terms.analogy: Emptying the grocery bag and putting each thing in its place. If the store crams it all together with a flyer on top, a person can still manage; a machine chokes.
terms.confusion: With reading. Reading is understanding what it says; parsing is extracting the data into fixed fields. A person reads "I'll call you Tuesday" and knows the date; a program needs someone to have parsed that into a date field, or as far as it's concerned, that data doesn't exist.

terms.short: The package of data inside a notification when a service calls your flow.
terms.long: It literally means "useful cargo." When someone fills out your form, your webhook doesn't just receive "a notification" — it receives a payload with the name, email, and message, each field labeled. The first thing you do with it is look at it in full, in the box's right-hand column, because those exact field names are what you'll be writing into expressions later (the formulas between double braces that pull a value from the previous step). Skip that look and you'll spend half an hour fighting with a field that was actually called full_name, not name.
terms.analogy: The contents of the package, not the package itself. The delivery driver rings the bell; the payload is what's inside the box.
terms.confusion: With the body. Very similar, but used in opposite directions: a payload is usually what arrives to you, and a body is what you send out. In practice plenty of people mix them up and nothing terrible happens.

terms.short: The document format that looks the same on any screen; underneath it can be text or photos.
terms.long: PDF stands for Portable Document Format, and its whole point is looking identical on any computer and when printed. Underneath there are two very different kinds that look the same on screen: one carries real text you can copy a sentence from, and the other is a stack of photos of scanned pages. It's the format you'll work with most here, because your manuals, contracts, and invoices are all in it. And it takes up more space than it looks: a forty-page PDF eats around 30,000 of the tokens an AI counts, so uploading five to a chat fills the table before you've asked a single question.
terms.analogy: A photocopy versus a typed page. Both read equally well by eye, but only one lets you search for a word.
terms.confusion: With a Word document. A PDF is built to not be touched: you view it, print it, sign it — but editing it is always a fight. If something's going to keep changing, keep it in its original format and only export the PDF at the very end.

terms.short: Requiring it to say where every fact came from, with a link or document, instead of just stating it.
terms.long: It goes in the prompt as one more rule: every figure, date, name, or legal reference comes with where it's from, and if there isn't one, it says so. You'll need this the moment a value leaves the chat and ends up on your website, on an invoice, or in an email to a client — exactly where the course teaches you to hit the brakes. And there's a step almost nobody takes: opening the link and searching the text with Ctrl+F. A page existing doesn't prove it says what's being claimed, and with web search enabled, fabrication comes disguised as a source, which is worse, because the link relaxes you.
terms.analogy: Asking for the receipt instead of trusting the price the clerk calls out. Receipt in hand, you can go check it at the register. Without it, all you have is their word.
terms.confusion: With having the fact already verified. Handing you a source verifies nothing: the source might not exist, might exist and not say that, or might be a page from two years ago. Asking for sources saves you the work of finding where to check — checking is still on you.

terms.short: Giving each program only exactly what its task needs, and not one thing more.
terms.long: It's the golden rule whenever you connect an AI or a flow to your accounts. If the script only needs to read your email subjects, request read access and labels — don't hand it "send on your behalf" or "permanently delete" for convenience, because someday it'll get used. In the course you apply this on Google's permissions screen and when setting up n8n credentials. The practical rule: always start read-only, because a read mistake fixes itself in ten seconds and a write mistake sometimes never does.
terms.analogy: The key you leave with the gas meter reader. It opens the entryway and the meter room, not your whole apartment.
terms.confusion: With distrusting the tool. That's not what this is about. Excess permission hurts on the day the tool malfunctions, someone copies the access, or an email arrives with hidden instructions that the tool is about to read.

terms.short: An AI search engine: it answers your question in a paragraph and lists the links each fact came from underneath.
terms.long: The difference from a normal chat is that it doesn't answer from memory: it searches the internet first and shows numbered sources next to each sentence. That makes it useful exactly where the course keeps telling you to ask for sources: prices that change seasonally, regulations, industry data. The decision doesn't change because of that: open the links and check they actually say what it summarized, because sometimes the source exists and doesn't say that.
terms.analogy: An intern who brings you the summary with the photocopies stapled behind it. You still have to check the photocopies.
terms.confusion: With a normal search engine. Google gives you a list of links and you do the searching; Perplexity gives you the answer already written, with links as backup. It's more convenient, which is exactly why people trust it without opening a single one.

terms.short: A call from your flow to another service over the internet, with a response coming back.
terms.long: Every request has four parts: the method (what you're doing), the address (who you're calling), the header (who you are), and the body (what you're sending). The response that comes back carries a number that sums it all up: 200 went fine, 401 you haven't identified yourself, 403 you've identified yourself but lack permission, 429 you're going too fast, 500 the failure is on the other end. That number is the first thing you check when a box turns red, because it tells you whether the fix is yours or you just need to wait and retry.
terms.analogy: Calling a company on the phone. You dial a number, say who you are, ask for something, and get an answer — even if it's a no.
terms.confusion: With the API. The API is the catalog of everything that service lets you ask for; a request is one specific call from that catalog. When someone says "I ran out of API," they almost always mean their requests aren't going through anymore.

terms.short: The add-on that teaches Postgres to store vectors and search by meaning.
terms.long: You switch it on with one line, "create extension vector," and from then on your ordinary database can also answer questions from your own documents. In the course you use it inside Supabase, which includes it even on the free plan. The advantage of doing this here instead of in a separate vector service is that permissions live in the same tables as the documents: filtering by area and sorting by similarity is a single query. With two separate systems you'd have to sync them by hand, and that's exactly where information leaks sneak in.
terms.analogy: Adding one more shelf to the bookcase you already have at home, instead of buying a whole new piece of furniture for three books.
terms.confusion: With a dedicated vector database, like Pinecone or Qdrant. Those are a separate service you have to maintain and keep in sync; pgvector is your regular Postgres with one more capability. If you're already using Postgres, you don't need the other.

terms.short: Any piece of data that lets you identify a specific person.
terms.long: Name, email, phone, address, ID number — but also combinations that together point to someone. If you handle this in Europe, GDPR applies to you, and the three practical rules are: ask only for what you need, don't route it through services that don't require it, and don't leave it written in searchable places, like a team chat.
terms.analogy: Someone else's wallet. You're carrying it, but it's not yours.
terms.confusion: With confidential business data. Personal data also has an owner and rights attached: they can ask you to delete it.

terms.short: A small version with an end date, to test with real data before committing to everything.
terms.long: It's the step between a demo and building the whole system, and in the course it comes with three things written down before it starts: how long it runs, over which slice of the work (a hundred of their real emails, not the full 420), and what number decides whether to continue or stop. That number gets agreed beforehand or never agreed at all: leave it for the end, and whoever talks loudest in the meeting makes the call. A pilot is also for getting to know each other: if a client won't let you see their data but demands guarantees, you find that out over $300 instead of $3,000.
terms.analogy: A bar trying out a new dish for two weeks, Thursdays only, before putting it on the printed menu.
terms.confusion: With a free trial. A pilot is billed, even if it's a small amount: in the course, the entry point is an audit around $300 with a report of hours and costs. What's given away for free, nobody prioritizes — not the client, not you.

terms.short: Python's package installer. You type pip install and it downloads whatever piece the project's missing.
terms.long: You'll see it in every project in the course: `pip install pytest pytest-cov` to be able to run tests, and `pip install -r requirements.txt` to install everything a project needs in one go when someone downloads it. A golden rule half the class skips: activate the project's virtual environment first. Install without activating it and the packages go into the whole computer's Python install, and the day you generate requirements.txt you'll freeze half your system into that list instead of just your project's four things.
terms.analogy: An order to a supplier. You ask by name and the box arrives; what matters is which warehouse you unload it into.
terms.confusion: With brew and npm, which also install things but each in its own world. And there's a second trap inside pip itself: depending on the computer, the command might be `pip`, `pip3`, or `python -m pip`, and if it says it doesn't recognize one, try the other two before giving up.

terms.short: Another automation site like Zapier or Make, built for people who don't mind writing a bit of code.
terms.long: It works the same way as the others (something happens, tasks get done), with the difference that between steps you can write a few lines to transform the data your way. That's what makes it powerful, and it's exactly why it's left out of this course: here we work with Make, Zapier, and n8n, all manageable with no code written. If someone recommends it to you, the question to ask yourself is whether you'll be able to maintain that piece of code six months from now. If the answer's no, stick with the others.
terms.analogy: A kitchen with an induction cooktop and also an open flame. You can do more, but you have to trust your own hand.
terms.confusion: With n8n, which also lets you insert code. The practical difference is where each one lives: n8n you can install on a computer of your own; Pipedream always runs on theirs, so there you don't choose where your data ends up.

terms.short: The chain of automatic steps your change travels through from being pushed to being live.
terms.long: It literally means "tubería": a pipe. It's the umbrella term: installing dependencies (other people's pieces your project needs), running tests, building the project, and deploying, in that order, each step waiting on the one before. If a step fails, the pipeline breaks right there and nothing after it even gets attempted — which is exactly what you want. In the course your first pipeline has two jobs, "tests" and "deploy," and the second only fires if the first finishes clean.
terms.analogy: A supermarket checkout belt. Something jams at the scanner, and nothing behind it moves forward.
terms.confusion: With an n8n flow. An n8n flow moves your business data (emails, leads, invoices); a pipeline moves your code from your computer to the internet. They look similar on the diagram, not in what they're for.

terms.short: A template's blank slot. Literally "the thing holding the spot."
terms.long: It's the English word for what the course calls a "hueco": the part of a prompt that changes each use and that you mark between brackets. You'll read it this way in Claude's and ChatGPT's documentation and in any template you download online. A well-named placeholder fills in in ten seconds; a badly named one, like [X], forces you to reread the whole prompt to remember what went there. The decision: what's a placeholder and what's fixed text. Anything that'll be identical next week, leave written out.
terms.analogy: The dotted line on a mail-in form. The paper's already printed; that line is the only spot where you write.
terms.confusion: With a programming variable. You fill in a placeholder yourself, by hand, copying and pasting; a variable gets filled in by a machine automatically. The same word gets used for both, which is exactly why it's confusing.

terms.short: The minimum unit of video: one continuous scene with duration, framing, and movement.
terms.long: With AI video, it's better to think in short shots rather than whole videos in one go. Each shot should specify what's visible, how long it lasts, what the camera does, what changes, and how it gets reviewed. Seedance, Runway, or Higgsfield can produce powerful individual shots, but professional video comes from stitching together shots that carry intent and continuity.
terms.analogy: A sentence within a text: it can stand fine on its own, but what matters is how it fits with the one before and after.
terms.confusion: With a scene. A scene can contain several shots; a shot is the continuous piece you generate or edit.

terms.short: An already-written, saved request with blanks to fill in, that you reuse without rethinking it.
terms.long: It has two parts: what always stays the same (who the AI is, your tone, your format, what it must never do) and the blanks that change every time. In the "save your prompts" lesson you build yours and keep it in a text file, not inside the chat, because the chat closes and the file doesn't. The decision is how many blanks to leave: two to five works well; hit twelve and you've written a form, and filling it in will tire you out more than starting from scratch.
terms.analogy: A lease agreement. The body hasn't changed in twenty years, and by hand you only fill in the name, the unit, the date, and the amount.
terms.confusion: With a chat that turned out well and you bookmark. That's good for one specific case; a template is built beforehand to work for every similar case, which is why it separates what's fixed from what changes.

terms.short: A flow someone else already built that you copy and adapt instead of building from scratch.
terms.long: In the course you find them in two places: the four in this portal's n8n guide (email drafts, WhatsApp, website monitor, and failure alerts) and n8n.io's public library, where people upload their own. You use one before building anything: search two or three words describing your process in English, open a couple of similar-looking ones, and see how someone else solved it. None of them works as-is, because every template ships with blanks only you can fill: the credentials, meaning the permissions to access your accounts, and your own business details. The decision is honest and simple: if you don't understand what each box does, don't turn it on.
terms.analogy: A recipe from a cookbook. It gives you the order and the amounts, but it's your own oven, and you end up eyeballing the salt.
terms.confusion: With a finished flow. A template is deliberately half-done: it's missing your accounts, your filters, your text. Paste it in and switch it on without touching anything, and it either doesn't start or starts doing something you never wanted.

terms.short: A robot that opens your website on its own, clicks buttons like a person would, and reports if something stopped working.
terms.long: It literally means "playwright," as in a dramatist. You write the journey once (open the page, type this email, hit send, check the thank-you message appears) and from then on it repeats that whole thing in seconds every time you touch the project. In the course it shows up in the quality and auto-publish section: tests pass green, it publishes; one fails, it doesn't. What it forces you to decide is which two or three journeys can never be allowed to break, because writing them all out is something nobody actually does.
terms.analogy: A mystery shopper who walks into your store every morning, always makes the exact same purchase, and calls you if the register doesn't work.
terms.confusion: With testing it yourself by hand. You test it once, with judgment; this tests it a thousand times, identically, and only checks what you asked it to. Whatever Playwright doesn't look at, nobody looks at, and that's exactly where bugs sneak in.

terms.short: How long you keep each piece of data before deleting it. It's your decision, and it has to be written down.
terms.long: In the course it comes up in the operations kit with a line worth remembering: a log that grows forever is a liability, not a virtue. Every case that passes through your flow leaves behind a row of someone's data, and those rows pile up on their own while you're not looking. You set a period per data type (closed cases six months, emails a year, whatever's reasonable for your purpose) and note it in your record of processing activities. The practical rule: if you can't automate the deletion, set a calendar reminder and do it by hand, because "just in case" isn't a retention period.
terms.analogy: Invoices in a drawer. The ones the tax authority requires, you keep for the required years; 2019 supermarket receipts, nobody with any sense keeps.
terms.confusion: With storage space. You're not deleting because it doesn't fit — you're deleting because you no longer have a reason to keep it. And the more you keep, the bigger the mess the day there's a breach.

terms.short: The page explaining what data you collect, why, who sees it, and how to request or delete it.
terms.long: In the course it comes up when publishing any website or form, and the mistake you'll see on the quiz is always the same: linking the site's general policy and assuming that's enough. That policy was written before your new form existed, so if it doesn't mention text being sent to an outside provider for classification, it doesn't cover it. It has to state five things: what the text is used for, how long it's kept, which providers see it, who's responsible for that data, and how to request review or deletion. The rule: it gets updated every time you add a new tool to the flow, not once a year.
terms.analogy: A product's ingredient label. Change the recipe and not the label, and the label becomes a lie.
terms.confusion: With the legal notice. A privacy policy discusses people's data; a legal notice states who you are, with name, tax ID, and contact info. Two separate pages, and Spain requires both.

terms.short: The rules a company sets for itself about which tools to use and with what data.
terms.long: It's not the law — it's what your client or your company decided on their own, and it's almost always stricter than the law. Which AI tools are approved, what can be pasted into a chat, who signs a license. In the course you run into this the day you go to install Docker on a work laptop, because past a certain company size, that license gets signed by someone else, not you — you ask beforehand, not after installing it. And if your delivery depends on internal approval from someone, write that down as a pending blocker instead of just crossing your fingers.
terms.analogy: A building's HOA rules. The law lets you have a dog; the HOA can decide it has to be carried in the elevator.
terms.confusion: With GDPR and laws in general. The law applies to you no matter where you are; internal policy changes from client to client. And breaking it doesn't end in a fine — it ends with you off the project.

terms.short: Going and checking every few minutes for updates, because the other service doesn't notify you.
terms.long: Gmail doesn't call you when an email arrives, so n8n has to go check: that's why a flow watching your inbox can take up to ten minutes to react, while a form that actually notifies you fires off the Slack message in three seconds. The decision is the interval: check too often and you burn calls on empty results, check too rarely and you're late. If the service offers a webhook, polling is unnecessary.
terms.analogy: Peeking out at the balcony every five minutes to see if the delivery's arrived, instead of them ringing the buzzer.
terms.confusion: With a webhook. They're two sides of the same coin: with polling, you ask and arrive late; with a webhook, they call you and it's instant. When someone complains "the automation is slow," it's almost always on polling, and the interval is the culprit.

terms.short: The disposable memory where whatever you just copied sits.
terms.long: Hit copy, and what you copied doesn't get saved to any file — it sits in the clipboard, a temporary spot managed by your system. Paste, and you retrieve it. Copy something else, and the previous thing disappears. That's why, if you copy a long prompt and then copy something else before pasting it, it's gone, and you have to go get it again.
terms.analogy: The tray you use to carry a plate from the counter to the table. Only one fits, and the next one bumps the previous one off.
terms.confusion: With saving a file. Copying doesn't save anything anywhere permanent: turn off the computer and the clipboard goes with it.

terms.short: A folder with three or four of your works, presentable, that prove what you can actually do.
terms.long: The course's minimum portfolio is three pieces: an n8n flow, a prompt-based assistant or system, and a code or documentation project. Each with its README, its screenshots, its risks, and a rehearsed explanation in case you're asked about it. It doesn't need to be large — it needs to be legible, honest, and defensible, because eight mediocre pieces bury the two good ones. And there's a serious warning: everything shown gets anonymized. A real client name in your portfolio is a complaint waiting to happen.
terms.analogy: The folder a photographer brings to an interview: twenty chosen photos, not the three thousand sitting on their hard drive.
terms.confusion: With a resume. A resume says where you've been and for how long; a portfolio shows what comes out of your hands and holds up to being asked how you did it and what went wrong. In this trade, the second matters far more than the first.

terms.short: The method meaning "I'm sending you something for you to create or process."
terms.long: It's what flows use for actual work: creating a contact in the CRM (the program storing your clients), adding a row in Airtable, sending text to the AI to classify. Data goes in the body, and who you are goes in the header. And it's the method that forces the most important retry decision: repeating a POST can create the same contact twice, or charge the same $34.90 twice. Before switching on automatic retries on a POST box, check what happens if it runs twice in a row.
terms.analogy: Dropping a letter in a mailbox. Drop it twice and two letters arrive, with no way to pull the first one back out.
terms.confusion: With GET. GET looks and leaves no trace on the other end; POST changes something. Use GET where POST was needed, and usually nothing happens — the service politely returns an error; do it the other way around, and something can actually happen, and it doesn't always undo itself.

terms.short: The serious, free database engine sitting underneath almost everything you build in this course.
terms.long: Its full name is PostgreSQL, and nobody says it that way — everyone just says Postgres. It handles millions of rows and several things writing at once without stepping on each other, it's been running for thirty years, and it costs nothing — what you pay for is the computer it lives on. In the course you never install it — you use it through Supabase, which is Postgres with a dashboard on top. With an add-on called pgvector it also stores vectors, the lists of numbers used to search by meaning: ask for shipping complaints and it pulls up "the package arrived three days late," where the word "shipping" never even appears.
terms.analogy: A car's engine. Almost nobody buys a loose engine, and yet everyone ends up driving one.
terms.confusion: With having to install it yourself on your computer. In the course you never install it — it comes already set up inside Supabase or n8n. You only go looking at the engine directly the day you want to switch providers and take the data with you.

terms.short: The free, serious database this course uses. Everyone just calls it "Postgres."
terms.long: You don't install it — in the course you use it through Supabase, which underneath is Postgres with a web dashboard and a SQL editor on top. It handles millions of rows and several things writing at once, and with the pgvector add-on it also stores vectors, the lists of numbers representing a text's meaning. The decision isn't whether it's good, it's when you need it: under a few thousand rows, with one thing writing, a spreadsheet does the job.
terms.analogy: A warehouse with numbered shelves and a supervisor inside. Overkill for four boxes, indispensable once trucks start showing up.
terms.confusion: With Supabase. Supabase is the service that serves it to you already set up, with accounts and a dashboard; Postgres is the engine underneath, and you can take that same engine somewhere else if you ever move.

terms.short: Microsoft's presentation program. Files are .pptx, and some skills can build them on their own.
terms.long: In the course it shows up in the skills chapter, because Anthropic publishes ready-made skills for PowerPoint, Excel, Word, and PDF: hand it the content and it returns a finished `.pptx` file, slides and all. It's the clearest example of what a skill is for — not having to explain, every single time, how to do something you always do the same way. The decision stays yours and never gets delegated: what gets said, in what order, and what's left out. What you delegate is the assembly, the boring part that eats all the hours.
terms.analogy: The neighborhood print shop. You bring the text and decide what goes on each page; they handle the paper, the staple, and the finish.
terms.confusion: With asking a chat "make me a presentation." A chat hands you text with slide titles you then copy one by one; the skill hands you the finished file. The difference isn't the quality of the text — it's who does the manual assembly.

terms.short: Windows's terminal: the window where you type commands instead of clicking.
terms.long: Search "PowerShell" in the Start menu and a blue window opens. It's where the course has you install Claude Code, start n8n with Docker, and generate a long random key. There's a trick that saves headaches from day one: open your project's folder in File Explorer, click the address bar at the top, delete what's written there, type `powershell`, and hit Enter — it opens already sitting in that folder, saving you from navigating blind. On Mac and Linux the equivalent program is called Terminal, and quite a few commands differ between them.
terms.analogy: The counter at an old-school hardware store. No shelves to browse — you say exactly what you want and they hand it to you.
terms.confusion: With Command Prompt, the classic black window called cmd. They look similar but don't understand the same commands. Rule of thumb: when a tutorial says "open the terminal" and you're on Windows, open PowerShell.

terms.short: A set figure agreed before starting, that doesn't move even if the work takes more hours than planned.
terms.long: In the course you only go fixed-price when you can write in one line what you're delivering; if you can't, it's an hours pool or an entry audit — never a fixed price with your fingers crossed. It's also used for maintenance: delivery includes thirty days of adjustments, and after that there's a monthly checkup billed at a fixed price. What it forces you to do is have your out-of-scope list written down, because at a fixed price, you alone absorb the risk of the work growing.
terms.analogy: A prix-fixe menu: you know what you'll pay before you sit down, and if the fish got expensive for the restaurant today, that's their problem.
terms.confusion: With an hours pool. A pool gets used when there's exploration to do and you don't yet know what you'll find, and there the risk falls on the client. "I want to automate customer service" is an hours-pool job disguised as a fixed price, and that's where money gets lost.

terms.short: The figure you give a client for a job, along with what it includes and how long it stays valid.
terms.long: In the course's running example, the quote is two lines: $900 for setup and $45/month for maintenance, with a three-week timeline and thirty days of validity. That expiration date isn't decoration — without it, someone comes back demanding the same price eight months later. Before writing the figure, you need to have already decided whether you're going fixed-price or hours-pool, and that comes down to one thing: can you say in one line what you're delivering.
terms.analogy: A repair shop's estimate: one number, what it includes, the timeline, and a date after which it's no longer valid.
terms.confusion: With a spending cap set on an AI platform to avoid overcharges. Different things: one is what you charge, the other is a cap on what you pay. And watch out — the second often only warns you and doesn't actually cut anything off.

terms.short: A test copy of your website with its own address, for showing off and breaking without touching the public version.
terms.long: On Vercel it creates itself: you push a branch (a parallel path where you test changes without touching the good one) and a comment appears on GitHub with a link like myapp-git-branchname-yourusername.vercel.app. It's what you send a client to get feedback before it exists for the world. Two things always trip people up: if you marked a variable for Production only, the preview breaks; and if the link asks your client to log in, you need to remove that deployment's protection.
terms.analogy: A dress fitting before the wedding. Same outfit, but it can still be changed and nobody's seen it yet.
terms.confusion: With the live preview Lovable or Claude show you while writing code. That's only visible inside the tool; Vercel's Preview is a real internet address you can send over WhatsApp.

terms.short: A very tight framing, where a face or object fills almost the entire screen.
terms.long: It's the shot with the most impact, and the one that gives AI-generated video the most trouble, because getting closer reveals details, and that's exactly where it breaks: hands, fingers, eyes, letters. In the course it comes up as a warning when planning an ad: if your shot has hands in close-up, better to rethink it before spending credits. The decision it forces on you is either framing tighter or wider so whatever tends to break just doesn't end up on screen.
terms.analogy: Getting very close to a painting done in broad brushstrokes. From far away it's a portrait; up close it's four smudges.
terms.confusion: With "shot" on its own, the video unit, the continuous five-to-ten-second piece. A close-up isn't a piece of video — it's how near the camera is within that piece.

terms.short: Turning something you custom-build every time into a fixed package with a name, price, and set contents.
terms.long: It's the idea holding up the course's entire business module. Instead of improvising over the phone what your work includes, you have a service sheet with a name, what's included, what's not included, timeline, price, and what the client has to provide. Underneath it works the same way: figures in a single file, a recorded demo, and a proposal that generates itself from those figures. What you have to decide is what you stop doing, because a package that accepts any request quietly turns back, a month later, into a custom job billed at package price.
terms.analogy: A restaurant's set menu versus cooking whatever each table asks for: same kitchen, far less chaos, and better margins.
terms.confusion: With selling software. Productizing isn't about having software — it's your service being explained, quoted, and delivered the same way the twentieth time as the first. The classic mistake is putting a nice price on the website and still accepting changes that aren't on the sheet.

terms.short: The request you write to a model.
terms.long: A prompt that works isn't longer or full of magic formulas: it says who you are, what you want, with what data, in what format, and what it shouldn't do. The single change that improves results the most is dropping "write something about X" and instead asking for the concrete result with its limits stated.
terms.analogy: A brief to a professional. The clearer it is, the fewer rounds of revisions.
terms.confusion: With the system prompt. Yours changes with every message; the system prompt is the fixed instruction that always comes first.

terms.short: One that can be read two ways, and both are reasonable. The AI picks one and doesn't tell you.
terms.long: "Summarize the report for tomorrow" could mean tomorrow's report, or a summary for you to read tomorrow. You have the answer in your head; the machine only has the sentence. The memory lesson has a fix that always works: close the message with "if anything is ambiguous or you're missing information, ask me now." The decision: answer three questions now, or find out half an hour later that it understood something else and throw the work away.
terms.analogy: Sending someone for "the usual bread" when the neighborhood has two bakeries you always go to. They come back with bread — just not yours.
terms.confusion: With a vague prompt. An ambiguous one states something concrete that admits two readings; a vague one never gets around to saying anything concrete. Ambiguous gets fixed by clarifying one word; vague has to be rewritten entirely.

terms.short: The fixed instruction set for the model before any message.
terms.long: It defines the role, the tone, the language, and the limits, and applies to the whole conversation without repeating it. It's where whatever must never change goes; specific data goes in the message, not here. Never paste text from outside sources in here — this is exactly the door prompt injection walks through.
terms.analogy: A job's operating manual, versus the day's specific task.
terms.confusion: With the first message. The first message fades back as the conversation grows; the system prompt stays up front always.

terms.short: A request several paragraphs long. Not a problem in itself: what gets in the way is filler, not length.
terms.long: The master prompt used to build your first website runs nearly two pages, and every block is plugging a specific, recurring mistake — so long isn't bad. The real limit is something else: everything you write takes up room in the context window, and a prompt stuffed with adjectives and pleasantries burns the exact same space as one full of your own real data, while delivering far less. The decision when reviewing it: for every paragraph, ask if it takes a decision away from the machine. If it doesn't, cut it.
terms.analogy: A two-page shopping list is fine for forty items. It's terrible for four items and thirty-six sentences explaining why you like ham.
terms.confusion: With a good prompt. Some people judge a request's quality by its bulk. The real measure is how many decisions you've stopped delegating, and that sometimes fits in six lines.

terms.short: A long, tightly specified request that does the whole job in one go and gets pasted almost as-is.
terms.long: The course has several; the best known is the one that builds your first website. It carries who you are, your real data, what you don't want, how it must be delivered, how it needs to look on mobile, and the checklist you'll verify it against. And it ends with a move that looks like a detour and isn't: it forbids building anything right away and forces the model to summarize what it understood in five lines and ask you no more than three questions. Those ninety seconds are what separates a website with your real prices from one with made-up prices.
terms.analogy: The spec sheet you hand a carpenter: measurements, wood, hardware, timeline, and what to do if something doesn't line up. Not a conversation — a spec sheet.
terms.confusion: With a template. A master prompt covers a whole job and gets pasted nearly whole; a template is smaller and built to be reused often, changing just two or three blanks. In practice, a master prompt you use every week ends up turning into a template.

terms.short: A saved prompt with a fixed part and blanks in capital letters you fill in each time.
terms.long: The fixed part is everything that doesn't change from one Monday to the next: who the AI is, what it does, in what tone, in what format, how many words, and what it must never do. The blanks are what changes, written in CAPITALS between brackets with a name that explains itself, [PRODUCT NAME] and not [X], because capitals jump out before you hit send. In the course you build five of these into a file and use them every week. The rule that decides if you've overdone it: two to five blanks is fine; hit twelve and you've built a form, and filling it in will tire you out more than writing the request from scratch.
terms.analogy: A carpentry shop's order form. The body's printed and hasn't changed in years. By hand you only fill in the measurement, the wood, the date, and the name.
terms.confusion: With digging back through your chat history for the one that worked that day. History sorts conversations by date, not by what they were for, and the search box only finds words you remember typing. What ends up happening is you rewrite it from memory, and memory always gives you the first attempt's version, not the fourth — the good one.

terms.short: One that says nothing concrete. "Make me a website": ten thousand answers are correct, and the machine picks among them.
terms.long: It's mistake number one, and almost nobody notices, because the AI doesn't object: fed "make me a website" it happily starts building, and three wasted afternoons begin right there. It's recognizable with a two-second test: if your sentence would work just as well for a competitor, it's vague. The cure isn't writing more — it's inserting data only you have: your exact prices, your city, who visits the page, and what you want them to do after reading it. In the course you see this live, asking something deliberately vague and getting back six one-line bullet points, all true and all useless.
terms.analogy: Walking into a clothing store and saying "I want something nice." You get shown whatever sells most, which is exactly what everyone else is already wearing.
terms.confusion: With a short prompt. A one-line request with your three specific facts works better than a full page of adjectives. What's missing isn't length — it's information the machine can't guess.

terms.short: A request for an image or video AI, written with subject, composition, light, camera, and constraints.
terms.long: It's not written the way a text prompt is. It has to describe what's visible: a specific subject, environment, action, framing, lens or camera, light, style, proportions, any visible text, and elements that must stay out. For video, add duration, movement, pacing, and continuity. A good visual prompt also states what the piece is for and how it'll be reviewed.
terms.analogy: A shooting order or an art direction sheet, not an inspirational sentence.
terms.confusion: With a general creative prompt. "Make it modern" controls nothing; "product centered, clean background, soft side light, no text" does.

terms.short: Writing well what you ask AI for. Not a trick — a craft you learn.
terms.long: In the course you work it through five ingredients: role, context, task, format, and success criterion. Every ingredient you add is one more decision you're no longer leaving to the machine. The five-ingredients lesson has you send the same request five times, adding one ingredient at a time, so you see with your own eyes which one changes the result top to bottom and which barely registers. The decision it forces on you: which part of the task you write yourself, and which part you let it invent.
terms.analogy: Hiring a builder for a job. Say only "fix my bathroom" and they fix it their way. Give them measurements, tile, budget, and timeline, and they fix it your way.
terms.confusion: With knowing clever phrasing. There are no magic words: what changes the result is the concrete information you put in (your prices, your client, your format), not the tone you ask in.

terms.short: The data you pass into a component so it renders with your content instead of the placeholder example.
terms.long: Short for "properties." It's what lets the same card serve Product A and Product B: you swap the name, price, and photo, and everything else stays the same. When the AI hands you back a component with made-up data hardcoded inside, what you need to ask for is that data coming in as props instead of being written by hand. Skip that, and you'll have to open the code every single time a price changes.
terms.analogy: The envelope on a form letter. The letter's always the same; you fill in the name and address on each mailing.
terms.confusion: With a regular variable. A variable lives inside a piece and only it can see it; props come in from outside, decided by whoever places the component.
