terms.short: The short document stating in writing what you'll do, what you won't, how much it costs, and by when.
terms.long: In the course it's five sections on two pages, no more: problem and goal with the client's own figures, scope, out of scope, price and timeline, and how the result gets measured and who approves it. You'll meet it in the business module and in the delivery kit, where a PROPOSAL.md file generates itself from figures you've already measured. The section almost nobody writes is what the client has to provide: access, a named point of contact, sample data. Leave that unwritten, and any delay ends up being your fault.
terms.analogy: The paper the shop hands you before touching your car: what's wrong, what they'll do, how much, and by when.
terms.confusion: With a quote. A quote is the figure; a proposal is the full document explaining why that figure makes sense and what's excluded from it. Sending only the number, without the rest, is exactly what opens the "I thought this was included too" argument.

terms.short: A proposal written to sell, not to work from: the one read by whoever decides whether to pay you.
terms.long: It carries the same five sections as any proposal, but who reads it changes, and that changes everything: it leads with their own figures (fourteen hours a month done by hand, $143.94 in net savings) instead of your methodology. The course's rule is one that holds forever: if your pitch sentence has a word the client would have to look up, it isn't your pitch sentence. Nobody buys AI — they buy getting ten hours a month of their people's time back, and out-of-scope goes in even though it feels like it's subtracting.
terms.analogy: The estimate a shop gives you doesn't list every screw's part number: it lists what's wrong with the car, what they'll do, and how much it costs.
terms.confusion: With a technical proposal, which explains how it works underneath. You need that one, and sometimes the client's IT person does too, but not whoever signs. Send the technical version to whoever's paying, and the meeting turns into explaining jargon instead of deciding.

terms.short: The company the model you're using comes from: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Mistral.
terms.long: It's who gives you your API key, who sets your per-minute limits, and who sends the bill at the end of the month. It's also who can quietly swap your model underneath you without warning, which is exactly why your saved test cases with expected outputs are the only tripwire you have. There's a part almost nobody checks until a serious client shows up: send it personal data, and that provider becomes a data processor, requiring a contract with them. Choosing a provider isn't just choosing quality — it's choosing who you're signing with.
terms.analogy: The wholesaler stocking your inventory. You don't care who they are until the day they swap the product without telling you, and your customers notice before you do.
terms.confusion: With the app. ChatGPT is the website you talk through; OpenAI is the company behind it, the one you get the key from and that bills you. And you can use one provider's model inside a completely different tool — it happens constantly.

terms.short: The number identifying which program a connection on a computer is meant for.
terms.long: It shows up at the end of a local address: localhost:3000, localhost:5678. Only one program can occupy a given number at a time, which is where every beginner's most repeated error comes from: "port already in use" almost always means the same project is already running in another window you thought you'd closed.
terms.analogy: A building's unit number. The street is your computer; the unit is the program.
terms.confusion: With an internet address. A port only makes sense inside a machine or a network.

terms.short: Downloading the changes on GitHub so they exist on your computer too.
terms.long: It's the opposite of push: instead of sending your own work, you bring down whatever's new in the repository. Working solo you barely touch it, but it becomes essential the moment there are two of you, or the moment you've edited a file straight from GitHub's website and want to keep going on your own computer. Skipping a pull and editing on top of an outdated version is the number one way to end up with a conflict.
terms.analogy: Opening the mailbox and bringing inside the letters that arrived while you were out.
terms.confusion: With a pull request, which sounds similar and is something else. A pull is downloading files, and you don't need anyone's permission; a pull request is asking for your changes to enter the good version, and someone has to accept it.

terms.short: A proposed change that someone reviews before it goes in.
terms.long: It bundles the diff, an explanation of why the change is being made, and a place to comment line by line. Even working alone, it forces you to look at everything about to go in, all at once, and that's where half of all mistakes get caught.
terms.analogy: Handing over a draft before it goes to print.
terms.confusion: With a commit. A commit is already a saved change; a proposal is a pending change awaiting acceptance.

terms.short: Uploading to GitHub the changes you've already saved on your computer.
terms.long: It's the step that gets your work off your hard drive and into the online repository: until you push, nobody else sees it, and a laptop failure takes everything with it. In this course you won't type git push in the terminal — either Claude Code does it for you, or you upload files by dragging them onto github.com. What matters isn't the command, it's the habit: three hours of work without a single push means no safety net.
terms.analogy: Writing the letter is one thing; dropping it in the mailbox is another. Push is dropping it in the mailbox.
terms.confusion: With saving, which is the commit. A commit leaves a snapshot on your computer; a push sends it to the internet. You can have twenty commits made and zero pushed, which is exactly the situation where a broken drive costs you the week's work.

terms.short: The program that runs a Python project's tests and tells you which pass and which fail.
terms.long: You install it with `pip install pytest`. In the course it shows up in the expenses project and in the GitHub Actions recipe: you write tests in a `tests/` folder, run `pytest -v`, and get one line per behavior that works and a detailed failure for each one that doesn't. Add `--cov` and it also tells you how much of your code those tests actually touched. It forces one important decision: you write the list of what needs checking beforehand, because tests written alongside the code only prove the code does what the code does.
terms.analogy: A car inspection. It fixes nothing — it runs a checklist and hands you the paper listing what's wrong.
terms.confusion: With a linter. A linter looks at how the code is written — indentation, names, dead lines — without ever running it; pytest actually runs it with real data and checks the outcome. A project can look flawless to a linter and still return the wrong total.

terms.short: The programming language almost all the code examples in this course are written in.
terms.long: It's the most common language for working with data and talking to model APIs. You'll see it in the projects doing very down-to-earth things: reading an `invoices.csv`, summing the base column, applying 21% VAT, and printing the total. You won't be the one writing it: the AI writes it, and you read it, run it, and decide whether it works. What is your decision is the version, because the course works with Python 3.11 or higher, and a project built with one version and run with another fails for reasons that have nothing to do with your actual code.
terms.analogy: The common tongue of a professional kitchen. Not the only language, but the one most of the recipes you'll come across are written in.
terms.confusion: With JavaScript. Both show up in the course and do different jobs: Python for data, files, and terminal programs; JavaScript for what moves inside a webpage. Paste one where the other belonged and you get a syntax error that won't tell you the real reason.

terms.short: Feeding the model your documents at question time, so it answers using them.
terms.long: The process is always the same: documents get chunked, stored, and when a question comes in, the most similar chunks get pulled and placed in front of it along with an instruction to never make up anything not in there. When it answers badly, check FIRST which chunks it retrieved: nine times out of ten the failure is there, not in the model.
terms.analogy: An open-book exam instead of one from memory.
terms.confusion: With fine-tuning. RAG changes what information it answers with; fine-tuning changes how it answers.

terms.short: A paid platform where you leave a program of yours running day and night without setting up a whole server.
terms.long: It comes up when you build something that has to be listening constantly, like a program receiving WhatsApp messages or a webhook of your own: it works on your computer, but shuts off the moment you close the laptop. You connect your GitHub project, paste your keys into its "Variables" tab, and it hands you a public address you can give to Meta or whoever needs it. It runs around $5-7/month for something small and bills per active service, so switch off what you're not using or the bill climbs on its own.
terms.analogy: Renting a storage unit with an outlet. You plug your device in, leave it plugged in, and pay every month whether you visit or not.
terms.confusion: With Vercel. Vercel is built for sites that get assembled and served; Railway is for programs that need to stay awake and listening, like a bot or a database.

terms.short: A parallel line of work where you can test things without touching what already works.
terms.long: You open a branch, make the changes, test it, and only once it's good do you merge it into the main one. It's what lets you experiment without anxiety: if it goes wrong, you delete the branch and nothing happened.
terms.analogy: A photocopy of the blueprint to scribble on.
terms.confusion: With copying the folder. A branch knows where it came from and knows how to merge back; a copy doesn't.

terms.short: A box's red output: the failure exits through there so the flow doesn't stop dead.
terms.long: By default, when a box fails, the whole flow stops — silently, too. You change that by opening the box, going to the "Settings" tab, and setting the "On Error" list to "Continue (using error output)": the box then grows a second, red output on the right, and that's what you hang the notification and the log off of. In the course you do this on the two or three most fragile boxes, always the ones talking to an outside service and the ones using credentials, because those expire. The line repeated throughout the lessons sums up the rule: a flow without an error branch isn't a finished flow.
terms.analogy: A signed detour around a closed road. Without it you're just stuck at the roadblock; with it you continue another way, and someone notes there was a closure.
terms.confusion: With a retry. A retry tries the same thing again in case it was a passing hiccup; an error branch is what you do once you've already accepted that it failed. They go in sequence: retry first, and if it's still broken, it exits through the red output.

terms.short: The project's good copy, the one that gets published; on GitHub it's called main.
terms.long: Every repository has a main branch, and every other branch is a parallel copy for testing things without touching the good one. Working solo, this course tells you something almost no tutorial dares to: just stay on main and save directly. You lose exactly zero safety, because history still has your back, and you skip half the concepts entirely. Separate branches start earning their keep once two people are touching the same file — not before.
terms.analogy: The original contract sitting in the folder. Branches are photocopies where you pencil in corrections to try out.
terms.confusion: With believing the main branch is untouchable and you always have to work somewhere else. It's not — it's simply the one that counts. You can write to it every single day, as long as every change gets saved with its own note.

terms.short: The cap on how many requests a service lets you make in a given time.
terms.long: It's signaled with a 429 code. It almost always shows up when a process loops through a list calling one item at a time. The fix isn't waiting longer between calls — it's grouping them and sending them together, which is also faster and cheaper.
terms.analogy: A supermarket checkout: go item by item and the line behind you gets annoyed.
terms.confusion: With running out of credit. That also returns 429, but the message will mention quota: one gets fixed by slowing down, the other by paying.

terms.short: The model's slow mode: it pauses to think before answering, and gets logic, numbers, and chained steps right more often.
terms.long: It's the long gear. The short one answers instantly; the long one spends a few seconds writing intermediate steps to itself before giving you the result. In ChatGPT you pick it from the dropdown at the top, where the model's name includes "Thinking" or similar; in Claude there's a button next to the text box. The decision is when to switch it on: for rephrasing an email, it's throwing away money and time, because it takes longer and those intermediate steps get billed; for a pricing calculation or a flow with conditions, it's the difference between getting it right and not.
terms.analogy: The scratch-work sheet in a math exam. It takes longer to hand in, but the arithmetic actually comes out right.
terms.confusion: With the model understanding what it's saying. It doesn't — it's still calculating which chunk of text comes next, just now giving itself more text to lean on before finishing. That's why a reasoning model still makes things up, and it needs checking just the same.

terms.short: A very widely used tool for building large websites piece by piece. The AI will suggest it whether you asked for it or not.
terms.long: It's a framework: instead of a single file for your page, it hands you folders of pieces that get assembled together. In the course it mostly comes up as a warning, because when you ask an AI or a tool like Lovable for a website, you get back folders with names you never chose — that's React or Next.js imposing its own way of working. That's why the "your first website" lesson has you explicitly ban it in the prompt, along with npm and the terminal. Decision: for a single page you're showing a client, you don't want it; for an application with users and several screens, it's the normal choice.
terms.analogy: Custom-fitted kitchen cabinets versus a loose table. To set out one table, building a whole kitchen is absurd; for an entire kitchen, a loose table won't cut it.
terms.confusion: With your project's name. The course warns: don't name your folder `my-project-react`, because you'd be naming the tool instead of what it does, and a year from now the tool will be different and the name will lie.

terms.short: The file that explains in two minutes what this project is and how to start it.
terms.long: It literally means "read me." It goes in the project's root (the main folder, not tucked into any subfolder), is named README.md, and is the first thing anyone sees opening your folder or your GitHub repository. In the course you write it with AI's help, and the brief is very specific: write it for exactly one reader, yourself six months from now, once you've forgotten everything. A project without a README means that in six months you won't even know how to start it.
terms.analogy: The instruction sheet sitting on top when you open a furniture box. It's not the furniture, but without it you assemble it wrong.
terms.confusion: With the client's user manual. A README is technical and lives inside the project: how to install it, how to start it, what keys it needs. The client manual is a separate document, jargon-free, and goes with the delivery.

terms.short: Something that calls itself and repeats inward until it hits bottom.
terms.long: A recursive function (a piece of code that invokes itself) solves part of a problem and calls itself again with what's left. In the course you mostly see the word "recursive" inside tools: LangChain's document chunker splits text by levels, and folder scans go into their subfolders too. The decision it always forces on you is where it stops: every recursion needs a clear end point, or it calls itself forever and crashes the program.
terms.analogy: You open a box and there's another box inside, and another inside that, until one is empty. That empty one is what lets you stop.
terms.confusion: With a loop. A loop repeats the same list of steps start to finish; recursion goes one level deeper each time and then unwinds back out. And when you see "recursive" checked as an option in a program, it almost always means: and inside subfolders too.

terms.short: Rewriting your request, rather than asking the AI to redo its answer. It's the correction that saves the most.
terms.long: When something comes out wrong you have two paths: keep correcting inside the chat, or stop and fix the request. The second is the one that pays off forever, because you close the chat but keep the request. In the course you do this literally: take the prompt that finally worked on the fourth try and rewrite it as a template, separating what's fixed from what goes in brackets, and that text is what gets saved. Warning sign: twelve rounds of corrections in the same conversation means the problem isn't the answer anymore — it's the request.
terms.analogy: If the delivery arrives wrong three times in a row, it's not the driver's fault — the order slip itself needs rewriting.
terms.confusion: With regenerating. Regenerating is rolling the dice again with the same instructions; rewriting is changing the instructions. If the answer fails twice for the same reason, regenerating is a waste of time.

terms.short: Reorganizing a program's internals without changing anything visible on the outside.
terms.long: You do it so the code is easier to understand or easier to extend without suffering — not to fix anything visible. And that's where the danger lies: done right, nobody notices; done wrong, something that had worked for months breaks, in a spot nobody's watching. In the course it shows up as one of the warning signs when reviewing AI-written code: you ask for one small change and get back thirty files touched. The rule that saves headaches is never mixing the two: refactoring and adding a new feature never go in the same change, because if something breaks, you won't know which one caused it.
terms.analogy: Reorganizing a shop's back stockroom. The storefront stays the same, but get a shelf wrong and nobody finds anything Monday morning.
terms.confusion: With improving the product. Refactoring adds no features and fixes no bugs: if the user notices anything different afterward, it wasn't a refactor — it was something else sold to you under that name.

terms.short: Asking it to answer the same message again. It's the two-arrows-in-a-circle button under the response.
terms.long: It works because the AI doesn't always give the same answer to the same text — there's randomness involved, so a second try sometimes sounds better. Use it when the answer is basically on track and all that's bothering you is how it sounds. Don't use it when it fails for a specific reason (a fact is missing, it broke your format, it made up a price), because with the same instructions you'll get the same failure in different words. The decision: two regenerations failing the same way mean it's time to rewrite the request, not roll the dice again.
terms.analogy: Flipping the coin again hoping for the other side. Sometimes it works, but if what you actually need is a six, the problem isn't the roll.
terms.confusion: With rewriting the prompt. Regenerating changes nothing about what you asked for — it just replays the round. Since it costs no effort, it's exactly where time slips away unnoticed.

terms.short: The document logging what data you process, why, how long you keep it, and who accesses it.
terms.long: Many people assume being small exempts them. It doesn't: if the processing isn't occasional (and an automated flow that runs daily isn't), you need one even with fewer than 250 people. In the course it gets built alongside the flow, not after: a table with what comes in, for what purpose, which provider sees it, in what region it's processed, and how long it's kept. The rule: date-stamp each line when you checked it, because that's what turns the document into an actual defense instead of decoration.
terms.analogy: A repair shop's logbook. Which car came in, what got done to it, who touched it, and when it left.
terms.confusion: With your flow's execution log. That one's technical and reports what happened each time the automation ran; this one's legal and reports what data you process and why. They sound alike and don't substitute for each other.

terms.short: Something that used to work and stopped, because of a change made somewhere else.
terms.long: It shows up the moment you ask AI for changes to a project that was already working fine: you ask it to tweak a button's text and the contact form breaks, because they shared a file. You test the new thing, which is natural, and nobody tests the old thing. That's how a regression can spend weeks miscalculating shipping costs without you noticing, and it's the most expensive kind of failure there is. The decision it forces on you fits on one page: write down, once, the five paths that would kill your business if they broke, and walk through them after every change.
terms.analogy: The plumber fixes your kitchen faucet and leaves without checking the shower. The shower's had no hot water since Tuesday, and you find out Sunday.
terms.confusion: With a new bug. A new bug lives in what you just asked for and shows up immediately; a regression lives in something older and only appears if you deliberately go looking. Without that list of paths written down, your regressions are going to be found by a client.

terms.short: Trying a failed step again, instead of writing off the whole flow as broken.
terms.long: Many failures are momentary: the service was overloaded, the network hiccupped, you got back a 500. Retrying once fixes that without you even noticing. The decision — the important one — isn't how many times to retry: it's whether that step can be repeated without consequences. Re-reading a sheet or re-checking a price is free; re-charging $34.90 or re-sending the same notice to a client isn't.
terms.analogy: Redialing when the line's busy. Repeating the call bothers nobody; repeating the pizza order does.
terms.confusion: With actually fixing the problem. If the failure's yours — an expired key, a misspelled address, a field that doesn't exist — retrying a thousand times gives you the same error a thousand times. Retries only work against temporary failures on the other side.

terms.short: n8n's setting that repeats a failed step on its own, without you. Switched on box by box.
terms.long: It lives in each node's settings, with two numbers: how many times it tries again, and how long it waits between attempts. The course's rule is blunt: automatic retries only on what can be repeated without consequences; on anything moving money or talking to a client, you press retry yourself. And that decision gets made on a calm Tuesday afternoon, not at three in the morning once whatever had to happen already has.
terms.analogy: A phone's auto-redial. Handy for reaching a friend; a bad idea when every call costs you money.
terms.confusion: With an error alert. Retries act inside the box, trying to save that round before it's lost; an alert acts once it's already been lost, so you find out. You need both, and neither substitutes for the other: retries alone mean the day all three attempts fail, nobody tells you.

terms.short: A named, dated version you tag by hand the day the project works.
terms.long: On GitHub you create it from the right-hand column of your project: "Releases," "Create a new release," and give it a name like v1-working. From then on that version has its own page, with a "Source code (zip)" link that downloads the entire project exactly as it stood that day. It lets you get back to a good point with one click, instead of digging through the save history reading notes. The decision it forces on you is when you say "this works": tag nothing, ever, and a month from now you'll be guessing which day was the good one.
terms.analogy: The photo of the finished renovation, dated on the back and kept separate from the roll with a thousand construction shots.
terms.confusion: With a commit, which is every ordinary save. You'll make dozens of commits and none stands out; a release you mark by hand, and a normal project has two or three. Tag twenty releases and you're back to an undistinguishable pile.

terms.short: Like Railway: you host a program there to keep it always awake, and it has a free plan with a catch.
terms.long: It's worth knowing the free plan's catch before trusting it: it shuts your service off after fifteen minutes with no visitors, and the first request that arrives while it's spinning back up gets dropped. Fine for learning; not for a client's webhook. The small paid plan runs around $5-7/month, and in the course it also shows up as the target of automatic deployment: when tests pass green, Render gets notified to publish.
terms.analogy: A shop that pulls its shutter down if nobody walks in for fifteen minutes. Call and it comes back up, but you were left waiting outside a moment.
terms.confusion: With the English word "render" used in video and image work, meaning to process and export the final file. Unrelated — here it's the name of a hosting company.

terms.short: How long something takes to respond once it actually has real data in it.
terms.long: The symptom is always the same: something that ran smoothly with twenty rows drags with twenty thousand. In the course's search project, a query drops from four seconds to thirty milliseconds just by adding the right index. The rule is never optimizing by ear: measure with real data first, find which specific step is slow, and fix that. On a spreadsheet dashboard, every formula added "just in case" is a little bit of permanent slowness too.
terms.analogy: A supermarket checkout line. With three customers it doesn't matter how it's organized; with fifty, it shows who opened another register in time.
terms.confusion: With cost. A slow query can be free, and a lightning-fast one can cost you money every single time. They're measured separately, even though both get worse as volume grows.

terms.short: A site where you run other people's models on their machines and pay by seconds of use, not by month.
terms.long: It's for the middle case: you want an open image, audio, or video model, but your computer can't run it and you don't feel like setting up a server. You send the request via API and it hands back the result. The decision here is financial: you pay for machine time, so a heavy model stuck inside a loop of 500 rows can get very expensive with nobody stopping it. Set a spending cap before letting it loose.
terms.analogy: Renting a hammer drill by the hour instead of buying one. Worth it for one hole; not for a hundred a day.
terms.confusion: With Hugging Face and Ollama, which always come up in the same conversation. Hugging Face is the model's store, Ollama runs it on your own computer, and Replicate runs it on someone else's, billing you by the minute.

terms.short: A site where you write and run programs right inside the browser, nothing installed, with AI that builds alongside you.
terms.long: It's an entire programming computer packed into one browser tab: file list, text, command window, and a publish button, all on the same screen. Its AI feature, which they call Agent, builds the project on its own from what you tell it. In the course it comes with the same warning as Bolt: it's their computer, not yours, so download the project occasionally and save the copy with a date in the name.
terms.analogy: A rented-by-the-hour kitchen. Everything's set up and you don't do the dishes, but whatever you leave in the fridge on the way out stops being yours.
terms.confusion: With VS Code. VS Code installs on your computer and the files are yours even without internet; Replit lives on their website, and offline you can't open anything. If you're going to work on a train, this won't do.

terms.short: A project's folder with its entire history inside.
terms.long: It's the project plus its book of changes. It can be private or public, and that's where one of the trade's most expensive slip-ups lives: accidentally publishing a repository with keys inside. Before uploading anything, check the .gitignore.
terms.analogy: A filing cabinet holding the work and every dated draft.
terms.confusion: With an ordinary folder. Without Git inside, there's no history to consult.

terms.short: The same thing, on a different computer or six months from now, coming back together and working identically.
terms.long: It's one of two things Docker solves in the course: inside the container sit the exact versions that worked, so it behaves the same on your laptop, your client's, and a rented server. Without it comes the classic "it worked on my machine," which on a client delivery is a wasted afternoon. It also applies to prompts: saving the version you used and which model is what lets you reproduce a result. Watch out — the model contributes its own randomness: what's reproducible is the setup, not the response word for word.
terms.analogy: A recipe measured in grams instead of "a handful." Anyone can make it in their own kitchen and get the same cake.
terms.confusion: With backups. A backup preserves your data; reproducibility preserves the conditions to build it all back up again. You can have a perfect backup and still not be able to get it running again.

terms.short: The file with the exact list of pieces your Python project needs.
terms.long: One line per piece, shaped like package==number, and that number is the whole point: it pins the version so six months from now the same one installs instead of a newer one that breaks things. It's generated on its own, with pip freeze, and never written by hand. In the course you use it two ways: when someone clones your project and starts it with pip install -r requirements.txt, and inside the Dockerfile. There's a trap that catches a lot of people: generate it without your virtual environment activated, and you freeze your computer's entire Python install, producing a bizarre list of packages you never installed.
terms.analogy: A shopping list with the exact brand and size. "Milk" gets you anything; "whole milk, one-liter carton" always gets you the same thing.
terms.confusion: With package.json, which plays the same role in JavaScript. If your project has both, it's because it involves both worlds. And don't confuse the list with what's installed: the file weighs two kilobytes, the packages weigh hundreds of megabytes, and those never get uploaded.

terms.short: How many dots make up an image or video: the higher, the more detail and the heavier the file.
terms.long: In the course it matters for the money, not the aesthetics. Runway's habit that saves the most credits: test in low resolution until framing and movement are decided, and only then generate in high. And in reverse, once something's turned out well, download it at the highest quality your plan allows. The decision it forces on you is when you bump up the quality, because regenerating just because you only saved a small version costs you all over again.
terms.analogy: Photocopying drafts while correcting them and only printing the final copy at good quality. Just as readable for working, and much cheaper.
terms.confusion: With quality. A huge image can still be badly framed with deformed hands: resolution fixes none of that, it just shows it bigger.

terms.short: The person who decides what's allowed to leave the company and what isn't. On a project of your own, that's you.
terms.long: In the course you mostly use it as a role you assign the AI right before publishing: "review these files as if you were my business's security officer and tell me everything that shouldn't leave my computer." What that review turns up is usually similar: keys and passwords, database addresses, people's emails and phone numbers, even folder paths carrying your username inside them. At a mid-sized company the role genuinely exists, and it's whoever approves tools and signs licenses — so you don't decide there. On your own project there's nobody, which is exactly why the role falls to you, and it helps to hand it explicitly to the machine before uploading anything.
terms.analogy: The floor manager who checks the tables before opening. They don't cook or serve, but they're the one who says whether this goes out as-is or not.
terms.confusion: With the IT person who fixes computers. That person keeps things running; a security officer decides what's allowed, and their answer is often no even when something works perfectly.

terms.short: A page rearranging itself to fit the screen width: phone, tablet, or computer.
terms.long: It literally means "that responds." It's not two different websites — it's the same one adapting: one column on mobile, three spread out on a laptop. Lovable, v0, and similar tools give you this by default, so you'll rarely need to ask for it, but you do need to check it, because it's where things break most: menus covering text, buttons spilling off the edge, tables that don't fit. The course's rule is to always check it on your own actual phone before showing a client.
terms.analogy: A kitchen shelving unit that reorganizes itself to fit the space: vertical in a small apartment, spread wide in a big one.
terms.confusion: With it looking fine when you narrow your computer's browser window. Not the same thing: on a phone the font size changes, the keyboard pops up and covers half the screen, and your finger is far fatter than a mouse pointer. Open it on a real phone.

terms.short: What you forbid it from doing. Written beforehand, inside the request, not after seeing the answer.
terms.long: They're lines like "no emojis," "90 words max," "never make up a review," "don't touch what already works." The first website's master prompt has an entire section called WHAT I DON'T WANT, and every line in it is patching a mistake that recurs constantly. Without constraints, the AI doesn't come up short — it overdoes it, adding a blog, a cart, and three testimonials that never existed. The rule: write down the ban the first time something bothers you, instead of fixing it by hand every week.
terms.analogy: The instructions you leave a painter. Not just "paint the living room" — also "don't move the couch and don't touch the ceiling."
terms.confusion: With acceptance criteria. A constraint says what it can't do while working; the criterion says how you check, at the end, whether the result is good. You need both, written in different parts of the request.

terms.short: Changing one piece of an image or video you already have, instead of regenerating the whole thing.
terms.long: It's what saves a shot that's ninety percent good. In the course it's done with Runway: you mark the object that doesn't belong and it removes it, filling in the gap, or it separates a subject from the background. The decision it forces on you is when to stop pushing regeneration: three attempts in and the shot fails on just one detail, it's cheaper to retouch that detail than to ask for the whole shot again and lose what you already liked in the process.
terms.analogy: Sewing a button back on instead of buying a new shirt. The rest of the shirt was fine.
terms.confusion: With regenerating. Regenerating changes everything, including what you liked; retouching only changes the piece you marked. Miss this distinction and you spend the afternoon chasing a result you already had in hand.

terms.short: What a function hands back when it finishes: the result the next step can use.
terms.long: A function is a named piece of code doing one specific thing; the return is what it delivers when it's done, written as "return" in the course's code. In the email agent, the function that saves the draft returns a record saying whether it succeeded and which file it landed in. It matters because the next step can only work with what got returned: if a function returns nothing, whoever calls it is left in the dark. When something fails midway through a flow, check first what the previous step is returning.
terms.analogy: Ordering coffee at the counter. The return value is the coffee handed to you — not the time the barista spent at the machine.
terms.confusion: With return on investment, which shows up in the client proposal as how many months it takes to pay for itself. Same word, different things: here it's a value coming out of a piece of code, there it's dollars. Context makes it obvious which is which.

terms.short: The first meeting with the client, where what's being done, with what data, and by when gets nailed down.
terms.long: It's for closing three very specific things: what systems get touched, what data gets used, and who grants you access. In the course it comes up as part of a classic mistake: sending a vague proposal trusting that "the details will get sorted at the kickoff." It doesn't work, because whatever gets discussed in a meeting with no minutes doesn't exist by month two, when you and the client remember it differently — leave that meeting having written up the minutes with scope and exclusions, and email them the same day.
terms.analogy: The day you hand over the keys to a renovation crew. Before touching anything, they walk the house with you noting what gets done and what doesn't.
terms.confusion: With the sales meeting. In sales you're persuading and discussing possibilities; by kickoff it's already decided and you're just closing details and access. If you're still negotiating price at kickoff, the proposal was never actually closed.

terms.short: The European law regulating what you can do with someone's data.
terms.long: In daily practice it's four things: ask only for what you need, say what you're using it for, keep it only as long as necessary, and know exactly which companies you're passing it to, because an AI service processing your clients' data counts too. Most scares don't come from fines — they come from having fed client data into a tool without checking what it does with it.
terms.analogy: Food-handling rules: boring until someone gets sick.
terms.confusion: With computer security. You can have everything encrypted and still be non-compliant, if you're collecting data you don't need.

terms.short: A staged plan with dates: what you deliver by day 30, 60, and 90.
terms.long: It literally means "road map." In the course there are three, organized not by topic but by delivery: by day 30, fundamentals and first exercises; by day 60, projects and automations; by day 90, portfolio, service proposal, case study, and defense. Each stage carries its own deliverables and checkpoints, and that's exactly what separates a plan from a list of good intentions. The rule it forces on you is blunt and useful: a week without a finished piece is a week without progress, no matter how many hours you put in.
terms.analogy: A renovation's work plan. It doesn't say "renovate the kitchen" — it says the tile is going in Thursday the 12th.
terms.confusion: With the backlog. A roadmap carries dates and commitment; a backlog is the list of what might get done someday. Dumping the whole backlog into the roadmap is the fastest way to fail to deliver it — and for the client to notice.

terms.short: Return on investment: how long a job takes to pay for itself, and what it leaves behind after.
terms.long: In the course it's always defended with subtraction, right in front of the client: $189 in hours saved a month, minus $45 maintenance, minus $0.06 in model billing, comes to $143.94 net a month. With that, the $900 setup cost pays for itself in 6.3 months, and the first year leaves the client $827.28 ahead. Subtracting your own costs in front of them is exactly what separates you from someone selling smoke. And if you can't measure how many hours it used to take before, you don't have an ROI — you have a promise.
terms.analogy: Switching to LED bulbs: you spend $60 today and by month eight you've already earned it back on the power bill.
terms.confusion: With gross savings. Savings that haven't had your bill or the hours spent fixing the tool's own mistakes subtracted convince nobody experienced. The number that lands is always the one after the subtraction, even when it's smaller.

terms.short: Going back to an earlier version that actually worked.
terms.long: It's what turns a disaster into a bad afternoon. It only works if a save point existed before the change, which is why a commit happens before touching something, not after. On publishing platforms it's usually a single button: re-promoting an older version.
terms.analogy: Reverse gear. It exists precisely for the moments you drove somewhere you shouldn't have.
terms.confusion: With actually fixing the bug. A rollback gets the service back to working right now; fixing it comes later, calmly.

terms.short: The piece of your website that decides which screen to show based on the address typed in.
terms.long: On a multi-page site — home, pricing, contact — there aren't twenty loose files hanging around: there's a list saying what gets rendered when the address ends in /pricing. That's the router, and its name will jump out the moment you touch Next.js or Vercel, where you'll see "App Router" written. It causes a very specific, very repeated failure: everything works on your computer, you publish, and reloading a page that isn't the homepage throws a 404. It's almost always hosting configuration, not code, and gets fixed in one message if you tell the AI which tool you built it with.
terms.analogy: A building's doorman. Tell them which floor you're going to and they send you to the right elevator; without them you're stuck in the lobby staring at mailboxes.
terms.confusion: With your home router, the blinking-light box from your internet provider. Unrelated beyond the name: yours splits internet between your devices; this one splits addresses inside your website. When someone mentions routes and 404s, it's this second one.

terms.short: A table saying what gets checked and how much each thing is worth. Keeps scoring from being a guess.
terms.long: In the course it shows up in two places that look different and are actually the same: evaluating your projects and your oral defense, and judging AI responses without letting the day's mood decide. You write it before looking at the result, with criteria that can be checked: "the three exact prices show up" works, "looks professional" doesn't. What it gives you over a loose checklist is weight: you know which failure is serious and which is a minor detail. The decision: how many criteria to include. Past six, nobody actually uses it; three well-chosen ones get used every time.
terms.analogy: A driving examiner's sheet. It doesn't decide whether they liked you: it notes whether you checked the mirror, shifted correctly, and crossed the solid line.
terms.confusion: With a checklist. A checklist is yes-or-no; a rubric grades and weighs. If yours is just "there or not there," skip the rubric and use a checklist — it fills out in a minute.

terms.short: AI video tools for fixing and extending footage you already have, on top of generating shots.
terms.long: What sets it apart is its toolbox for working on material that already exists: erasing an object from a scene and filling the gap, separating a person from the background with no green screen, extending a shot that ran too short, or changing the style of an entire video. It's the tool for someone who already has footage and needs to save it, more than for someone starting from a sentence. Credits get spent per second generated and per tool used, so the same plan lasts you a long time or almost none depending on what you do — check consumption before promising a delivery date.
terms.analogy: A body shop. It doesn't manufacture cars; it takes the dented one you bring in and hands it back presentable.
terms.confusion: With Higgsfield or Seedance, built for generating a shot from scratch. The question that separates them is short: do I have footage already? If yes, Runway.

terms.short: Asking for the response written with braces and quotes, so another program can read it without misreading anything.
terms.long: JSON is a way of writing data that machines always understand the same way. You'll need it the moment the AI's output feeds into an n8n flow or a spreadsheet, because the next step needs to know exactly which fields it's going to receive. The course's rule fits in one line: ask for it only when something automated is going to read the response; if you're reading it yourself, don't, because JSON reads far worse than a paragraph. And watch out: asking for it in the prompt helps but doesn't guarantee it. One day it answers with a friendly paragraph and breaks the whole chain.
terms.analogy: A shipping company's manifest versus a handwritten note. You can understand the note; the warehouse's machine reads the manifest without hesitating.
terms.confusion: With true structured output. Asking for JSON inline is a request, and it can get skipped; structured output forces the model to comply with a schema. If your automation crashes whenever the format fails, you need the second one.

terms.short: What you've written down beforehand should come out for a specific case.
terms.long: It's the missing half for almost everyone who claims to "test" their prompts: without noting beforehand what should come out, you correct by eye, and it always feels like it improved. With ten or twenty real cases and their expected output next to them, every change gets run against the list, and in a minute you know whether you broke something elsewhere. It's also what alerts you the day a provider quietly updates the model underneath and responses shift without you having touched anything. Writing it is tedious, and it's exactly the work separating a toy from something you can hand a client.
terms.analogy: An exam's answer key. Without it, every grader approves whatever sounds right to them that day.
terms.confusion: With an ideal word-for-word answer. Don't look for exact text matches, since the model never repeats the same sentence twice: note what can't be missing and what can't appear, and compare against that.

terms.short: Forcing the model to answer with an exact shape, instead of free text.
terms.long: You give it a schema and the system guarantees the response fits: the same fields, every time. It's what makes plugging a model into an automated process possible, because the next step knows exactly what it's going to receive. Without this, one day it answers with a friendly paragraph and breaks the whole chain.
terms.analogy: A form instead of a letter.
terms.confusion: With asking for it in the prompt. Asking helps; guaranteeing it with a schema is something else entirely.

terms.short: The invisible character saved when you hit Enter. You can't see it, but it's there.
terms.long: It's the culprit behind half the course's silly errors. Copy an API key (the long password a service gives you) and paste it into the .env file, and a trailing line break often sneaks in: the key looks correct to the eye and the service still says it's invalid. The same happens pasting a web address into an n8n node. And in the "test before delivering" lesson, deliberately inserting a line break into a text field is one of the attacks you're supposed to run against your own flow.
terms.analogy: An extra space at the end of a password. Looks correctly typed to your eyes, and it still won't let you in.
terms.confusion: With a blank space. Both are invisible and both break pasted keys, but a line break also splits the text into two pieces for the program reading it. Trick: if you suspect one, go to the end of the line and backspace until you're touching the last real letter.

terms.short: An isolated space where something runs without being able to touch anything else.
terms.long: It's how you test code you didn't write yourself, including AI-written code: if something weird happens inside, it stays inside. It's also the name for payment services' test mode, where you can simulate charges without moving real money.
terms.analogy: A kids' playpen: they can do whatever they want in there.
terms.confusion: With a virtual environment. An environment separates program versions; a sandbox separates permissions and risk.

terms.short: The trigger that fires by the clock: every day at 9, every Monday, every hour.
terms.long: In n8n the box is called Schedule Trigger, and it's the first one you actually build for real: pick Days, leave 1 in "Days Between Triggers," and set an hour and minute. It's perfect when what you want IS a moment: the morning summary, the invoice on the 1st. And it's a trap when you use it to watch for something that happens on its own schedule, because it condemns you to choosing between checking too often for nothing or finding out too late. Check the timezone before switching it on — that's failure number one.
terms.analogy: An alarm clock. It goes off at the time you set, whether anything interesting happened that night or not.
terms.confusion: With an app trigger (Gmail Trigger, Sheets Trigger). That also checks every few minutes, but it keeps track of what it's already delivered and only gives you what's new. With a plain Schedule, you have to build that bookkeeping yourself.

terms.short: How far a key or an integration is allowed to reach.
terms.long: It's the difference between "can read your emails" and "can read, write, and delete your emails." The rule is to grant the bare minimum needed and review it periodically: when something returns a 403 despite being properly identified, this is almost always why. Adding a new permission usually requires reinstalling the integration, and that's the step everyone forgets.
terms.analogy: A building's keys: you don't hand the full set to whoever's here to change a lightbulb.
terms.confusion: With being identified. A 401 means it doesn't know who you are; a 403 means it does, and still won't let you in.

terms.short: A short program that does one specific task, or the named shortcut that runs it.
terms.long: The word covers two things, and you'll see both. One: a loose file doing a job, like one that reads your invoices from a CSV and pulls out totals, or one you paste into Apps Script inside a Google Sheet. Two: the named shortcuts living inside package.json that you launch by typing npm run dev. Either way, the same rule applies: never run a script you don't understand — ask the AI to explain it line by line first, because it runs from start to finish, no questions asked, and whatever it deletes doesn't go to a trash bin.
terms.analogy: A recipe written on paper. You follow it top to bottom without thinking, which is exactly why you should read the whole thing before turning on the stove.
terms.confusion: With an application. A script does one thing and ends; an application stays open waiting for you to use it. If something runs and closes the window, it was a script.

terms.short: Any piece of data that grants access to something: keys, passwords, tokens.
terms.long: They live outside the code, in environment variables, and get declared again on the server when you publish. If one gets published by mistake, deleting it from history isn't enough — you have to revoke it and generate a new one, because anything that was public has to be assumed copied.
terms.analogy: The key to the vault, not what's inside it.
terms.confusion: With personal data. A secret opens doors; personal data identifies a person. Both need protecting, for different reasons.

terms.short: GitHub's key vault, where you store them so its robots can use them without leaving them written anywhere.
terms.long: They live under "Settings" → "Secrets and variables" → "Actions" in your repository (your project's folder as stored on GitHub, with its history), and you add each one by hand, one at a time. In your instructions file you don't write the key — you write ${{ secrets.NAME }}, and GitHub substitutes it at run time. Write it directly instead and it stays in the history forever, and on a public project someone finds it in under a minute. Once saved, a secret can never be read again, not even by you — only replaced, which is why you also keep it in your own password manager.
terms.analogy: A hotel's safe. Staff can put your suitcase inside, but nobody opens it again to look at what's in there.
terms.confusion: With the "variables" on that same screen, right next to it. Variables are ordinary settings, visible in plain sight in logs; secrets appear masked. When in doubt, save it as a secret.

terms.short: A video generator from text or a still image, with reasonably coherent shots.
terms.long: Give it a sentence, or a starting image, and it hands back a few seconds of video; its strength is that within one shot, things move sensibly and the character's face doesn't shift midway. In the course it comes with the same warning as its neighbors: one strong shot isn't a video. Video comes from chaining shots that carry intent and continuity, so the storyboard gets written before generating anything, or you end up with six beautiful pieces each pulling in a different direction.
terms.analogy: A brilliant session musician recording loose bars. If nobody wrote the song, you have twenty bars and no song.
terms.confusion: With Runway and Higgsfield. All three generate video, and you pick by testing which gives the best result for your kind of shot; the real divide isn't between them — it's between generating shots and actually editing a video together.

terms.short: The word every read-only query starts with, changing nothing. It means "select."
terms.long: It's the first word worth learning to recognize, because it tells you whether a piece of SQL is safe. A statement starting with select just looks; one starting with delete (removes rows), update (changes them), or drop (throws away the whole table) touches things, and there's no undo bin. When the AI writes SQL for you, read its first word before hitting Run. And avoid select *, meaning "all columns": ask only for what you're going to use.
terms.analogy: Window shopping versus walking in and taking things. Select is looking: the worst that can happen is it takes a while.
terms.confusion: With assuming a select can never hurt. It doesn't delete anything, but an unfiltered one against a massive table can keep the server busy and the dashboard frozen for everyone in the meantime.

terms.short: Installing it yourself, on your own computer or a server of yours, instead of paying a fee to use it on someone else's.
terms.long: It means "hosted by yourself." In the course it shows up mostly with n8n, which you can use on their cloud paying a monthly fee, installing nothing, or set up yourself: free in license, and with your account handling maintenance. The decision isn't about money — it's about whose phone rings when something breaks on a Sunday. Self-host it, and updates, backups, and outages are yours, and if the flow belongs to a client, that responsibility needs to be written into the proposal.
terms.analogy: Renting a storefront versus buying the ground floor. Buy it, and you pay no rent, but the day the boiler breaks, you're the one who calls someone and pays for it.
terms.confusion: With it being free. The license costs nothing, everything else does: the server, your time, and the scare. And there's a trap that catches a lot of people: install it on your laptop, and the automated flow only works while the laptop's on, so at three in the morning nothing runs at all.

terms.short: A number that pins down part of the randomness so you can reproduce or get close to a result.
terms.long: Many generative tools use controlled randomness. Save the seed and you can more easily reproduce an image or a similar variant, though it won't always come out identical, since model, version, reference, and other parameters also play a role. In institutional projects it gets saved alongside the prompt, the date, the tool, and the approved image.
terms.analogy: Writing down the recipe and the oven temperature: doesn't guarantee the same cake, but saves you from starting over.
terms.confusion: With saving the final file. The seed helps recreate; the final file is the approved evidence.

terms.short: A computer running twenty-four hours a day whose only job is answering when someone asks for a page or a piece of data.
terms.long: It has no screen or keyboard: it sits in a data center cabinet, and you operate it by typing commands from your own machine. In the course it comes up when you decide where whatever you built will live: a small server to keep n8n always awake runs $5-15/month, and that price doesn't include the hours you'll spend on it. Setting it up right the first time is a full afternoon; afterward you have to update it, back it up, and be available if it goes down. That's why the advice is not to rent a server until you have something working that someone's actually using.
terms.analogy: A bartender who never closes. You order, they serve, and it doesn't matter that it's four in the morning.
terms.confusion: With "the cloud." The cloud is the rental model; the server is the specific machine you're renting. And watch a different use of the word: an "MCP server" isn't a rented computer — it's a program that lends tools to the AI.

terms.short: Your own computer acting as a server, so you can see your project in the browser before publishing it.
terms.long: It opens at an address like http://localhost:3000, and that number after the colon is the door it answers through. It doesn't reach the internet: send that link to a colleague over WhatsApp and they'll get an error, because on their computer "localhost" means their own machine. That, which sounds like a limitation, is its best feature: you can break everything and nobody sees it, and it costs nothing. The classic mistake is typing 3000 into the browser when the tool actually started on 3001 because 3000 was taken — the right number is written on your own screen from the start.
terms.analogy: Cooking at home instead of opening a restaurant. You can burn the eggs four times and nobody knows.
terms.confusion: With having the site actually published. Seeing it in your own browser doesn't mean it exists on the internet. The test takes a minute: open it on your phone using mobile data, with home wifi off. If it doesn't load, it's still local.

terms.short: A continuous stretch of work with a tool, from when you open it to when you close it.
terms.long: In a chat, a session is the conversation, and it dies with it: close it and the context empties out with nothing left behind. In Claude Code it's also the unit your cost gets measured in, and there the difference is huge: two hours of a session within a roughly $22/month plan cost you not one extra dollar, and those same two hours on an API key with no cap set can run $8 to $20. In n8n, watch out — manual runs from a testing session might not even get saved to history. The habit that saves whole afternoons: before closing, ask for a written handoff and save it yourself.
terms.analogy: A kitchen shift. Whatever you don't write down before hanging up the apron, the next shift won't know.
terms.confusion: With an account. An account is yours and lasts years; a session lasts as long as it lasts and leaves nothing behind except what you saved by hand. And don't confuse it with the context window: the window can fill up long before you consider the session over.

terms.short: The program that reads what you type into the terminal and runs the command.
terms.long: The black window is the terminal; whoever understands your commands inside it is the shell. It matters because they don't all speak the same way: Windows's default is PowerShell and a Mac's is zsh, so a command written for one might not work in the other. That's the real reason a tutorial can fail on you without you doing anything wrong. When asking the AI for help, tell it what system you're on first — otherwise it'll give you the other one's command.
terms.analogy: The waiter taking your order. The bar's always the bar, but depending on who's behind it, they either understand "an espresso macchiato" or give you a blank look.
terms.confusion: With the terminal. The terminal is the window; the shell is who's inside listening. Almost everyone uses the two words interchangeably, and you only notice the difference the day a Mac command won't run on your Windows.

terms.short: A set of instructions that teaches an assistant to do a task your way.
terms.long: It's not code: it's your own way of working, written down so it's followed consistently, with its steps, its output format, and its limits. Done well, it turns "depends how you ask" into a repeatable result.
terms.analogy: The procedure taped to the workshop wall.
terms.confusion: With a loose prompt. A prompt gets written every time; a skill gets defined once and reused.

terms.short: A skill's file: says when to use it and how to do that job, step by step.
terms.long: A skill is a named folder with this file inside. At the top goes the header — the name and a description of when to use it and when not to; below, the procedure written in Markdown. The course's example is called `getafe-bathroom-quote`, runs 120 lines, and took 40 minutes to write with AI's help. Windows Notepad trap: pick "All Files" in the Type dropdown and UTF-8 under Encoding, or it'll save a `SKILL.md.txt` that's worthless. And a security decision: installing someone else's skill without reading the whole SKILL.md is the same as running a stranger's program.
terms.analogy: The laminated recipe card in a restaurant kitchen. Whoever's working that night pulls off the same dish without needing to ask the chef.
terms.confusion: With CLAUDE.md. CLAUDE.md is a specific project's rules and always gets read; SKILL.md is a procedure that activates only when a task matches its description, and you carry it from one project to another.

terms.short: The deadline you commit to: how quickly you respond or resolve. Stands for Service Level Agreement.
terms.long: It's a written commitment like "we respond within 24 business hours." It comes up when you sell a client an automation, because the moment your flow starts handling their emails, you're the one promising that deadline. Before signing any, check two things: what happens on weekends, and what happens if the service on the other end is down. A deadline with no alert firing before it's missed is useless, because you find out only after you've already failed to deliver.
terms.analogy: A courier's "delivered in 24 hours." It's worth exactly as much as the alert that fires when the package has been sitting still for twenty hours.
terms.confusion: With your average turnaround time. You calculate the average after the fact; an SLA is a promise met or missed case by case. Promising your average means missing it half the time.

terms.short: Work chat, with rooms split by topic. Your flows can drop messages into those rooms on their own.
terms.long: In the course you don't use it to talk to coworkers — you use it as a notification mailbox: every form someone submits shows up in a channel in under five seconds, and a broken flow alerts you there instead of in an email you'll read Thursday. The free plan is more than enough, with two limits you'll notice: you only see messages from the last 90 days, and you only connect 10 external apps, and your automated alert counts as one of those ten. Decide what goes to Slack and what goes to email: whatever needs to interrupt you buzzes your pocket; the rest doesn't.
terms.analogy: An office with several desks, and you sit at whichever one you need: orders, invoices, coffee talk.
terms.confusion: With using WhatsApp or Telegram for the same thing. All three buzz your phone; the difference is that in Slack the notification sits in a channel the whole team can see, searchable months later.

terms.short: The bit of text deliberately repeated at the end of one chunk and the start of the next.
terms.long: Splitting a document into pieces, a cut sooner or later lands in the middle of an important sentence, splitting it between two chunks so neither one answers well. The fix is repeating the end of each chunk at the start of the next — in the course you'll usually see it written as "overlap." In the document search project it's around two hundred characters, enough that a sentence sliced by the cut still sits whole in at least one chunk. The decision is how much: too little and you keep losing sentences at the seams; too much and you're storing and paying for the same text multiple times.
terms.analogy: Roof shingles. Each one laps a bit over the one below, and that repeated bit, which looks wasteful, is exactly what keeps water from getting through the seam.
terms.confusion: With having saved the document twice by mistake. Here the repetition is deliberate and small. And watch a different thing the course also calls "overlapping": when two classification categories step on each other and the same email could fit both. Same word, different problem, fixed by writing better definitions, not by chunking differently.

terms.short: The box that splits a long list and releases it a little at a time, instead of all at once.
terms.long: It literally means "split into batches"; in newer n8n versions the same box is called "Loop Over Items." You need it when a step hands you 200 rows and the next one fires 200 calls in a row at a service that can't take that pace and returns a 429 error, meaning "you're asking me for too much." The fix is lowering the batch size inside it, and if it still complains, adding a one-second Wait beforehand. The decision is one of patience: batching takes noticeably longer, but it reaches the end instead of dying halfway.
terms.analogy: Doing laundry in two loads instead of stuffing it all in at once. Takes twice as long, but you don't blow out the drum.
terms.confusion: With saving money. Splitting into batches doesn't reduce the work: the 200 calls still happen and still get billed the same, just spread over time. If you actually want to spend less, you need to process fewer things, not the same amount more slowly.

terms.short: The language used to ask a database what it has stored.
terms.long: It's written in statements starting with select (fetch), insert (add), or delete (remove), and they run instantly. In the course you don't write it — the AI writes it for you, and you paste it into Supabase's SQL editor and hit Run. Your job is reading the first word before running it and knowing whether that statement only looks or also changes things. A .sql file you don't understand gets tested on a copy, never on real data.
terms.analogy: The order you place with the warehouse clerk. They know where everything is; you just have to say it right, in the right order.
terms.confusion: With the database itself. SQL is the language; PostgreSQL or SQLite is the warehouse that understands it. Change warehouses and the language stays almost the same.

terms.short: An entire database packed into a single file, no server, nothing to install.
terms.long: It's what n8n ships with by default: your flows, your encrypted credentials, users, and the entire history live inside one file called database.sqlite. That's both a huge advantage and a trap. The advantage: copying that file is your complete backup. The trap: start n8n in Docker without properly mounting the folder, and the file gets created inside the container and disappears with it. Someone in the course lost three weeks that way, which is why that check happens on day one.
terms.analogy: A portable filing box versus a warehouse. You can carry it under your arm — and also leave it forgotten on the train.
terms.confusion: With it being a toy database. It holds up far better than people think: you switch to PostgreSQL once volume gets heavy or once you're running several workers in parallel, not before.

terms.short: A way to connect to another computer or to GitHub over an encrypted channel, no password typed.
terms.long: It works with a pair of keys, one that stays on your computer and one you hand to the service, which then recognizes you afterward without asking for anything. In this course it's on the list of things you can skip: everything with GitHub is done from the browser, and setting up SSH keys on day one will only cause headaches. It comes up for real the day you rent your own server, because then it's the only door in.
terms.analogy: The building key handed to you once: you never buzz the intercom again, but lose it and the lock has to be changed.
terms.confusion: With a password. A password you know by heart and type; an SSH key is a file living on your computer that you never type. Steal the laptop and the key goes with it, which is why it's also protected with a passphrase.

terms.short: The table or sequence of shots defining a video before it gets generated or filmed.
terms.long: Before spending credits on video, you decide what happens shot by shot: duration, subject, framing, movement, audio, text, transition, risk, and approval criteria. In tools like Seedance or Runway, a storyboard prevents you from asking for an entire video with a vague sentence and then discovering every shot pulls in a different direction.
terms.analogy: A house's blueprint before buying materials.
terms.confusion: With a script. A script says what's being told; a storyboard says what's visible and how it changes.

terms.short: Showing the response as it's generated, word by word.
terms.long: It doesn't make the model any faster: it makes the wait far less noticeable, since there's something to read from the very first second. It's the difference between an interface that feels alive and one that feels frozen.
terms.analogy: Getting served bites while the rest of the meal is still cooking.
terms.confusion: With latency. Streaming doesn't reduce the total time, only the time to the first word.

terms.short: A value that's text, not a number, which is why it always sits in quotes.
terms.long: It literally means a chain, as in a chain of characters. You'll see it written exactly like this inside schemas passed to a model: "type": "string" means "this needs to come to me as text." The costly trap is that a number in quotes stops being a number: "640" is text and can't be added without converting it first. Even worse, "false" is also a string, and in JavaScript any non-empty text counts as true.
terms.analogy: A phone number written in an address book. It's digits, but nobody adds them up — it's a label, not a quantity.
terms.confusion: With a real number. If it's in quotes, it's text, no matter how much it looks like a number. This is the exact failure that keeps an amount from adding up correctly, or lets a consent field marked "false" slip through validation as if it were a yes.

terms.short: The most-used payment gateway: it's what charges cards on your behalf inside your website.
terms.long: In the course it comes up mostly in security and errors lessons, and for good reason. Its keys that move real money start with `sk_live_`, and that exact prefix is what scanning bots hunt for among accidentally published keys. It also shows up in the errors lesson, inside the most-copied CORS error message in the world, and in the webhooks lesson, because Stripe retries the same notification for days if you don't answer fast enough. The rule with no exceptions: that key never enters the code — it goes in an environment variable, and everything is tested first with the test keys.
terms.analogy: A shop's card reader. Someone else installs it, takes a cut of every transaction, and the one unforgivable thing is leaving the register's access code taped to the counter.
terms.confusion: With the test keys. Stripe gives you two nearly identical-looking sets: with the test ones no money moves, with the `sk_live_` ones it does. Checking the prefix before pasting anything is the two-second check that avoids the scare.

terms.short: A separate flow that another flow calls to handle a piece of the job and hand back a result.
terms.long: It literally means "underneath flow." It exists so you don't repeat the same piece in five places: you build "notify via Telegram" or "clean up the client's name" once, and other flows call it when needed. The payoff shows up the day you change something, because you change it in exactly one place and it's fixed everywhere. In the course it shows up in the n8n vocabulary, among the fifteen words you need to follow the forums, and it's not something you build on day one — the moment is when you're about to copy-paste the same three boxes for the third time.
terms.analogy: The base sauce you make Monday in a big pot and use Tuesday, Wednesday, and Thursday. You don't cook it from scratch every time.
terms.confusion: With the error workflow. Both are flows separate from the main one, but you deliberately call a sub-workflow mid-job, while the error one fires on its own, only when something breaks.

terms.short: A helper the main assistant hands part of a job to, getting back only the result.
terms.long: It serves two purposes: dividing up work that can happen in parallel, and isolating tasks that would generate a lot of noise, so the heavy lifting stays out of the main conversation. The main assistant keeps only the conclusion, not the whole process.
terms.analogy: Sending someone to the library to look up one fact instead of everyone going.
terms.confusion: With opening a separate conversation. A subagent returns its result to the main flow; a separate conversation knows nothing about this one.

terms.short: The written text appearing on video with what's being said.
terms.long: In the course they're always part of editing, never of generation: AI video can't write — it draws something that resembles letters. They get added on top in the timeline, where you also get them crisp and at whatever size you want. The decision it forces on you is facing how your video actually looks: the course's check is watching it on a phone with the sound off, since that's how most people will actually see it.
terms.analogy: A fish market's price sign. It doesn't get painted onto the fish — it goes on a chalkboard in front, easy to read and easy to change.
terms.confusion: With dubbing. Subtitles get read and never touch the audio; dubbing changes the voice you hear. And with asking the AI to write text inside the shot itself, which is burning credits in exchange for unreadable letters.

terms.short: The warehouse where your application stores whatever needs to still be there tomorrow: users, orders, messages, photos.
terms.long: Underneath it's Postgres, but handed to you already set up: a web dashboard, sign-up and login already built (email, password, a Google login button), and record-level locking so each client sees only their own data. It's what Lovable and similar tools usually plug in underneath the moment your application needs to remember something. Two things about the free plan worth knowing before promising anyone anything: it pauses if nobody touches the project for a week, and it doesn't take automatic backups.
terms.analogy: A 24-hour open office's filing cabinet, with its own drawers and a guard checking whose record it is before letting you see it.
terms.confusion: With Postgres. Postgres is the engine; Supabase is the whole car, keys, seats, and garage included. You can take that engine elsewhere if you ever move, and your data goes with you.

terms.short: You pay a fixed amount every month and use the app until you hit a message limit.
terms.long: It's one of two ways the course explains paying for AI; the other is pay-per-use, which runs through the API and has no default ceiling. With a subscription it's materially impossible to get a surprise bill: hit the limit, and the app tells you to wait a while and charges you not one extra cent. Entry-level plans all sit in the same range, around $23/month with tax. The decision is simple: as long as you're the one writing and reading, a subscription is all you need.
terms.analogy: A phone's flat-rate plan: talk however much you want, pay the same at month's end, no surprises.
terms.confusion: With pay-per-use. They look similar since both charge your card, but one has a ceiling and the other doesn't. The day someone tells you "create an API key and paste it here," you've switched worlds, and that's when caps need to go on before anything else.

terms.short: A list of records with the same fields: each row is a record and each column is a piece of data.
terms.long: It's the basic building block of any database. In the course's document search project there are three tables: people, documents, and chunks, and each stores exactly one thing. The decision comes earlier than you'd think: which tables exist and what fields each carries gets decided before the first piece of data goes in, because changing it later, with data already inside, is costly and risky.
terms.analogy: A drawer of client cards. They all have the same fields filled in, which is exactly why you can search by any of them.
terms.confusion: With a spreadsheet. They look alike, but a table won't let you type text into a slot meant for a date, and a spreadsheet will. That refusal is exactly what makes it reliable.

terms.short: A named label you put on a point in the history, like v1-working, so you can come back to it.
terms.long: In the course you create it from your project's GitHub homepage: scroll to "Releases," "Create a new release," open "Choose a tag," type v1-working, and pick "Create new tag on publish." On the day you set it, it seems useless; the day something breaks, it's the difference between digging through fifty changes and downloading the entire project from the good date in two clicks. Name it so future-you understands it in six months: "v1-the-one-I-showed-the-client" beats "v1.0.3" by a mile.
terms.analogy: A yellow sticky note on the right page of a manual. The book stays the same — you've just marked where the working part was.
terms.confusion: With a branch. A branch is a parallel path you keep working on, and it moves with you; a tag is a nail driven into one specific point in the history that never moves again.

terms.short: A way of setting colors, sizes, and spacing by writing short labels directly inside the page file itself.
terms.long: Instead of storing styles in a separate file, every piece of the page carries loose words attached to it saying how it should look: blue background, large text, some breathing room around it. It's what comes out by default when you ask v0 for a screen or convert a Figma design into code, so you'll see it whether you chose it or not.
