In your first website, though, the lesson tells you to explicitly ban it in the prompt: for a single loose file, it forces you to install things and open the terminal, and gives you nothing in return.
terms.analogy: Clothing with the washing instructions sewn onto each garment, instead of a list taped to the closet door. Faster to check, uglier closet.
terms.confusion: With the old-fashioned stylesheet, that separate file. They do the same job: one writes everything together right in the page, the other keeps it apart. See a pile of odd words crammed inside the tags — that's Tailwind.

terms.short: A messaging app used in the course as an alerter: your flow texts your phone when something breaks.
terms.long: It's chosen because setting up a bot that sends you messages is free, fast, and requires no paperwork, unlike WhatsApp. In the "make sure it doesn't break" lesson it's the alarm example: the order with the blank phone number that comes in at 3:14 AM reaches your pocket instead of sitting in a red list you'll never open. If Telegram feels like a hassle, a Slack message or an email with phone notifications enabled works just as well. What doesn't work is one more email among forty others.
terms.analogy: A home alarm system. You don't set it up because it looks nice — you set it up so it goes off at three in the morning the day something happens.
terms.confusion: With WhatsApp. For a program to message you, Telegram is free and takes ten minutes to set up; WhatsApp requires Meta's official channel, approved templates, and pay-per-message. To alert yourself, Telegram; to talk to clients, that's a different conversation entirely.

terms.short: How much improvisation the model is allowed, from 0 to 1.
terms.long: At 0 it answers the most predictable, repeatable way, which is what you want for extracting data, classifying, or returning JSON. Push it toward 0.7 and it gains variety and flair, which is what you want for drafting. It's the setting most people leave to chance without even knowing it exists.
terms.analogy: How much room you give someone to go off script.
terms.confusion: With quality. More temperature isn't better — it's just different every time.

terms.short: The window where you give the computer commands by typing them.
terms.long: You type a line, hit Enter, and it answers with text. Two habits prevent 90% of scares: checking which folder you're in before running anything, and never pasting a command you don't understand, no matter how convincing whoever handed it to you sounds. Whatever gets deleted from here doesn't go to a trash bin.
terms.analogy: An "order whatever you like" counter, with no menu and no buttons.
terms.confusion: With a code editor. The editor is where you write files; the terminal is where you run things.

terms.short: The conditions you accept when using a tool, or the ones you impose on whoever uses yours.
terms.long: They're those two checkboxes you tick without reading the first time you open Google AI Studio, and they're also what decides whether you can charge a client for what you've generated. In the course this turns into a specific, repeated check: before accepting a job, look at whether your plan allows commercial use and what rights you have over what the tool produces. Vercel's free plan, for instance, doesn't allow commercial use, and neither do several video and image tools. The rule: check this before accepting the job, never after delivering it, because finding out late has no cheap fix.
terms.analogy: A commercial lease. It states whether you can open a bar or only run an office, and you find that out before signing, not after you've installed the bar.
terms.confusion: With the privacy policy. Terms of use say what you can do with the service and what happens if you overstep; the privacy policy says what the service does with your data. Here it's the commercial-use clause that can actually cost you money.

terms.short: A short quote signed by a client explaining what you solved for them.
terms.long: On a website it's proof you exist and that someone's actually paid you, and the course has an explicit warning built into its site-building prompts: never invent reviews, testimonials, awards, logos, or client figures you didn't write yourself. A useful testimonial doesn't say "very professional" — it says what that person did before and what they do now. When requesting one, ask for it with those two guiding questions, in writing, with a name and permission to publish. No written permission, no publishing.
terms.analogy: A plumber's Google review, except you know the person is real and knows you've posted it.
terms.confusion: With putting a client's logo on your website. That's not a testimonial — that's using their brand, and it needs their permission just as much, if not more. Same with screenshots: if a client's name is visible inside, it's not portfolio material until you cover it.

terms.short: The mode where you only write a description and the AI invents the entire image.
terms.long: You'll see it written in tools as "text to image," literally that: from text to image. It's how Midjourney works by default. What decides the result isn't adjectives ("modern," "striking") but the description of what's visible, and in order: subject first, then environment, then light, then framing. The decision it forces on you is whether you're truly starting from nothing or have a photo of your own to use as reference, because with a reference you get it right far sooner and spend far less.
terms.analogy: Describing a piece of furniture over the phone to a carpenter who can't see it. Say "a nice table" and you get anything; say measurements, wood, and finish, and you get yours.
terms.confusion: With text to video, the same thing but in motion and with far more discards. And with providing a reference image: with text to image you show it nothing — you have to describe everything in words.

terms.short: Generating a video shot with only a written description, starting from no photo at all.
terms.long: Tools show it as "text to video." It's the most open-ended mode, and the one that throws away the most attempts, because the entire starting point gets invented by the machine. The course's Higgsfield guide recommends saving it for when you have no material of your own or you're going for something abstract. The decision it forces on you is about budget: expect a lot more discards per shot with text to video, and every discard costs credits.
terms.analogy: Ordering a dish over the phone with no photo of the menu. It can come out delicious, or it can arrive looking nothing like what you had in mind.
terms.confusion: With image to video. There you start from a photo of your own and the result is far more predictable. If you have a photo of the product or your storefront, always start there, and save text to video for when you have nothing at all.

terms.short: Every client request turned into a record with a status, so it doesn't get lost.
terms.long: In customer support it's the unit of work: an email comes in, a ticket opens, someone picks it up, it gets answered and closed. It's the typical input of the course's support automations: the AI reads the message, decides what type it is and how urgent, and leaves it ready for whoever handles it. A line from the course worth remembering: a ticket doesn't announce its own urgency. Urgency is set by whoever classifies it, so check that classification for a few weeks before trusting it.
terms.analogy: The number you take entering a deli counter. As long as your number is still active, nobody can say you weren't served.
terms.confusion: With a loose email. An email gets read and forgotten; a ticket has a status, open or closed, and an owner. If a client is losing requests, they're almost always working with emails instead of tickets.

terms.short: The maximum time a step waits for a response before giving up and failing.
terms.long: It literally means "the time is up." In n8n's request nodes it's set in milliseconds: 15000 means fifteen seconds. You'll run into it when an outside service is slow and your flow hangs waiting forever, which is worse than failing outright. The decision is yours: how long you wait before giving up, and what you do with that case once you do.
terms.analogy: You call the shop and let it ring ten times. On the eleventh you hang up and try something else, instead of holding the phone to your ear all afternoon.
terms.confusion: With the service having failed. A timeout doesn't say the other side made a mistake — it says it didn't answer in time; the work may have gone through fine on the other end anyway. That's why, before retrying a timeout, check whether it already happened.

terms.short: What kind of thing each column accepts: text, number, date, or yes/no.
terms.long: It's what a schema declares for each column, and what stops you from storing "tomorrow" where a date belongs. On a spreadsheet the opposite happens, and you have to defend against it: Google converts anything that looks like a number, so a phone number starting with 0 loses its zero and a code like 1-2 turns into a date. Mark those columns as text before data goes in, not after — what's already been converted doesn't revert on its own.
terms.analogy: The slots on a coin bank. The euro slot won't take a button, and that's exactly what you want.
terms.confusion: With format. Format is how a value looks (08/25/2026 or 2026-08-25); type is what it is. Changing the format doesn't change the type, which is why a date that displays correctly can still be text underneath.

terms.short: The typeface: the shape of the letters, not what they say.
terms.long: It shows up in the course in the website you build and in the changes you ask the AI to make. And it carries a specific trap: link a font hosted elsewhere, and your page stops looking the same offline — one of the course's checks is opening it with wifi turned off. It also shows up in the "asking for changes" lesson, where a "make it more modern" came back with a different font and half the page rewritten. The decision it forces on you is picking two typefaces at most and writing them into the request.
terms.analogy: A letter's handwriting. It says the same thing whether it's scrawled in a hurry or set in print type, and you don't trust it equally either way.
terms.confusion: With the text itself. Typography is the shape of the letters, not the content. And with size: changing typeface changes the whole site's feel, changing size only changes what's legible from a distance.

terms.short: The small piece text gets split into for counting and billing.
terms.long: Tokens aren't words: a long word can be two or three tokens, and Spanish produces more of them than English for the same text. Everything gets measured this way: what fits in the context, what a call costs, and how fast it responds. As a rule of thumb, roughly 750 words comes to about 1,000 tokens.
terms.analogy: Casino chips: inside, you play with chips, not dollars.
terms.confusion: With a character or a word. It matches neither, which is why you need a tool to count them, not a guess.

terms.short: A temporary pass a program shows to enter your account without ever learning your password.
terms.long: When you click "Allow" on Google's screen, you're not handing your password to anyone: Google gives the program a pass, and that pass is the token. The nice part is it expires and you can revoke it anytime from myaccount.google.com/permissions, without touching anything else. In the course you also call "token" the long string BotFather hands you when creating a Telegram bot, and the one you paste into an n8n credential: in practice they behave like a password. The rule: it goes into a password manager and never appears in a screenshot or a chat.
terms.analogy: A festival wristband. It doesn't carry your name, it's good for a few days, and if it falls off, whoever finds it gets in.
terms.confusion: With a password. You type a password and it stays yours; a token belongs to the program and can be revoked without changing anything else. Revoking a token knocks out only whatever was using it — exactly what you want.

terms.short: Everything you send the model, counted in pieces. It's what you pay for it to read.
terms.long: Every time you hit send, it's not just your message that goes out — the entire conversation from the start gets resent, plus any files you uploaded. All of that is input tokens, which is why a long session building a website can rack up over a million input tokens on its own. That's where the biggest money-saving decision in the course lives: once a chat runs on forever, don't keep pulling the thread. Ask for a status summary, open a fresh chat, and paste that in instead.
terms.analogy: The weight of the package you take to the post office. You pay for what you put inside, not for what they write back.
terms.confusion: With output tokens. Each input token is cheaper than an output one, but there are far more of them, because the entire history travels again with every message. In a long conversation, almost your entire bill is input.

terms.short: What the model writes, counted in pieces. They cost quite a bit more than input tokens.
terms.long: It's the half of the bill you can actually control through the request itself. Summarizing two hundred emails a month runs around three hundred thousand input tokens and sixty thousand output ones: with a small model that's cents, with the priciest model it's several dollars for the same job. And there's a detail that catches everyone: switch on reasoning, and the intermediate steps you never see also count as output. The move is asking for genuinely short answers, no intro, no closing summary, because every filler line gets billed.
terms.analogy: A taxi charges you for the distance covered, not for whatever you told the driver along the way.
terms.confusion: With max_tokens. Output tokens are what actually got written and what you're billed for; max_tokens is just the ceiling you set. Setting a high ceiling costs nothing extra by itself — it's filling it up that does.

terms.short: Giving the model the ability to call real functions instead of only writing text.
terms.long: You describe which tools exist and when to use each; it decides, and you execute. It's what fixes its weak spot: for counting, checking an exact fact, or acting on a system, it doesn't guess — it uses the tool. Each tool's description matters enormously, because it's the only thing it's choosing from.
terms.analogy: No longer asking from memory, and instead handing it access to the filing cabinet and the calculator.
terms.confusion: With a plugin. A plugin is a product; tool use is the mechanism underneath it.

terms.short: A dial that decides among how many candidate words the model can choose. Lower means more predictable and blander.
terms.long: The p stands for probability. At each step the model has a list of possible continuations ranked from most to least likely; top_p says how far down that list it's allowed to pick from. In the course you only run into it when building your own model in Ollama, in the config file, with a value like 0.9 already set. The honest move is leaving it alone: for more predictable answers, lower the temperature and leave this dial untouched, because moving both at once is the fastest way to lose track of which one wrecked your result.
terms.analogy: In a shop with a hundred t-shirts, top_p decides whether the clerk only looks at the ten best-sellers or checks the whole shelf before recommending one.
terms.confusion: With temperature. Both control the same thing — how much variety is in the response — through different paths: temperature changes how bold the choice is, top_p changes the size of the list it's choosing from. The industry norm is touching one or the other, never both.

terms.short: The step where you reshape data so it fits wherever it's headed.
terms.long: What arrives almost never has the shape the destination needs: a "full name" field comes in, and the table wants "First Name" and "Last Name" split apart. In n8n this is done with the Set node, shown on screen as Edit Fields, and with expressions, no code written. It's the tedious work that fills half of any flow, and skipping it is the most common reason the final step fails without explaining why.
terms.analogy: Moving groceries from the store bags to the pantry shelves. Same stuff, arranged how whoever's about to cook actually needs it.
terms.confusion: With normalization. Transforming changes structure: splitting one field into two, merging three into one. Normalizing gives content a stable format. They happen at the same time, in the same node, which is exactly why people mix them up.

terms.short: The internal architecture almost every language model today is built on.
terms.long: It's the building's plumbing: it explains how the machine distributes attention across the words in front of it before writing the next one. In this course it comes up exactly once, and only to tell you to ignore it, along with "attention" and "mixture of experts." It changes not a single decision you'll actually make: not which model you pick, not what prompt you write, not how much you pay. If someone sells it to you as essential knowledge for using AI at work, they're selling smoke.
terms.analogy: Knowing where the building's pipes run. You can live perfectly well in the apartment without ever having seen them.
terms.confusion: With Hugging Face's Transformers, spelled identically and a different thing: a code package for downloading and running models on your computer. And don't confuse it with the model itself either: transformers is the blueprint, the model is the finished building.

terms.short: The summary you write so someone who wasn't there can pick up exactly where you left off.
terms.long: In the course you use it mostly once a conversation with the AI has gotten long or stuck: you ask it to write a handover document with the goal, what already works, what's been ruled out, and the next step, then open a fresh chat and paste it in. The signal to do this is clear: three corrections in a row with no progress means the chat is weighed down. The same piece applies when finishing a client job, and there the handover is what you leave them so they don't have to depend on you.
terms.analogy: The note the morning shift leaves the afternoon shift at a bakery: what's done, what's left, and which dough not to touch.
terms.confusion: With copying and pasting the whole conversation. That drags the failed attempts along and weighs down the new chat all over again. A handover is written for someone who wasn't there, and what you ruled out matters as much as what you achieved — as long as you say it in two lines, not forty messages.

terms.short: The movement where the whole camera physically moves, usually sideways, following what it's filming.
terms.long: It literally means "traveling," which is exactly what the camera does. It's on Higgsfield's list of movements and shows up in the course's ad template as the calm shot, the one that presents the problem. The decision it forces on you is one of pacing: a slow tracking shot calms things down, which clashes head-on with a hook shot, which needs abrupt movement so people don't scroll past.
terms.analogy: Watching shop windows go by from a bus moving slowly. You're the one moving; the shop stays still.
terms.confusion: With a zoom. In a tracking shot the camera actually moves through space and the background shifts position; in a zoom the camera is fixed and only the image gets magnified, like using binoculars.

terms.short: Being able to prove what happened with a specific case: what came in, what the system decided, and who approved it.
terms.long: Your system working is one thing; being able to show someone, six months later, why it answered what it answered is entirely different. You get it by logging, for every call to the model, one line: what you sent, which model, what it answered, and what it cost. With an agent you can also ask for it live: which tool it used, which file it opened, and which line the data came from. The day a client complains, or a lawyer asks a question, you either have that or you have your word.
terms.analogy: A signed delivery note. Without it, arguing over whether the order arrived is one person's word against another's.
terms.confusion: With observability. Observability is for you, to check whether the system is behaving today; traceability is for showing someone else about a specific case from last month. They lean on the same logs and serve different purposes.

terms.short: A board of cards you drag between columns to see where each task stands.
terms.long: In the course it comes up as a reference, not a required tool: when Obsidian's entry discusses the Kanban plugin, it explains it as "drag-and-drop card boards, like Trello," with one difference that matters — there, the board is saved as an ordinary text note on your computer. That's the decision: in Trello your tasks live on a company's website and you see them from anywhere; in your own file, they live with you, readable by any AI that has access to that folder.
terms.analogy: An office whiteboard with sticky notes: to-do, in progress, done. Same idea, on screen, and nothing peels off.
terms.confusion: With a task list. A list says what needs doing; a board also says what stage each thing is at and who has it. If you never move the cards between columns, what you actually have is a list with more clicks.

terms.short: What makes an automation fire.
terms.long: It can be an incoming notification, a specific time, or a change in a sheet or database. Two things always get forgotten: many triggers only see what happens AFTER the flow is switched on, and others check every few minutes instead of instantly. If something "isn't firing," start there.
terms.analogy: The doorbell. Until it rings, nobody gets up.
terms.confusion: With the action. The trigger only decides when; what happens after are the actions.

terms.short: The trigger that only fires when you press the button. It's for testing and for delicate things.
terms.long: While you're building any flow, it's the one you use a hundred times: hit "Test workflow," bottom center, and watch the boxes turn green one by one. But it has a second, much more serious role: processes that must NOT start on their own — a mass mailing to clients, a data migration, a deletion — get deliberately left on manual. There, requiring a human to physically press the button is the feature, not the limitation. It's a button with a person standing in front of it.
terms.analogy: A paper shredder's button. You don't want it to start on its own — you want someone actually watching it.
terms.confusion: With activating the flow. Testing isn't activating: you can hit Test a hundred times and the flow stays off. The "Active" toggle, top right, is the only thing that makes it run unattended. The classic day-one accident is going home happy and finding out a week later it never ran once.

terms.short: Splitting a long document into small pieces so the AI only reads the ones that actually matter.
terms.long: A model can't read an eighty-page manual to answer one question, and even if it could, it'd be expensive and answer worse; that's why the document gets split and only the few relevant pieces get shown to it. In the course's document search project you build this by hand, in a file called trocear.py, producing pieces around two hundred words. What you're really deciding isn't so much the size as where you cut: by paragraph, not by character count, because cut through the middle of the sentence carrying the fact, and that fact stops existing for the search box. When the system answers badly, check first which chunks it retrieved, before blaming the model.
terms.analogy: Slicing bread for canapés. Cut it where it belongs and each slice holds whatever you pile on top; cut it carelessly and half the slices fall apart and are useless.
terms.confusion: With summarizing. Chunking doesn't lose a single word, it just distributes them; summarizing throws away whatever someone decided was extra, and that could be exactly what was being asked about. Also with "chunk": chunking is the action, a chunk is the piece that comes out of it.

terms.short: When a response gets cut off mid-sentence because it hit the ceiling on how much text it could write.
terms.long: It's not that the AI ran out of ideas: there's a cap on how much it can write in one go, and hitting it stops it cold, sometimes mid-word. This happens especially when you ask for a whole file or a very long piece of text, and it's the cause of the classic "...rest stays the same as before" showing up mid-code. On top of that, reasoning models spend part of that same cap thinking, so they cut off sooner than you'd expect. The decision: ask for it across consecutive messages but complete, rather than settling for a cut piece you don't know how to fill back in.
terms.analogy: A page that runs out mid-letter. What's written is fine — there just wasn't room for the rest.
terms.confusion: With it forgetting what you asked. If it cuts off suddenly at the end, that's the writing cap. If from the start it's ignoring things you said a while ago, that's the context window — a different problem, fixed a different way.

terms.short: A middleman that sends SMS and WhatsApp messages from your programs, billing a fee plus per message.
terms.long: It comes up in the course's WhatsApp entry, among four ways to automate messaging, alongside 360dialog, Wati, and Respond.io. It's the paid route: instead of fighting Meta's official API yourself, you hire someone who's already set it up and gives you an easy way to use it. The course makes you put real numbers on the table before choosing, because there are two separate costs that add up: the monthly fee and the per-message surcharge. Decision: calculate what your real volume costs monthly, and what breaks if that volume is multiplied by ten.
terms.analogy: The courier company delivering your packages. You could go to each door yourself; you pay so you don't have to, and you pay per package.
terms.confusion: With sending a WhatsApp from your regular phone. Replying by hand within the 24-hour window costs nothing; the moment you automate it, you're under Meta's business rules, with approved templates and price per conversation.

terms.short: JavaScript with tags warning of a mistake before anything runs. Files end in .ts.
terms.long: It's the same old JavaScript, but it forces you to state what type every value is: that `price` is a number and `name` is text. In exchange, the editor underlines the mistake in red while you write instead of it blowing up once the client's already looking at it. In the course you don't choose it — it shows up because website-building tools add it on their own, and suddenly `.ts` and `.tsx` files appear in your folder. Decision: don't convert it to JavaScript "to simplify," because you'll break the whole project solving a problem you never had.
terms.analogy: Pantry labels. You cook the same way, but you don't mix up the salt jar with the sugar jar because it's written on the outside.
terms.confusion: With a separate language. It isn't: before running, it gets converted into plain JavaScript, and the browser never sees TypeScript at all. That's why a type error stops the build on your computer and never breaks the already-published site.

terms.short: Enlarging an image or video you already have so it shows more detail.
terms.long: It literally means "scaling up." In Midjourney these are the U1 to U4 buttons under the four proposals: click one and that image jumps to full resolution. Runway has the same thing for video. The decision it forces on you is when to hit it, because it costs credits: first pick which one you want by looking at the four small versions, and only enlarge the one you picked.
terms.analogy: Printing a large photo of only the one you picked from the roll. The rest stay small because you're never hanging them anywhere.
terms.confusion: With regenerating at high quality. An upscale starts from the image you already liked and preserves it; regenerating gives you a different image even with the same text. And enlarging doesn't fix bad framing or a six-fingered hand.

terms.short: A page's complete address, what you type at the top of the browser.
terms.long: A URL has several pieces: starting with https means the connection is encrypted, then comes the site's name, sometimes a door number (the port), and then the path down to the specific page. Miss a letter or add an extra space and the browser can't get there. Once you publish your site, the URL is exactly what you'd send someone over WhatsApp.
terms.analogy: A complete mailing address: street, number, floor, and door. With just the street name, the mail carrier can't get there.
terms.confusion: With a site's name. "my shop" isn't a URL; "https://myshop.com/products" is. And a URL can also point to something on your own computer, not just the internet.

terms.short: Being allowed to use what you generate in something you charge for. Many free plans don't allow it.
terms.long: It shows up in almost every tool entry in the course, always with the same warning: check it before accepting the job, not after delivering it. Vercel's free plan forbids charging for a site published there, and ElevenLabs' free plan won't let you sell the audio either. On Midjourney it also depends on your company's revenue, not just what you pay. It's a two-minute check: open the tool's pricing page, look for those exact two words, and only then tell the client yes.
terms.analogy: A regular driver's license versus a taxi license. With the first you drive your friends around; charging for the ride needs a different paper, even though the car's the same.
terms.confusion: With the watermark. Removing it is an aesthetic matter; commercial use is a permission matter. A plan can strip the watermark from your video and still not let you bill anyone for it.

terms.short: The encoding you should always pick: it's the one that knows how to write accented letters, special characters, and emoji.
terms.long: It comes up at three specific moments in the course, always the same way: saving your README.md, saving your first web-1.html, and saving SKILL.md, in Notepad's Encoding dropdown. It's also inside the projects' code, at every file open. The tell that you got it wrong is unmistakable: open the file and where it said "café" there are now odd symbols. The fix is going back to Save As and choosing UTF-8, without rewriting anything.
terms.analogy: The universal plug for text files. Not the only one out there, but the one that fits everything you'll be using.
terms.confusion: With the extra-.txt problem. They're two separate failures in the same save dialog: the Type dropdown decides whether your README.md ends up called README.md.txt, and the Encoding dropdown decides whether accents display. Both need changing.

terms.short: Vercel's tool that turns a sentence into a drawn, working screen, ready to copy.
terms.long: You describe a screen (the homepage, the contact form, the sales dashboard) and it hands it back built, usually in two or three versions to compare before you start editing. What you get is that screen: code to paste into your project, or a published link to show it off. And here's the decision: the buttons can look gorgeous and do nothing, and the data you see is invented for the demo, so don't show it to a client saying "it's already done" — you'd be committing to an impossible deadline.
terms.analogy: The storefront of a shop that hasn't opened yet. Looks great from the street, and behind it there's neither a stockroom nor a register.
terms.confusion: With Lovable or Bolt, which build the entire application including its data storage. v0 handles the visible part, and does it very well; you have to build what's behind it yourself.

terms.short: Checking that a value follows the rules before letting it in.
terms.long: It ranges from the cheapest option — in Google Sheets, "Data" then "Data validation" so a column only accepts new, in progress, or closed — to a table's not null, which stops a row from being saved without what's essential. The real decision isn't what you validate — it's what you do with what fails: send it to an error branch where someone reviews it, or let it drop silently. The second is the standard way to lose orders without ever noticing.
terms.analogy: Airport baggage screening. It doesn't change what you're carrying — it tells you whether you can bring it through and sets aside what you can't.
terms.confusion: With cleaning. Cleaning fixes what it can; validation fixes nothing — it decides. Validate before cleaning and you'll throw out good data over one extra space.

terms.short: What gets stored automatically when you say nothing: today's date, a starting status, a zero.
terms.long: In the course's tables you'll see it as default now(), stamping the current time on an entry date, or default 'new' for status. It saves work and avoids nulls, but it decides for you, and that has consequences: if everything comes in as "new" and nobody reviews that list, the database fills up with cases that look handled just because they have a status set. Choose defaults that are true, not ones that just look tidy on the dashboard.
terms.analogy: The daily special. Don't choose, and you still get served something — not always what you'd have ordered.
terms.confusion: With a required field. A default value fills in for you when you stay silent; a required field forces you to speak up. They're opposites, and get confused because both prevent blank slots.

terms.short: A name you give a value so you can use it later without repeating it.
terms.long: Write price = 11.50, and from then on you use the word price instead of the number, so the day it goes up you change it in one place instead of forty. You'll see this in n8n's expressions and in any code the AI gives you. There's one case worth looking at closely: on a website, any variable whose name starts with NEXT_PUBLIC_ or VITE_ gets sent to the browser of every visitor. Put a real key in there, and you're not storing it — you're publishing it.
terms.analogy: A jar label in the kitchen. It says "flour," and you don't have to open it to know what's inside.
terms.confusion: With a constant. A variable can change value while the program runs; a constant is set once and never touched. And an "environment variable" is something else entirely: that one lives outside the code, in configuration.

terms.short: A value the program reads from outside its own code.
terms.long: It's where keys live. On your computer they're in a .env file that never gets uploaded; on the server they're declared by hand all over again. And here's the number-one cause of a project working locally and failing when published: they're read at build time, so after adding one you have to deploy again.
terms.analogy: The information written on the envelope, not printed on the flyer itself.
terms.confusion: With ordinary configuration. These change without touching the code, and differ at every place the project runs.

terms.short: The settings and keys your program reads from outside, so they change from place to place without touching the code.
terms.long: They're name-and-value pairs, like ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-whatever, and the code asks for the name without ever knowing the value. On your computer they live in the .env file; on Vercel, under "Settings" → "Environment Variables"; on GitHub, in repository secrets. The course's number-one failure is this: your code reaches the platform but your keys don't, because they're deliberately excluded from what gets uploaded, and the site starts up, asks for the key, can't find it, and crashes. There's a nearly-as-common second failure: you create them correctly but never redeploy, so they haven't taken effect yet.
terms.analogy: Price stickers in a store. The product is the same in every store; the sticker changes depending on where it is.
terms.confusion: With writing the key directly into the code. There it stays in history forever, and on a public project, bots find it in under a minute. Also watch names starting with NEXT_PUBLIC_ or VITE_: those are sent to the browser by design and stop being secret.

terms.short: A long list of numbers representing a piece of text's meaning, so it can be compared with others.
terms.long: It's the piece that makes an assistant answering from your documents possible: every text chunk gets converted into a list of numbers, and searching means finding the chunks whose numbers sit closest to your question's. You'll see this in the "answer with sources" project, written as "vector store" or vector database. The course is blunt about this, and it's worth listening: don't build a vector database until the dumb version — pasting the whole document into the chat — has genuinely failed you. With twenty documents, pasting wins.
terms.analogy: A place's map coordinates. Two bars with similar coordinates are close together; two texts with similar vectors talk about the same thing.
terms.confusion: With keyword search. A keyword search finds "invoice" only if it literally says "invoice"; a vector search finds the document even if the client wrote "receipt" or "the billing paper." That's the whole point, and also why it sometimes brings back something similar but wrong.

terms.short: The maximum amount of text a model can have in front of it at once.
terms.long: It's measured in tokens and includes your instructions, the conversation, and any documents you've pasted in. Once it fills up, the oldest material drops out, which explains why a long chat starts contradicting itself. A huge window doesn't always help: the more you cram in, the more the important part gets diluted.
terms.analogy: The size of a table. Whatever doesn't fit ends up on the floor.
terms.confusion: With long-term memory. Nothing gets saved here: the conversation ends and it's gone.

terms.short: The Python command that creates a box of packages that only exists inside that folder.
terms.long: Short for virtual environment. You type python -m venv .venv once inside the project folder and then activate it; you'll know it's active because (.venv) appears in parentheses at the start of the terminal line. Everything you install from that point stays inside and doesn't mix with the rest of your computer. And it has to be activated every time you open a new window: no (.venv) visible means it's not active, and any pip install you run goes into the general Python install, leaving cross-contaminated versions everywhere.
terms.analogy: A travel toiletry bag. What you pack there goes with that specific trip and doesn't mix with the bathroom cabinet.
terms.confusion: With Docker. A virtual environment isolates Python packages and nothing else; Docker also isolates the operating system and Python version. That's why "it works for me" with venv doesn't guarantee it works for your teammate, and with Docker it does.

terms.short: The site where you leave your website for anyone to see, with an address you can send over WhatsApp.
terms.long: It takes your project's files, saved on GitHub, assembles them, and publishes them on its own, in under a minute, every time you change something. The free plan is called Hobby and is more than enough to learn and to show off your idea, with two conditions worth reading first: it's for personal, non-commercial use, and you can only publish a hundred times a day. What saves a bad day is the history: if today's change breaks the site, you go back to yesterday's version with one button.
terms.analogy: A rented storefront on a busy street. You put what's visible inside; they provide the building, the lighting, the shutter, and the security guard.
terms.confusion: With GitHub. GitHub stores your files and their change history; Vercel takes them from there and shows them to the world. You need both, in that order: first push to GitHub, then Vercel publishes on its own.

terms.short: The copy of your project from before the last change, that you go back to with one click when something breaks.
terms.long: On Vercel it's under the "Deployments" tab: find the last deployment that said "Ready," click the three dots, "Instant Rollback," and your site is back to how it was in seconds. GitHub has the other route: if you tagged the version from the day everything worked with a name, its page carries a link to download the entire project exactly as it stood that day. This is what makes publishing feel calm, because you know any disaster has an undo. What you can't do is stop there: going back stops the bleeding, but the bug is still there and will return the next time you push.
terms.analogy: Word's undo button, but for your entire site, with people looking at it right now.
terms.confusion: With a backup. A backup preserves your data; going back to a previous version changes the program, not the data. If the bug ate client information, this won't bring it back.

terms.short: Saving every state of the work so you can return to it.
terms.long: It applies to code with Git, but also to prompts: save each version with its date and what you changed, and never edit one that's already run in production. The day quality drops, that list is the only thing that'll tell you what you touched.
terms.analogy: A contract's numbered drafts.
terms.confusion: With saving a file. Saving overwrites; versioning preserves what came before.

terms.short: The program where a project's files get written and organized. It's free and needs no account.
terms.long: Short for Visual Studio Code. It has three zones, and that's all you need: your file list on the left, text in the center, and a small window at the bottom, the terminal, where you give the computer commands by typing them. In the course it's where you work once you leave a tool's website behind and have the project folder on your own computer. A rule that saves whole afternoons: always open the entire folder, never a loose file, or half of what you're told won't show up where it should.
terms.analogy: A restaurant kitchen: the pantry on one side, the counter in the middle, the stove underneath. Everything in one room so you're not running between spaces.
terms.confusion: With the terminal. The terminal is only that small window at the bottom, and it exists outside this too; VS Code is the whole room. Plenty of people say "open VS Code" when they mean "type this into the terminal."

terms.short: A box that pauses the flow for however long you tell it, then lets it continue.
terms.long: In n8n you add it by pressing Tab and typing "wait." You use it for two completely different reasons: slowing down so you don't machine-gun a service that cuts you off if you call it 200 times in a row (a second between calls is often enough), or holding the flow until something happens, like a person approving the next step before anything gets sent to a client. Every wait stretches out the whole execution, and that's the decision you face: if the pause is hours long because you're waiting on a human, splitting the flow in two usually works better.
terms.analogy: A yellow light at a poor-visibility intersection. It doesn't forbid you from going — it forces you to go slowly enough to avoid a collision.
terms.confusion: With a timeout. A Wait is something you set on purpose, and the flow calmly continues afterward; a timeout is the limit past which the system gives up and returns an error. One's a pause, the other's a surrender.

terms.short: A notification a service sends to an address of yours when something happens.
terms.long: It flips the usual way of working on its head: instead of checking every minute for updates, you get notified. That address is a key: whoever has it can send messages pretending to be the service, so it's never shared, and if it leaks, you generate a new one. And watch out for receiving the same notification twice: it happens, and you need to be ready for it.
terms.analogy: The delivery driver ringing when they arrive, instead of you checking the balcony every five minutes.
terms.confusion: With a hook. A webhook crosses from one service to another over the internet; a hook happens inside the same tool.

terms.short: A webhook's permanent address. It only exists once the flow is switched on.
terms.long: It carries /webhook/ in the middle, and it's the one you paste into the outside service — your web form, Meta, the payment gateway — once you've finished building. Until you flip the "Active" toggle, that address literally doesn't exist, and whoever sends something to it gets an error. And it carries a requirement that decides where you host n8n: it has to be reachable from the internet, so n8n on your laptop won't do — you need the cloud or a server.
terms.analogy: The phone number you put in the shop window. Publishing it only makes sense if the shop is actually open.
terms.confusion: With the test one. The test one carries /webhook-test/ and only listens while the editor is open; this one carries /webhook/ and only listens while the flow is active. Mix them up and no error goes off — nothing simply ever happens, which is far worse.

terms.short: A webhook's temporary address: it only works while n8n's editor is open.
terms.long: It carries /webhook-test/ in the middle and switches on by clicking "Listen for test event" inside the webhook box. It's for one essential thing: sending yourself a fake notification and seeing exactly what data actually arrives, with each field's real name, before building the rest of the flow. The moment you close the editor, or a while passes, it stops listening, and anything sent to it gets lost with no warning to anyone.
terms.analogy: A doorbell that only rings while you're home waiting for the gas company. Leave, and they can knock all they want — nobody's there to hear it.
terms.confusion: With the production one, and this is the mix-up that costs the most afternoons. Half of every "my webhook isn't receiving anything" forum post is pasting the test address into the real service. Rule: if it needs to run unattended, the address carries /webhook/, not /webhook-test/.

terms.short: Not one thing — three: the regular app, WhatsApp Business, and the official channel for a program to write on its own.
terms.long: That third one is called the WhatsApp Business Platform, and it's what comes up in the course when you want a flow to talk to clients. It works like a bank's phone system: you can only message first with sentences Meta has pre-approved, but if a client wrote to you less than 24 hours ago, you can reply with anything, for free. Signing up costs nothing, and you pay per message you initiate, on the order of cents. The decision is whether your case fits within that 24-hour window, because outside it, templates set the bill.
terms.analogy: An intercom with business hours. If the neighbor calls, you say whatever you want; if you call at an odd hour, you can only say the pre-approved lines.
terms.confusion: With sending messages from your phone using one of the workaround programs floating around out there. That's against Meta's rules and can get your number banned. The right route is the Cloud API, signed up for at developers.facebook.com.

terms.short: Microsoft's operating system, the most common one among the course's students' computers.
terms.long: It matters because almost every command and path changes depending on the system: on Windows the terminal is called PowerShell, the installer is winget, and folders are written with backslashes, like C:\projects\my-site. That's why guides carry a tab per system, and you need to find yours before pasting anything. Two warnings that save a whole afternoon: create the project folder outside OneDrive and outside the Desktop, because OneDrive touches files while they're being written and causes very strange errors. And turn on file name extensions in File Explorer, because Windows hides them by default, so you can't tell whether you've saved a real .html or a disguised .txt.
terms.analogy: The local language of the country you live in: the recipe's the same, but the ingredients get asked for in different words.
terms.confusion: With assuming any tutorial's command works on your machine. Most tutorials are written on Mac. If you get "command not recognized," before hunting for a bug, check whether that command belongs to a different system.

terms.short: Windows's program installer: tell it a name and it downloads and installs it on its own.
terms.long: You type it into PowerShell, Windows's command window, like this: winget install --id Python.Python.3.12 -e. It does exactly the same job as brew on Mac and apt on Linux, which is why the course's guides carry a tab per system instead of one universal command. There's a snag almost everyone hits on day one: you install something, it finishes with no errors, you type python --version in that same window, and it says it doesn't recognize it. You didn't do anything wrong — that window read its list of programs when it opened; close it, open a new one, and try again.
terms.analogy: Ordering from the neighborhood shop instead of trawling five websites. You give the exact name and it's handed to you over the counter.
terms.confusion: With downloading the installer from the official website. Both work, but mixing them leaves two versions of the same program living on your machine, and untangling that is a mess. Pick one route and stick with it.

terms.short: Microsoft's word processor. Good for reading documents, not for storing code or keys.
terms.long: In the course it shows up two opposite ways. In favor: a document with your old copy and your style rules is one of the best things you can upload to a project so the AI copies your tone instead of inventing one. Against it, and this repeats across several lessons: your API keys, your prompt library, and any line of code never go there. The reason is concrete and has ruined many afternoons: Word swaps straight quotes for curly ones and hyphens for long dashes, and that pasted text later fails without explaining why. Decision: documents go in Word; project files go in a plain-text editor.
terms.analogy: A typewritten letter with flourishes. Beautiful to read, useless if what you needed was the exact serial number.
terms.confusion: With a text file. Both carry text inside, but a `.docx` is a box with formatting, and a `.txt` or `.md` is just the text and nothing more. When a tutorial says "create a file," it never means a Word document.

terms.short: A sequence of steps defined ahead of time that runs on its own.
terms.long: It has three parts: what triggers it, what conditions filter out cases that don't apply, and what actions run, in what order. The filter is the piece that prevents the most trouble and gets forgotten the most: without it, the first day of real use, real things happen to cases that should never have gotten through.
terms.analogy: An assembly line. Every station does its own job, always in the same order.
terms.confusion: With an agent. Here the steps are pre-decided; an agent decides them on the fly.

terms.short: Linux running inside Windows, with no disk partitioning and no need for two computers.
terms.long: WSL stands for Windows Subsystem for Linux. You'll barely touch it by hand, but it sits underneath things you do use: installing Docker Desktop on Windows shows a pre-checked box saying "Use WSL 2 instead of Hyper-V," and it should stay checked as it comes. If Docker throws an error on day one, the usual fix is opening PowerShell as administrator and typing wsl --update, then restarting the computer. If the message mentions virtualization, that's not fixable from Windows anymore — it's turned off in the BIOS, the menu you reach by pressing F2, F10, or Delete right after powering on.
terms.analogy: Having an industrial kitchen set up in your home garage: the house is still yours, but cooking happens differently in there.
terms.confusion: With an old-school virtual machine. Here you're not booting a separate computer or waiting two minutes: it's always there, in the background, and its folders show up in the regular File Explorer.

terms.short: A text format for configuration files, written with colons and indentation instead of braces.
terms.long: Files end in .yml or .yaml. In the course you run into it three places: the file that makes GitHub run your tests automatically, the prompts.yaml where you store different versions of your prompts, and the config.yaml you touch when connecting a local model with Ollama. You don't need to know how to write it from scratch, but you do need to respect the indentation when copying it, because that's exactly where it breaks. Always open it in a code editor.
terms.analogy: A hand-written folder index: whatever's nudged further right belongs inside whatever's above it.
terms.confusion: With JSON. Both store the same kind of data; JSON uses braces and quotes and travels between programs, YAML uses indentation and is written and read by people. For a configuration file you'll be editing yourself, YAML reads better; for a response between machines, JSON.

terms.short: A site where you connect apps by dragging boxes, nothing installed. The easiest of all, and the priciest.
terms.long: It watches for something (an email arriving, someone filling out a form, it turning eight in the morning) and when it happens, runs the list of tasks you set up. It bills per task, and that's exactly the problem the course flags: the free plan gives about 100 tasks a month, gone in the first week, and past that you're in the $20-30/month range. The "connecting apps" lesson has a number that sums it up: Rubén's setup costs $0 built by hand and around $348 a year on Zapier. Choose it when your afternoon is worth more than that difference — not out of habit.
terms.analogy: A taxi. It gets you there without you knowing how to drive, and drops you at the door, but charges every trip. Worth it for a one-off; not for the daily commute.
terms.confusion: With Make and n8n, which do the same job. The difference is how they count: Zapier bills per task, meaning per step; Make per operation; n8n per full run of the flow. A flow processing 500 rows is 500 tasks on Zapier and a single loop pass on n8n.

terms.short: Asking for the task plain, with no worked example shown. Literally "zero shots."
terms.long: It's how almost everyone writes without knowing it has a name: you explain what you want and see what comes out. It's not inherently bad, and for an easy, one-off task it's the reasonable choice, since preparing examples takes time. It stops paying off the moment you repeat the task or the result has to sound like you: with no samples, you get the internet's average, which is exactly the text that sounds like nobody in particular. The decision: doing it once, go plain; doing it forty times, sit down and prepare three examples.
terms.analogy: Ordering "give me something to snack on" at a bar. Food shows up, sure — just not the food you had in mind.
terms.confusion: With a short prompt. You can write two full pages of context and still be zero-shot: what defines it is having no already-worked example inside, not how much space the message takes up.

terms.short: The video-call program. Here it matters for what it leaves behind: the recording and the transcript.
terms.long: In the course you don't touch it as an AI tool — you touch it as a source of raw material: a meeting produces a long text of what everyone said, and that text is exactly what you paste into the minutes template to get back a five-line summary, the agreements, and who's doing what. A warning that isn't minor: recording and transcribing a meeting means processing people's data, so you announce it at the start and strip names before pasting anything into a chat. Decision beforehand: check what gets stored and where before uploading the full transcript.
terms.analogy: A recorder sitting on the table at a neighborhood meeting. It saves you from taking notes, and precisely because of that, you have to say out loud that it's running.
terms.confusion: With the automatic summary meeting tools provide themselves. That one follows their own rules and format; pasting the transcript yourself into your own template lets you dictate exactly which sections you want and which get left out.

terms.short: The shell that comes preinstalled on today's Macs: the program interpreting what you type into Terminal.
terms.long: Always written lowercase. It matters in the course for a very specific reason: follow a video recorded on Windows with PowerShell while you're on a Mac, and you'll see commands you can't type and folder paths that don't exist on your machine. You're not doing anything wrong — they're just two different languages. Before following any terminal tutorial, check which system it was recorded on and ask the AI for the version matching yours.
terms.analogy: An assembly manual in a language you don't speak, furniture already in front of you. You half-understand it, and the measurements never quite line up.
terms.confusion: With Bash. zsh is Bash's successor and almost everything works the same way, but not everything. If a command from an old tutorial fails on your Mac for no apparent reason, this is usually why.
